t: Window Style Editor (app 12, "Windows")
h: Window Style Editor (app 12, "Windows")
x: Window Style Editor (app 12, "Windows") Native desk3 app, 860 x 600, icon Lucide app-window ( L_APPWIN , scripts/gen-icons.py ). Left: live preview (two sample windows, one focused, one inactive, on a wallpaper strip with a Light/Dark switch), themes, Export/Import. Right: colour picker (hue strip, saturation, lightness, the 16 style tokens, Follow) and the inspector in collapsible groups. Every control changes the real desktop at once. Controls Chrome: kind (style, card, lights, caption, none), glass window, glass title bar, blurred or sharp wallpaper, title bar opacity. Geometry: corner radius 0 to 28, title bar height 36 to 56, title side padding. Windows are fixed size: no minimum size or snap gap exist. Title bar: solid or gradient (angle in 15 degree steps), colours, alignment, font, title colours, inactive fade, separator. Buttons: light size, spacing, colours, glyphs (never, hover, always), hover highlight, button radius, inactive fade. Minimise (yellow light, caption button) really closes with the minimise animation; maximise only raises. Body: colour, opacity (below 256 turns glass on), border colour and width, inner shadow, scroll bar style (used by the editor itself: no other app has a scroll bar yet). Shadow and depth: blur, offset down (no sideways offset), strength inactive and focused, colour, focus glow, focus ring. Motion: open, close, minimise preset (fade, scale, slide), duration, easing (ease out, linear, in and out), reduce motion. Colour schemes: follow style, Light, Dark, Graphite, Midnight glass, Warm paper, Solarized, High contrast, Temple gold. A scheme also switches to a matching desktop style so app text stays readable on the new body colour. Themes (under the preview): the five desktop styles are read-only bases; Customize copies one into an editable user theme (8 slots), Save as new, Delete, Reset to base. Controls are greyed on a base theme. Rename is not implemented. Theme string ws1 nmNAME ba2 kd-1 gl-1 tg0 ... one two-letter key and a decimal value per field ( ws_fk in 03e), name with underscores. -1 follows the desktop style. Export prints it on COM1 ( WINSTYLE ... ), writes B:/WINSTYLE.TXT and shows it; Import reads that file (or the last export), checks ws1 , ignores unknown keys, clamps values, makes a new user theme. Nothing is persisted otherwise. Architecture ws[WS_N] (I64, defined in 01-core.HC) holds every value; -1 means follow the style, so the defaults equal the old constants. 01-winstyle.HC: WsChrome (fill, glass, gradient, border, title, buttons), WsShadow (shadow, glow, ring), motion helpers. 03e-windowstyle.HC: editor, themes, import/export. Frame (02-ui) now only animates the rectangle and calls them. Redraw by field: motion none; shadow fields only a screen redraw; title fields a 66 px strip of each layer; the rest all layers. Constants that became fields: TBAR (now ws_tb ), Rad(), shadow 34/16/16/50 and colour, card/border/separator/title/button colours, traffic light radius 7 and pitch 22, close box radius 8, open scale 0.94, time constant 90 ms, glass alpha 205, border hairline, shadow margins in DirtyWin and WinNear. Shadow tile cache NTK 4 to 8 (glow adds a tile). New hit ids ID_MIN, ID_MAX. Verified Aiwnios, 2x, five styles, four windows: screenshots with the defaults were pixel identical to the code before the edits (max difference 0, measured when the tree was quiet; aiwnios/winstyle-golden.HC ). Real pointer clicks and drags ( aiwnios/winstyle-drive.HC ) worked for Customize, kind, glyphs, gradient, colour swatches, angle slider. Shots: shots/window-style-*.png . Not verified: x86 VM run, drag frame times, all presets, import round trip, motion presets, hover, scroll wheel. Limits: chained comparisons with calls ( A(1)<=x<A(2) ) are wrong on Aiwnios, use && . Blur amount is on or off (the wallpaper blur is fixed).

t: Kosmos Browser: architecture and specification
h: Kosmos Browser: architecture and specification
x: Kosmos Browser: architecture and specification Status: specification, not code. Branch task/templeos-shell. Written 2026-10-27. Read with browser-features.md (what each feature is, priority, provider) and browser-test-sites.md (what we test on). It replaces the v0 design in browser-plan.md where they differ; v0 stays as the reader-mode fallback. Every number here is one of three kinds, and the text says which: [measured] (taken from this repo or the local Mac, with the command or file named), [reported] (taken from a source or from the project notes, not reproduced here), or [estimate] (our arithmetic; the M1 or M2 gate must confirm it). Anything marked (memory) is an API or flag name from memory, to be checked against the Chrome 156 protocol JSON at M1. 0. Summary of decisions The host runs a real engine. Google Chrome 156 (local, found at /Applications/Google Chrome.app ) driven over CDP. We do not write HTML, CSS or JavaScript engines in the guest. Transport to Chrome is --remote-debugging-pipe , not a port. No listening socket, no WebSocket client needed, no other program can attach. Requires a non-default --user-data-dir (Chrome 136+ rule, verified fact 2 in browser-features.md ). The guest receives a display list (positioned text runs, boxes, images, clip and scroll regions, link and control hit areas), cut into 256-px bands that the guest caches and asks for on demand. Input and navigation go back as binary messages. Pages are never rendered as pixels except in a fallback tile for canvas, video and WebGL. Extensions run in our own extension host on the host, because Chrome 137+ branded builds ignore --load-extension (verified fact 3). We implement a chrome.* shim for the MV3 subset in browser-features.md section 11. One throwaway profile per run, never the user's real Chrome profile. History, bookmarks and settings live in our SQLite store. Cookies live only in the throwaway profile and the host never sends them to the guest. a. Components text Copy TempleOS guest (HolyC, desk3) | Browser app (03b-browser.HC -> browser/*.HC) | | | | | Shell | | Omnibox | | Page view | | Panels | | DevTools UI | | | | tab strip, | | and menu | | display-list| | history, marks, | | Elements, Console, | | | | toolbar, | | suggest. | | painter, | | downloads, | | Network, Application| | | | bookmarks | | | | scroll, hits| | settings, perms | | (Sources, Perf later)| | | | | | | | Browser protocol client (protocol.HC) | | Channel: COM1 (QEMU, lockstep chunks) or Aiwnios socket | binary frames, section b | Host (macOS, Python stdlib; our bridge process) | | | | kb-bridge (scripts/browser-bridge.py, grows into browser/host/) | | | | | channel server | | session / tab | | DLIST builder | | Extension host | | | | framing, flow | | manager: tabs, | | DOMSnapshot -> | | manifest, shim, | | | | control, coalesce| | nav, input routing | | ops, bands, hits | | background, content | | | | scripts, popups | | | | | | | | | | | Engine adapter: CDP over --remote-debugging-pipe (cdp.py, engine.py) | | | | | fd 3 / fd 4, NUL-terminated JSON | | v | | | Profile store (store.py, sqlite3 stdlib): | Google Chrome 156 (headless, unified mode), | | | history, bookmarks, settings, downloads, | throwaway --user-data-dir, one browser context | | | extensions registry, per-site settings | per tab, page targets, service workers | | | Component responsibilities: Channel server. Owns the byte link to the guest. Frames, checksums, sequence numbers, flow control, input coalescing (section b). Session and tab manager. One record per tab: browser context id, page target id, session id, navigation history, last display-list version per band, dirty flags. Routes guest input to the right tab and turns Chrome events into guest messages. Engine adapter. The only code that knows CDP. Everything else calls engine.navigate(tab, url) , engine.input(tab, event) , engine.snapshot(tab) -> snapshot , engine.screenshot(tab, clip, scale) . This is the portability seam for the Aiwnios build (the guest-side transport is in section b1). DLIST builder. Turns DOMSnapshot output into ops (section c). Pure Python, no Chrome calls, so it can be tested on saved snapshots. Extension host. Section g. Profile store. SQLite via sqlite3 . Schema in section i (stream 6). Guest protocol client and painter. Section b and d. Host language and dependencies Python 3 standard library only: subprocess (with pass_fds ), json , sqlite3 , base64 , zlib (host side only), struct , hashlib , http.server (extension and helper pages on 127.0.0.1), threading , select . Not needed: a WebSocket client (the pipe transport avoids one), Node, Playwright or Puppeteer. Playwright is a fine reference for CDP usage but adds a Node dependency; we do not need it. Engine check at start-up: GOOGLE_CHROME=/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome , version from --version . Refuse to run below a version we tested (start at 156). Not bundled. We do not ship Chrome. The user installs Chrome (or a Chrome for Testing build) and the bridge finds it. See section k2 for the licence reasoning. Why CDP over the pipe, and not Chrome's own headless server --remote-debugging-pipe gives a bidirectional channel on file descriptors 3 and 4 with no TCP port. A port would let any local process attach to the engine, including other user processes, which is the same risk Chrome's own Chrome 136 change was made to reduce (verified fact 2). --headless (new mode, unified with headful in Chrome 132+; verified fact 5) gives the full rendering path, including fonts, images and Canvas, which we need for fidelity. The old headless shell is not enough for fonts. b. Wire protocol: guest and host b1. Transport and framing Transport: COM1 at the QEMU server socket (the v0 path, KS_SERIAL_PORT , default 4555), or a Unix socket on Aiwnios (the native build). The framing is the same on both. Frame layout (all integers little endian): Offset Size Field Meaning 0 1 sync 0xA5 1 1 type message type (table b2) 2 1 flags bit 0 more-fragments, bit 1 compressed (reserved, always 0 in v1), bit 2 urgent (input, navigation) 3 1 tab tab id (0 = global, 1..255) 4 4 seq sender sequence number, increments per frame 8 4 len payload length, 0 to 1 MB 12 len payload 12+len 4 crc32 CRC-32 (IEEE 802.3, the zlib polynomial) over bytes 0 to 11+len Overhead is 16 bytes per frame. Receivers scan for sync , then check length and CRC; a bad frame is dropped and the receiver sends a NAK (type 0x7F) with the expected seq . Frames are limited to 64 KB on serial (fragment with more-fragments ) and 1 MB on sockets. Why CRC-32: the serial link is emulated, so errors are unlikely, but a corrupt display list shows as garbage text on screen and is hard to diagnose. CRC-32 table in HolyC is 1 KB and costs one table lookup per byte; measure (M1) before choosing a cheaper one (Fletcher-32 is the fallback). Encoding: binary throughout. ASCII (the v0 KDoc form) is kept only for the debug dump ( --dump ), not for the wire, because hex or decimal text doubles the bytes. v0's OK <n> <c> header is replaced by framed messages; v0 and v1 are not wire-compatible, and that is fine because the guest and host ship together. b2. Message types Code Name Direction Payload (summary) 0x01 HELLO both version u16, capabilities u32, guest viewport w,h (u16, device px), scale u8 0x02 NAV G to H op u8 (load, back, forward, reload, stop, new-tab, close-tab), url string (UTF-8 bytes, ASCII in v1) 0x03 INPUT G to H kind u8 (mouse-move, mouse-down, mouse-up, wheel, key-down, key-up, char), x, y (CSS px * 16), button, modifiers, key code, char 0x04 SCROLL G to H container id u16 (0 = root), dx, dy (CSS px * 16) 0x05 RESIZE G to H viewport w, h (device px), scale (1 or 2) 0x06 DLIST H to G band index u16, band version u32, count of ops, string table, op stream (section c) 0x07 TILE H to G rect, format, pixel data (fallback for canvas, video, WebGL) 0x08 IMAGE H to G image id (hash), width, height, format (rgb565-rle, alpha-rle, rgba8-rle), data 0x09 RUNIMG H to G run hash, width, height, alpha or colour, data (non-Latin text, section h) 0x0A CURSOR H to G cursor kind (arrow, hand, text, wait, crosshair, not-allowed) 0x0B META H to G tab title, url, loading state, can-back, can-forward, zoom, security state 0x0C DOWNLOAD H to G download id, name, size, state, progress 0x0D PROMPT both prompt id, kind (permission, outward-send, download, install, dangerous-file, cert), text, default answer 0x0E PROMPT-ANS G to H prompt id, answer (yes, no, always, never) 0x0F DEVT both DevTools domain id, JSON or binary event (section f) 0x10 EXT both extension id, event name, JSON 0x11 BANDREQ G to H band index list (what to send next, priority order) 0x12 HAVE G to H image and run hashes the guest holds (bloom or short list), cache state 0x13 ACK G to H highest contiguous seq received, window bytes free 0x14 STATS both frame counters, bytes, ms, for the benchmark 0x7F NAK G to H expected seq 0x7E PING both nonce b3. Flow control Two modes, chosen at HELLO by the channel's caps flags: Lockstep chunks (serial, v1). The sender transmits at most c bytes, waits for one acknowledgement byte (0x06, as in v0), then transmits the next chunk. The guest reads its FIFO fully on every acknowledgement. M1 measures c in {32, 128, 512} on the emulated link as v0 did; the default follows the best result that passes a 20 KB checksum test. Sliding window (socket, Aiwnios; and serial if the M1 test shows the FIFO holds). Window of W bytes unacknowledged (initial 16 KB), the guest sends ACK with its free buffer, the sender stops at zero window. NAK retransmits from the expected seq. Caution (memory, to confirm in M1): QEMU's emulated 16550 holds a small FIFO, and the guest must drain it on each poll or bytes are lost. This is why the serial mode stays lockstep until M1 shows otherwise. The sliding window is not enabled on serial by default. b4. Throughput budget Serial figure. The v0 note reports about 47 KB/s over the QEMU serial socket [reported] . The native-apps plan records the older lockstep loader at 1.4 to 2.7 KB/s [reported] and sets a channel gate of 50 KB/s sustained [reported] . The 47 KB/s number is not in the repo's measured results that this pass read; M1 must reproduce it with the bench:N URL ( browser-plan.md M1 gate) before any budget depends on it. Real hardware. A physical UART at 115200 baud carries about 11.5 KB/s (10 bits per byte) [estimate] . We target QEMU and Aiwnios, not a real PC serial port, so this only matters if the guest is ever run on hardware. Consequence for pages [estimate at 47 KB/s]. Payload Time over serial 20 KB display list (a small article's first band set) 0.4 s 120 KB first-paint budget (bands 0 to 2 plus a few images) 2.6 s 400 KB (Wikipedia article with a long display list) 8.5 s one 400 x 300 photo, RGB565 uncompressed (240 KB) 5.1 s one 120 x 80 thumbnail, RGB565 (19 KB) 0.4 s Rules that follow: first paint is capped at 120 KB of data; images are sent only when visible and downscaled (section d); the rest of the page streams in the background at low priority, cancelled by any new request. b5. Delta updates and caching Bands. The page is split into horizontal bands of 256 CSS px. A band's ops are positioned relative to the page origin in its own range. The host keeps a hash of each band's op bytes and a version number (band version increments only when the hash changes). Delta. When the page changes (SPA update, input, timer), the host re-snapshots, rebuilds bands, and sends only bands whose hash changed. A band the guest does not hold is sent in full. There is no op-level diff in v1; band granularity is simple and the cost is at most one band (256 px) extra per change. Images. Keyed by a 64-bit hash of the downscaled bytes (FNV-1a 64 in HolyC; SHA-256 truncated on the host is also fine; the hash is over what is sent, so the key matches the bytes). The guest keeps an LRU of images within a memory budget (section d). HAVE lets the host skip resends after a reconnect. Fonts. Built-in bitmap faces are referenced by id and never sent (section h). Non-built-in text is sent as RUNIMG with a hash of (font, size, string, colour). Strings. Each DLIST has a string table; ops refer to strings by index. Repeated link URLs and class labels cost one entry each. b6. Input coalescing (guest side, host side) Input Rule mouse-move keep the latest position; send at most one per 16 ms; send immediately when a button is down (drag selection) wheel sum deltas for one frame; one SCROLL per frame mouse-down, mouse-up never coalesced; each sent with urgent flag key-down, key-up, char never coalesced, in order; a burst of char events may be packed into one frame of up to 64 bytes resize last value wins, 100 ms debounce zoom keys sent as NAV op, not as key events, so the host handles them once The host coalesces Page.scrollBy (or Input.dispatchMouseEvent wheel) the same way: summed per 16 ms. c. Display list format c1. What the host produces The host takes a DOMSnapshot per navigation or dirty tick and emits, in paint order, a sequence of ops. Coordinates are CSS px in units of 1/16 px (i32), so 800 px is 12800. The guest multiplies by the scale (1 or 2) when it paints. Opcodes (proposed; the M1 spike may reorder them): Op Name Fields Bytes [estimate] 0x01 BOX x, y, w, h (i32 each), fill (colour token, u8), border (token u8), border width (u8), radius (u8 in px), flags (u8) 21 0x02 TEXT x, y (i32), string index (u16), face (u8: built-in face id, see h), colour token (u8), decoration (u8: underline, strike, selected), flags (u8) 14 0x03 IMAGE x, y, w, h (i32), image id (u64), fit (u8: fill, contain, cover, none), flags 26 0x04 CLIP push: x, y, w, h (i32) 17 (push), 1 (pop, op 0x05) 0x05 CLIP-POP none 1 0x06 LINK hit x, y, w, h, link string index (u16) 18 0x07 CONTROL kind (u8: text, password (drawn as dots, no value sent), checkbox, radio, button, select, textarea, file, range), id (u16), x, y, w, h, value string index (u16), label string index (u16), state (u8: disabled, checked, focused) 26 0x08 SCROLL-BEGIN container id (u16), clip x, y, w, h, content h (i32), offset y (i32), overflow (u8) 23 0x09 SCROLL-END none 1 0x0A RUN-IMG run hash (u64), x, y, w, h 26 0x0B TILE tile id (u32), x, y, w, h 21 0x0C FIXED marks the next op as viewport-fixed (drawn at a fixed offset from the viewport) 1 0x0D STICKY the next op's y is clamped to [min, max] as scroll changes, with top inset; fields min, max, top (i32) 13 0x0E XFORM 2 x 3 matrix, i16 fixed 1/1000 (guest honours translate and uniform scale only) 13 0x0F DECOR x, y, w, h, kind (u8: hr, underline, strike, focus-ring, selection-rect) 18 0x10 STR string index (u16), length (u16), UTF-8 bytes (ASCII in v1; non-ASCII as RUNIMG) 5 + n Token values (colour and face) are indices into the guest's palette, not RGB: C_INK , C_PAGE and so on from desk3/01-core.HC . Page colours that are not in the palette map to the nearest token in the host (or go to a RUN-IMG if the difference is large, decided at M2 by eye and by the golden tests). This keeps the wire small and the guest palette consistent with the desktop; page colours that matter for legibility (text on a background) are preserved by the nearest-token mapping in the M2 gate. c2. Worked example A small page, illustrative numbers (not captured from a live browser; the M1 spike replaces them with real values): html Copy <!doctype html> < html >< head >< title > Example </ title ></ head > < body style = "margin:8px;font-family:Inter,sans-serif" > < h1 style = "font-size:32px;margin:21px 0 0" > Example Domain </ h1 > < p style = "font-size:16px" > This domain is for illustrative examples. < a href = "https://www.iana.org/domains/example" > More information </ a ></ p > < img src = "logo.png" width = "32" height = "32" alt = "" > < button > Go </ button > </ body ></ html > Readable dump ( --dump output; the wire carries the binary form of the same ops). Viewport 800 x 600 CSS px, scale 2: text Copy DLIST band=0 version=1 viewport=800x600 scale=2 page_h=600 STR 0 "Example Domain" STR 1 "This domain is for illustrative examples." STR 2 "More information" STR 3 "https://www.iana.org/domains/example" STR 4 "Go" BOX x=0 y=0 w=800 h=600 fill=C_PAGE border=- flags=root TEXT x=8 y=21 str=0 face=H1 col=C_INK TEXT x=8 y=72 str=1 face=REG16 col=C_INK TEXT x=326 y=72 str=2 face=REG16 col=C_ACC decor=underline LINK x=326 y=72 w=131 h=20 str=3 IMAGE x=8 y=108 w=32 h=32 id=0x7c1f0e3a5d2b9a10 fit=none CONTROL kind=button x=48 y=108 w=44 h=28 str=4 state=- Binary size of this band: 5 strings (about 90 bytes including headers) plus 8 ops (about 130 bytes) plus a 32-byte band header, about 250 bytes [estimate]. Compare: the v0 KDoc for the same page would be about 200 bytes of text but has no positions, colours or images, so the cost is roughly 1.3 times for a much better result. c3. How the hard cases are handled Case Handling Fidelity limit Scroll (root) the guest scrolls its own band cache; the host is told only the new offset (SCROLL) so it can prefetch bands; the list is in page coordinates none for static content Scroll containers (overflow: auto/scroll) SCROLL-BEGIN with clip and content height; the host owns the container's offset and reports it in META; the guest sends SCROLL with the container id; the host re-sends the band that holds the container's content a little latency (one round trip) when wheel-scrolling a nested container position: fixed FIXED flag; the guest draws the op at viewport coordinates and ignores the scroll fixed elements that depend on transforms are drawn as tiles position: sticky STICKY with min, max and top; the guest clamps y as the root scrolls, with no round trip the containing block must be a single band; very complex sticky chains fall back to a tile overflow: hidden CLIP push and pop around the children none z-index and stacking contexts DOMSnapshot paint order is used; the host emits in paint order, so the guest paints ops sequentially and no z-sort is needed the guest does not composite blend modes; mix-blend-mode is ignored (drawn normal) opacity drawn as a tile when the opacity is not 1 and the element has children; for leaf elements the host multiplies the colour token's nearest match approximate transforms translate and uniform scale use XFORM; rotate, skew and 3D go to TILE rotated text is a tile (not selectable) box-shadow, gradients not in the op set in v1; the host renders a TILE for the box area when the computed style has a shadow or gradient (the common ones: card shadow, header gradient) tile cost; this is the largest visual gap border-radius BOX radius (up to 16 px) larger radii are drawn as tiles text selection the host runs selection through Input events (drag or double-click) and reports the selected ranges as DECOR selection-rect ops; the guest never computes selection geometry selection on text in tiles is not possible form controls CONTROL ops; the guest draws a native-looking widget; the value comes from the host; typing goes to the host as key events, which edit the real input; the caret position is sent in META the guest's widget look is not the page's own look (fine); password values never leave the host (drawn as dots) iframes the host flattens same-origin iframes into the page's band (clip to the iframe rectangle); cross-origin iframes are attached as separate targets and flattened with the same mechanism (out-of-process frames need Target auto-attach and per-frame snapshots, M4) a cross-origin iframe with its own scroll or its own fixed elements is drawn approximately canvas, video, WebGL, <object> , <embed> TILE: the host screenshots the element's rectangle at device scale (Page.captureScreenshot with clip) at 2 to 5 frames a second for video, on change for canvas and WebGL no sound, no selection, latency of a tile round trip (about 100 to 200 ms [estimate]) SVG inline SVG drawn as a TILE in v1; SVG images are rasterised by Chrome as IMAGE vector quality lost at zoom; tile re-render on zoom change <select> dropdowns the host reports the option list in CONTROL; the guest draws the menu native OS popups are not used Print styles, @media print not used (we render the screen media) none Dark mode ( prefers-color-scheme ) the host sets the emulated media to light (default) pages that follow the OS setting are light Hover the host reports the hover target in META after each mouse move; hover-only styles are applied by Chrome, so the next band reflects them one band round trip of lag on hover Animations and transitions the host snapshots at settle time; animations are sampled at 4 Hz on change for visible bands (flag, off by default) not smooth c4. Honest fidelity limits (for the user) Layout is Chrome's , so line breaks, wrapping, tables and flex and grid are exact. This is the main gain over any custom engine. Glyphs are not Chrome's. Latin text is drawn with our bitmap faces (section h), so letter shapes differ from the page's own font, and widths can differ by a pixel or two per run. The positions come from Chrome, so lines do not drift. For non-Latin text, RUN-IMG uses Chrome's own rasteriser and the shapes are exact. Gradients, shadows and blend modes are approximate or drawn as tiles. Anything in a tile is not text: no selection, no find match, no accessible text. Latency of interactions is one channel round trip plus one Chrome frame. Scroll of the root is local and instant; clicks and typing are not. Video and audio are not played in the guest (section 15 of the features doc). d. Rendering budget d1. What the guest draws per frame Only ops in the visible bands and only inside the dirty rectangle. Visible bands are found by a binary search on the band index (bands are sorted by y). Text: one blit per glyph from a bitmap atlas. A glyph at scale 2 is about 18 x 30 device px [estimate]; a run of 40 glyphs is about 22 000 px of copying. Boxes: fill rectangles, border as four rectangles, radius as a small corner table (the desk already has shadow and corner tiles, NTK cache, see 01-core.HC ). Images: blit of a cached bitmap, scaled only when the fit mode says so (scaling is done on the host, so the guest blits 1:1 wherever possible). d2. Budgets (targets, to be measured at M2) Situation Target on Aiwnios (arm64) Target on QEMU x86 (TCG) Scroll by one wheel tick (dirty rectangle = the whole page area) under 16 ms under 150 ms (accept a visible step) Full redraw of the page area, 2880 x 1800 device px under 8 ms under 300 ms New band arrives and is painted under 20 ms of guest CPU under 200 ms Idle zero (no redraw without a change) zero Reference points, from aiwnios/README.md [measured] : the desk's full redraw is 3.9 ms (4.2 worst) on Aiwnios at 2880 x 1800, and the desktop with ten windows runs at 35 frames a second under the scripted drive. No measurement of the browser exists yet; these are targets, not facts. d3. Tile cache and band cache Band cache. The guest keeps parsed ops per band (array of op records). Budget 4 MB of ops per tab, LRU by band. A 1 MB op budget is about 4000 BOX and TEXT ops [estimate] which is a long article's first screen-fulls. Page bitmap cache (optional, M4). Rendered 256-px bands at device scale kept as bitmaps (2880 x 512 px at 4 bytes per px is about 5.9 MB per band, too large to keep many); so the default is no bitmap cache, and the optional one is only for the 3 bands around the viewport. Measure first; the desk's own shadow tiles ( NTK ) are the reference for what TempleOS can hold. Image cache. LRU, 8 MB budget in the guest (RGB565 bitmaps: about 1 MB per 1000 x 500 px image [estimate]). d4. Image downscaling on the host to exact paint size The host knows each IMAGE's paint rectangle in device px (box size times scale, from the layout snapshot). A helper page ( about:blank in a hidden target, a canvas) draws the decoded image at exactly that size with imageSmoothingQuality = "high" , then reads the pixels back with getImageData (memory: canvas API; verify the read-back size limit at M2) . Chrome does the decode, so AVIF, WebP and SVG work with no code of ours. The result is quantised to RGB565, run-length encoded per row, and hashed. Transparent images use an alpha plane (RLE) with the colour. Images are sent when their band is requested, not with the page. Images above a 300 KB per-page budget are sent in priority order (visible first) and the rest are placeholders with the alt text until requested. Paint size changes (zoom, resize) re-request the image at the new size; the old hash stays in the cache. Cost check [estimate] : a 400 x 300 px photo is 120 000 px, 240 KB as RGB565 raw; RLE does not help photos, so photos are the expensive case. Mitigations: the 300 KB budget, the size cap, and a later option of an 8-bit palette for flat graphics (M6). e. Security model e1. Isolation on the host Per-tab browser context. Each tab is a Target.createBrowserContext ( memory ; the method exists in the Target domain) with disposeOnDetach . Tabs do not share cookies, storage or cache unless the user opens a link in the same context (the default for ordinary tabs is a context per window, so tabs in one window share cookies as in Chrome). Incognito. A separate context with no store writes, cookies discarded when the window closes. Throwaway profile. --user-data-dir points at ~/Library/Caches/KosmosBrowser/run-<pid> (created at start, removed at exit). It is never ~/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome . Verified fact 2 explains why the non-default directory is also required by Chrome for the debugging pipe. No port. --remote-debugging-pipe only. The bridge must refuse to start if a --remote-debugging-port argument is ever added (a test in stream 9). Launch flags (to verify on 156). --no-first-run , --no-default-browser-check , --disable-sync , --disable-background-networking , --disable-component-update , --password-store=basic , --use-mock-keychain ( memory : the mock keychain flag exists in Chromium builds; check it still applies to Google Chrome 156), --disable-extensions (we run our own host), --disable-features=... only for a named, tested need. Preferences written into the throwaway profile before start: password manager and autofill off, default search as configured, third-party cookie setting, download directory set to the staging folder (section e4). e2. The guest never receives secrets No cookies, no Set-Cookie , no Authorization headers, no tokens, no password values, no form autofill, no certificate private data. The host sends the page's own DOM values for visible controls (what the user sees), except password fields, which are drawn as dots with no value. The Network DevTools panel shows headers, with Cookie, Set-Cookie and Authorization redacted by default. Revealing one needs a per-request prompt (P2). Passwords and payment data are out of scope (features doc, section 8); the host does no keychain access unless the user approves each use. e3. Extension permission model An extension has declared permissions and host permissions in its manifest. Each is shown at install (the warning list), and a new one disables the extension until accepted. Content scripts run only on URLs matched by their matches , in an isolated world. The extension's background cannot read a page's JavaScript objects except through its own content scripts. An extension cannot read another extension's storage. Manifest subset Supported keys (MV3): manifest_version (must be 3), name , version , description , icons , permissions , host_permissions , optional_permissions (requested at run time through the permissions API), content_scripts ( matches , exclude_matches , js , css , run_at document_start, document_end, document_idle, all_frames , world ISOLATED only), action ( default_title , default_popup , default_icon ), background ( service_worker as a file name; type module is accepted), web_accessible_resources (matches only), options_page (P2), commands (P2), minimum_chrome_version (ignored, reported). Not supported: externally_connectable , content_security_policy overrides (we apply our own strict CSP to extension pages), oauth2 , key , update_url (no auto-update in v1), incognito split (incognito mode off for extensions in v1), sandbox , MV2 keys. g2. Where extensions live and how they run Folders: ~/Library/Application Support/KosmosBrowser/extensions/<id>/ , with <id> the SHA-256-based ID (32 characters, a–p alphabet, as Chrome does (memory) ). Each folder is a copy of the unpacked source; the originals are never modified. Pages: extension pages are served by the bridge's local HTTP server on 127.0.0.1 at http://127.0.0.1:<port>/ext/<id>/... with a strict CSP. (A single port and a path prefix avoids a fake chrome-extension:// scheme. The origin is different from any web origin.) Background: a page target (not a Chrome service worker) loads background.html (generated by us from the service_worker file if it is not already a page) in its own browser context. This is not MV3 service-worker semantics: no DOM is a difference we accept (the background can use DOM APIs that an MV3 worker could not), and the background does not stop when idle (memory cost; a P2 timer can unload it). Alarms keep it alive when needed. Shim: before any extension script runs, Page.addScriptToEvaluateOnNewDocument installs chrome.* (the shim, host/ext_shim.js ). The shim calls the host through Runtime.addBinding (a binding named __kosmosExt ) with JSON messages; the host answers through Runtime.evaluate on the target ( memory : the binding API exists in the Runtime domain). Content scripts: Page.createIsolatedWorld gives each extension its own world on each frame; the content script is evaluated there ( Runtime.evaluate with the world's context id). The page's own JavaScript cannot see the isolated world's objects. Popup: default_popup is a page target at http://127.0.0.1:<port>/ext/<id>/popup.html , painted by the guest in a popup area (the same painter as pages, section c). Its size comes from the popup's content size, capped at 800 x 600 CSS px. g3. chrome.* subset implemented by the bridge Namespace Subset Where it runs chrome.runtime id, getURL, getManifest, sendMessage, onMessage, connect (port, P2), lastError shim plus host router chrome.storage local (get, set, remove, clear, onChanged); sync is an alias of local (documented) host-store, per extension chrome.tabs query, get, create, update, remove, sendMessage, onUpdated (basic) host tab manager; the tabs permission chrome.scripting executeScript (func or files), insertCSS, removeCSS, registerContentScripts (P2) host, into isolated worlds chrome.action setBadgeText, setBadgeBackgroundColor, setTitle, setIcon, setPopup, onClicked guest toolbar button chrome.alarms create, get, clear, onAlarm host scheduler chrome.i18n getMessage, getUILanguage from _locales in the extension chrome.permissions contains, request (prompt), remove guest prompt chrome.bookmarks, chrome.history, chrome.downloads, chrome.cookies P2, behind permission prompts host-store and engine chrome.contextMenus, chrome.commands P2 guest menus Everything else in browser-features.md section 11 is out of scope or P2. Install flow The user chooses "Load unpacked" in the Extensions page (guest) and picks a folder. The guest sends EXT "install-request" with the folder name, and the host opens a host-side folder chooser (Finder, through osascript ; memory : a standard approach, verify in the stream) so the user picks the folder on the Mac. The host reads manifest.json , validates it (the subset above), computes the ID and the permission list, and sends a PROMPT with the warnings from browser-features.md section 11. The user answers Yes or No in the guest. On Yes the host copies the folder into the extensions directory and registers it. On No nothing is copied. Updating an extension shows a diff of new permissions and disables the extension until the user accepts them. Chrome Web Store installs and .crx files are not supported in v1 (features doc, section 11; untrusted download path). A .crx is not unpacked or run without the user's explicit folder choice. g5. Non-Latin text, in more detail The host knows, from the layout snapshot, the font family and the glyph coverage of each text run. A run that needs a font outside stage A and B is sent as RUN-IMG. The helper page draws the run with fillText in the same font family and size at device scale, then reads the pixels back with getImageData (memory) . Right-to-left and mixed-direction runs are drawn as one string, so shaping and bidi are Chrome's. A RUN-IMG has an alpha mask and the colour token; selection colour is applied in the guest. Hash key: (font family, weight, size, scale, string, colour token). Cached in the guest's image cache, with the same budget as images. Cost [estimate]: a 20-character CJK run at 16 px at scale 2 is about 640 x 40 px; an alpha mask at 8 bits is 25 KB raw and compresses about 3 to 1 with row RLE, so about 8 KB per run. A page with 200 such runs costs 1.6 MB, which is too large for serial; the first-paint budget will hold only the first screen's runs, and the rest stream in. This is the main reason non-Latin pages are slow on the serial link (section k, risk 4). i. Work breakdown into streams Each stream names the files it owns. h: Browser v0 for the HolyC desktop

Browser v0 for the HolyC desktop Status: Stage 0 (plan). Branch task/templeos-shell. Scope: a first browser app in the guest, with the host doing all network work. Architecture Three parts. Nothing in the guest touches the network, TLS, or JavaScript. Host bridge apps/templeos-holyc/scripts/browser-bridge.py (Python standard library only). It connects to the VM's COM1 serial port (TCP, QEMU server socket), waits for GET <url> lines from the guest, fetches the page with urllib (redirects followed, 10 s timeout, 1 MB limit, gzip handled), converts it to KDoc (below), and sends it back. Also a --convert URL mode that prints KDoc to the terminal for testing, and a bench:N URL that returns N bytes of test data for channel measurement. Document format KDoc : one block per line, ASCII only, produced by the host's reader-mode simplifier. Guest browser app ( desk3/03b-browser.HC , window app id 10, "Browser"). It sends requests and reads replies with a non-blocking state machine polled once per frame, parses KDoc into laid-out runs once per page, and draws only the visible lines. Wire protocol (over COM1, 8 bits, no flow control) Guest to host: - GET <url>
 . The URL is ASCII with no spaces (the guest percent-encodes). Host to guest: - W
 heartbeat, sent about once a second while a fetch is slow. The guest ignores it and resets its silence timer. - ERR <message>
 on failure (the guest shows the message on an error page). - OK <n> <c>
 then n bytes of KDoc. c is the chunk size: the host sends c bytes, waits for one acknowledgement byte, and repeats (the last chunk may be shorter). Acknowledgement byte: 0x06, written by the guest after every chunk, so the guest is never overrun. Guest timings: each byte poll is non-blocking. Silence for 3 s during a request is an error ("no answer from the host bridge"). Total time for one request is capped at 30 s. The chunk size and throughput are measured, see the milestones. Host-to-guest bytes never contain a line the guest could mistake for a request, because the guest only parses lines while it is waiting for a header. Document format (KDoc v1) Plain ASCII lines, LF ends each line. Lines the guest does not know are ignored. URL <final url> : the address after redirects (first line). TITLE <text> : page title (optional). H1 text , H2 text , H3 text : headings. P text : paragraph. LI text : list item (bullet drawn by the guest). Q text : block quote. CODE text : preformatted line (drawn in the small font). HR : horizontal rule. IMG alt text : placeholder box with the alt text (no image decoding in v0). Links inside any text: [[url|link text]] . The URL is absolute, | and ]] never appear in it (percent-encoded), and the link text never contains [ or ] . Reader mode on the host: score candidate containers (Readability-like: each paragraph adds its length times one minus its link density to its parent and grandparent, with a class and id bonus or penalty), choose the best, skip script, style, nav, header, footer, aside, form, button, svg, iframe, noscript, template, and navigation-like classes (navbox, toc, reference, sidebar, ad, comment, share). Entities decoded, whitespace collapsed, curly quotes, dashes and other non-ASCII mapped to ASCII (NFKD, then drop), text capped at about 60 KB. Guest app Window 760 by 560 logical, icon: Lucide globe. Toolbar: Back, Forward, Reload buttons, then the URL bar. Page area with a thin scrollbar. Status line at the bottom: the URL being loaded, or the error, plus the time the load took. URL bar: click to focus, ASCII typed in, Backspace, Enter loads (adds https:// when there is a dot and no scheme; text without a dot becomes a DuckDuckGo html search), Escape unfocuses (only while focused, so Escape still quits the desktop otherwise). Links: accent colour with an underline; one hit region per link run; clicking pushes history and navigates. Scrolling: mouse wheel, Up, Down, PageUp, PageDown, Home, End while the browser is in front. History: back and forward (a list of URLs with an index). Layout is cached per page and per scale; drawing walks only the visible lines (binary search on line y). Milestones and gates M0 plan : this file committed. Gate: file reviewed in the commit. M1 channel : the guest sends GET and receives a test payload with bench:N at chunk sizes 32, 128 and 512. Gate: a 20 KB payload arrives intact (checksum over the bytes at both ends matches) for each chunk size; throughput in bytes per second is reported for each chunk size. Pass if at least one size reaches 2 KB/s; fail and report otherwise. M2 converter : browser-bridge.py --convert URL prints a sensible KDoc for the five test URLs. Gate: each gives at least 500 bytes of body text (except example.com, which is short), no HTML tags, no non-ASCII, links absolute. M3 app : the Browser window opens from the dock, loads a page from the bridge, shows links, scrolls, goes back and forward, and shows the Loading state while the bridge is slow. Gate: screenshots of the first four test URLs render legibly and clicking one link navigates. M4 polish and verification : the five URLs end to end in the VM, errors (bad URL, no bridge, timeout, unreachable host) show an error page, long pages do not freeze the desktop (the frame time while loading stays under 50 ms), screenshots in apps/templeos-holyc/shots/browser-*.png . Out of scope for v0 JavaScript (none, ever in the guest), forms and submitting, cookies and sessions, login, images (placeholders only), CSS (the host's reader mode decides the look), tables as tables (rows become lines), fonts other than the Inter set, text selection, find in page, tabs, bookmarks, persistence, HTTPS certificate checks beyond urllib's defaults (the host does TLS). Test URLs http://example.com/ (very small page, baseline) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oscilloscope (article with links, references and an infobox) https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/introduction.html (documentation with code blocks) https://paulgraham.com/greatwork.html (plain HTML essay) https://news.ycombinator.com/ (table layout, many links)

t: DLIST binary format (guest reader spec)
h: DLIST binary format (guest reader spec)
x: DLIST binary format (guest reader spec) Status: v1, written with stream 2 (M2 host half). The reference encoder is browser/host/dlist.py ; the reference painter is browser/host/dlist_paint_ref.py ; tests/browser/dlist_test.py decodes the hex example below. Decisions where the spec ( docs/browser-architecture.md c) was ambiguous are listed at the top of dlist.py (D1 to D19). Conventions All integers little endian. Coordinates are i32 in 1/16 CSS px, page origin (scroll 0). Band i covers 4096 units (256 CSS px): [i*4096, (i+1)*4096) . Colour refs are u8: 0xFF none, 0..254 index into the band colour table. String refs are u16: 0xFFFF none. Strings are UTF-8, ASCII in v1. Scale: device px = units * scale / 16 (scale 1 or 2). Band payload (one DLIST message, type 0x06) Offset Size Field 0 2 band index (u16) 2 2 flags (u16): bit0 last band, bit1 band holds FIXED ops 4 4 band version (u32) 8 8 band hash (u64), FNV-1a 64 over bytes 16 to end 16 4 band top y (i32, units) 20 4 band bottom y (i32, units, exclusive) 24 2 n_colours (u16, 0..255) 26 2 n_strings (u16) 28 4 n_ops (u32) 32 4 x n_colours colour table: R, G, B, A bytes then per string: 2 + len u16 length, UTF-8 bytes then per op opcode (u8), fields in the order below The guest reads header, colours and strings, then ops until n_ops are consumed. Any other byte count after the last op is an error. The hash lets the guest skip a band it already holds (BANDREQ/HAVE in b5). Ops Field codes: i i32, I u32, Q u64, H u16, B u8, h i16, b i8. Sizes include the opcode. Op Code Fields Size BOX 01 x y w h i, fill B, border B, bw B, rad B, flags B 22 TEXT 02 x y i, w H (px), str H, face B, col B, deco B, flags B 17 IMAGE 03 x y w h i, id Q, fit B (0 fill, 1 contain, 2 cover, 3 none), flags B 27 CLIP 04 x y w h i 17 CLIP_POP 05 none 1 LINK 06 x y w h i, str H 19 CONTROL 07 kind B, id H, x y w h i, val H, label H, state B 25 SCROLL_BEGIN 08 sid H, x y w h i, content_h i, offset i, overflow B 28 SCROLL_END 09 none 1 RUNIMG 0A hash Q, x y w h i 25 TILE 0B id I, x y w h i, kind B (low nibble kind, high nibble alpha 0..15) 22 FIXED 0C prefix for the next op (viewport coordinates) 1 STICKY 0D min i, max i, top i; prefix for the next op 13 (XFORM) 0E reserved, never emitted DECOR 0F x y w h i, kind B, col B 19 (STR) 10 reserved GRAD 11 x y w h i, a B, b B, angle B, rad B 21 SHADOW 12 x y w h i, dx h, dy h, blur B, spread b, col B, rad B 25 BOX: fill and border are colour refs; border is drawn bw px wide inside the box rectangle. flags bits are reserved (0). TEXT: face bits are bold (bit0), size class (bits 1-2: 0 <= 12 px, 1 <= 16, 2 <= 24, 3 larger), mono (bit3), italic (bit4), serif (bit5). deco bits: underline 1, line-through 2, overline 4. IMAGE: flags bits 0-3 alpha 0..15 (15 opaque), bit4 placeholder (no content yet), bit5 CSS background. TILE kind: 0 svg, 1 canvas or webgl, 2 video, 4 embed. CONTROL kind: 0 text, 1 password (val is 0xFFFF, never sent), 2 checkbox, 3 radio, 4 button, 5 select, 6 textarea, 7 file, 8 range, 9 submit, 10 reset, 11 other. CONTROL state bits: 0 disabled, 1 checked, 2 readonly, 3 required. GRAD: linear two-stop from a to b ; angle 0 = to top, 64 = to right, 128 = to bottom, 192 = to left. SHADOW: offsets in units, blur and spread in px. Prefix ops: FIXED and STICKY apply to the op that follows them, and nothing else. A STICKY op paints at y + shift , where shift = clamp(scroll_y + top, min, max) - min . Paint an op only in the band that holds its shifted top. FIXED ops are in band 0 and use viewport coordinates. Clip groups: CLIP (or SCROLL_BEGIN) opens a group, CLIP_POP (or SCROLL_END) closes it. Groups do not nest; the encoder never opens one inside another. h: Podcast service (svcpodcast.py): protocol for the HolyC side
x: Podcast service (svc_podcast.py): protocol for the HolyC side Service name podcast . Request REQ id podcast token op arg... ; reply records are TAB separated (recs.py), all text ASCII. Ids: show f + 10 hex (from the feed URL), episode 10 hex. The guest never sends a feed URL except in subscribe_url . ? = optional. Sizes measured by tests/test_podcast.py. Ops and replies categories -> K id label count x12. directory CAT|all OFFSET LIMIT(max 40) ?QUERY -> DH total offset count cat , then D fid title publisher cat tone subscribed desc . 10 entries: 984 bytes (worst case about 1.9 KB). 108 shows, 12 categories (fixtures/podcasts/catalog.json). subs -> S fid title publisher tone episodes unplayed fetched_epoch downloaded . subscribe FID , subscribe_url URL ?TITLE , unsubscribe FID reply with one S . No network, no approval. tone 0..11 = rose orange amber lime green teal cyan blue indigo violet purple pink (the app's cover colour). refresh FID ?force -> R fid result new total skipped title note ; result new same (304) cache (inside podcast_min_refresh_s) offline (saved list shown). Approval scope podcast:refresh:FID . No saved list and offline: ERR offline: cannot reach HOST (...) . episodes FID OFFSET LIMIT ?unplayed -> EH fid total offset count show publisher , then E eid yyyymmdd dur_s size_kb played downloaded pos_s title . Newest first, date 00000000 when unknown, title 72 chars. 10 episodes: 658 bytes (worst case about 1.4 KB). Needs a refresh first, else ERR . episode EID -> X (same fields as E plus host ) and up to 4 N text lines of 88 chars (show notes, tags removed). mark EID played|unplayed -> E . downloads OFFSET LIMIT -> DLH total offset count , then DE (same fields as E ). delete EID -> E . download EID -> DL eid state done_kb total_kb error ; state none run done err . Approval podcast:dl:EID (text names the title, size and host). Runs in a thread: poll dlstatus EID ; dlcancel EID . Limit podcast_max_mb. afplay cannot stream a URL (checked), so play of an episode that is not downloaded asks the same approval, downloads, then starts playing (the reply holds DL then PS ). Playback (through the music service, afplay): play EID ?START_S (default: resume), pause resume toggle stop seek S next prev volume 0..100 speed 0.75|1|1.25|1.5|2 sleep MINUTES|eoe|0 autonext 0|1 status . All reply PS state eid fid pos_s dur_s speed sleep_s autonext title ; state playing paused stopped loading ; sleep_s is seconds left, -1 for end of episode, 0 off. Poll status about 4 times a second while the window is open (it also saves progress). Position is saved every 5 s, on pause, stop, seek and sleep; an episode within 3 s of its end is marked played, then the next downloaded unplayed one plays if autonext is 1 (default; it never starts a download by itself). Pause/stop/seek answer ERR nothing from Podcasts is playing when the music service plays something else. cover FID|EID SIZE ?p4|565 , SIZE 32 40 48 64 96 (565 only up to 64) -> V id fmt w h nlines palette note , then nlines x Z hex (96 hex digits per line, last shorter). V ... none with a note when there is no image or no Pillow (the guest paints the tone block). Approval podcast:img:HOST . Cached on the host. Sizes: 40x40 1743 bytes, 48x48 2468, 96x96 9596 (the guest reply buffer is 12000). stats -> STATS requests user_agent . Cover record (the guest has no image decoder) p4 : palette = 64 hex digits = 16 colours of 4 digits each, the number is RGB565 (r5 g6 b5, F800 red). Data = rows top to bottom, left to right, two pixels per byte (left pixel = high nibble, index into the palette), 2 hex digits per byte, SIZE*SIZE/2 bytes. Concatenate the Z lines. 565 : no palette (empty field); data = SIZE*SIZE pixels, 4 hex digits each, the RGB565 number. The image is centre-cropped to a square, resized to SIZE (Lanczos), p4 is a 16-colour median cut (no dithering). Config (hub config.json; all optional) podcast_dir (default ~/.cache/kosmos-hostd/podcast: state.json, feeds/, audio/, covers/; outside the repo), podcast_max_mb 200, podcast_min_refresh_s 600, podcast_allow_loopback false (tests only), podcast_catalog (path), podcast_tick_s 0.5, contact (goes into the User-Agent KosmosTempleDesktop/0.1 podcast (contact) ). Registered in hostd.py build_hub (two lines). Security notes Network only after a one-time approval token naming the host (and size). Subscribing, browsing the directory, episode lists, status and play of a downloaded file are local. Feeds: http and https only, no user name or password, at most 3 redirects (each checked again), no proxy, identity encoding, 2 MB cap, 15 s timeout. Hosts that are or resolve to this Mac or a private network are refused (a lookup happens only after the approval; DNS rebinding between check and connect is not covered). XML: any DOCTYPE or ENTITY declaration and UTF-16 are refused before parsing (defusedxml is also used if installed), 100 episodes kept, titles cut to 300 chars. enclosure URLs that are not http/https (file://) are skipped and counted in skipped . Files: names are made from the episode id plus an audio extension, never from the feed; reads re-check the name and the real path inside audio/ (symlinks out are refused); ids are matched against ^f[0-9a-f]{10}$ and ^[0-9a-f]{10}$ . Downloads stop at podcast_max_mb, text/html answers are refused, partial files are removed. Covers: 3 MB cap, JPEG PNG GIF WEBP only, Pillow decompression-bomb limit 25 million pixels. The approval is a consent record for the UI, not a defence against a hostile guest (same as the other services).

t: sheet service (host half of Spreadsheets)
h: sheet service (host half of Spreadsheets)
x: sheet service (host half of Spreadsheets) svc_sheet.py registers service sheet in the hub (one line in hostd.py build_hub ). It drives GridCraft ( gridcraft-cli mcp , MIT OR Apache-2.0, alpha, third party) as one long-lived process. The workbook lives in that process; the guest only paints and types. Wire is the hub's: REQ id sheet token op arg... -> RES id OK + records (TAB fields, \t \n \\ escaped, ASCII only). Ops and replies (args are strings) op args reply records open file in workspace, or budget / sales / grades OPEN src title nsheets active dirty , then SH idx name used r0 c0 nrows ncols per sheet new [sample] same as open sheets / activate [name or index] SH records read range [sheet] (empty range = used range) RNG sheet range r0 c0 nrows ncols truncated , R rownum cell... , then ST records cell A1 [sheet] CELL ref input shown type flags bold italic (input is the formula text) eval formula, = optional (needs no open sheet) EVAL type text (errors: type e , text #DIV/0! ; a bad formula is ERR ) set cell text (text starting = is a formula) SET ref shown nsheets capped , then CH ref shown for every cell whose display changed (dependents included, max 200) format range bold=1 italic=0 fill=RRGGBB\|none align=left\|center\|right FMT range options save / export_csv path.xlsx / path.csv\|tsv [sheet] SAVED relpath bytes ; first try returns APPROVE fs:write:<abs path> close , status CLOSED ; STAT binary_found running pid rss_kb open title workspace Read layout. A window is at most 100 rows x 26 columns. Row record R n f1 f2 ... : field j is column c0+j; an empty cell is an empty field and trailing empty fields are cut. A field is one type char then the shown text (30 chars max, ASCII): s text, n number, c currency, p percent, d date/time, b bool, e error. Numbers are not re-sent as raw values; use cell for the formula/input. ST dcol drow flags align fill is sent only for cells that differ from the default (flags bit1 bold, bit2 italic; align l c r , default r for numbers else l ; fill RRGGBB or - ); dcol/drow are offsets in the window. Styles come from the engine's edit.copy html; if the window has merged cells the ST records are omitted. Config (config.json, git-ignored; see config.example.json) gridcraft_cli absolute path (else env GRIDCRAFT_CLI , else PATH; the service answers ERR "gridcraft-cli was not found" without it), sheet_workspace (default ~/.cache/kosmos-hostd/sheets , mode 0700), sheet_timeout_s (default 10, per engine call). Security Engine always under sandbox-exec -p <profile> (profile built in memory by make_profile , not a file): deny network* , writes only in the workspace, no reads under /Users or $HOME except the workspace and the binary's folder; env -i , HOME and TMPDIR in <workspace>/.sandbox/ , cwd there. Tests prove a raw open_workbook ~/.zshrc , a write to ~ , and mcp --connect <local port> fail. GridCraft MCP has no root confinement (docs/mcp.md), so the service checks every path first: no .. , no hidden component, no symlink at any level, must be inside the workspace, extension xlsx/xlsm/csv/tsv/json (save: xlsx, export: csv/tsv), 20 MB read limit. It exposes fixed ops only, never execute_command . File writes ask the guest (APPROVE naming the full path); the approval is used up by that one write. set / format need none. Limits: arg 1000 chars, window 100x26, engine line 4 MB, call timeout 10 s (the engine is killed, next call restarts it), at most 5 starts a minute. Supervision: started on first call; a dead or timed-out engine is replaced and the guest is told once that unsaved edits were lost; close() and atexit kill only the Popen pid. sys hello closes the workbook. Measured (M-series Mac, gridcraft-cli 0.12.1, tests/bench_sheet.py ) First call (start + new + eval) 50 ms; open sample 8 ms; read 20x12 2.4 ms; set with changed cells 0.8 ms; save 5 ms; reopen 2 ms. RSS 4.5 MB at start, 15 MB after the bench. Reply for a dense 20x12 window (240 cells, bold and fill rows): 2595 bytes; the budget sample: 923 bytes. Compare the hub's own cost: about 0.6 s for 20 KB on the serial link. What the CLI cannot do (or we do not use) No bulk style read (we parse edit.copy html; fonts, borders, number-format strings are not sent). No headless PNG; charts are not rendered (the sheet reports them in inspect_workbook only). Save writes xlsx only; xlsb/ods/xls open via gridcraft-cli convert , not this service yet. Sheet-qualified style reads work on the active sheet only. Alpha: function coverage is self-reported. Tests: python3 -I tests/test_sheet.py (fake engine always, real with GRIDCRAFT_CLI=... ).

t: Can the kosmos engine run on TempleOS, and what is the best way
h: Can the kosmos engine run on TempleOS, and what is the best way
x: Can the kosmos engine run on TempleOS, and what is the best way Feasibility study, 2026-10-27, branch task/templeos-shell. No engine crate was touched; all experiment code lives in the session scratchpad ( .../scratchpad/engine-on-templeos/ , not in the repo). Tags: [R] verified by running something this session. [S] verified by reading source (path given). [M] from memory or inference, not checked. 1. Answer in one paragraph Yes, in a limited and well-defined form. A deterministic slice of the engine, compiled by rustc as no_std for x86-64 and wrapped as a TempleOS .BIN , was loaded into TempleOS V5.03, called from HolyC, and returned the same 64-bit values as the native aarch64 build (blake3 state hash and a 10,000-tick f32/libm physics loop) [R]. That settles the hard questions for route 1 (ABI, loader format, SSE, float determinism, task switching). What is not settled is size: the real kosmos-sim and kosmos-physics pull bevy_ecs , rapier3d , serde_json , thiserror and HashMap , which need alloc and a std-free port of our own crates; that is weeks, not days, and was not attempted. The whole engine (wgpu renderer, winit, threads, files, network, MCP) cannot and should not run inside TempleOS. Recommended: route 3 now (already how the desktop works, zero risk), route 1 as a gated spike for the sim core only, and route 4 on Aiwnios as a cheap by-product of a C-ABI build. Do not hand-port to HolyC. 2. Hard facts established (section B) Toolchain available [R] rustup target list --installed for the active toolchain (1.97.1): aarch64-apple-darwin , wasm32-unknown-unknown , x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu . x86_64-unknown-none is not installed. Nothing was installed. nightly-2025-12-04 (rustc 1.93.0-nightly) has rust-src . rustc -Zunstable-options --print target-spec-json --target x86_64-unknown-none works without the target installed (the spec is built in), so a custom JSON can be derived from it. cargo -Zbuild-std=core,compiler_builtins fails offline : build-std resolves the whole std workspace and the registry cache has no dlmalloc (and no compiler_builtins ). Using it needs network access to crates.io (downloading source crates, no tool install). What the user would need to approve: either rustup target add x86_64-unknown-none (a tier-2 prebuilt core + compiler_builtins , about 30 MB, no network use at build time after that), or letting -Zbuild-std fetch std's dependencies. Either is needed for the soft-float variant with float code (see below). Workaround that needed neither: build libcore by hand with the nightly rustc from rust-src (7 s) into a private sysroot for the custom target, supply a 20-line stand-in compiler_builtins (memcpy, memmove, memset, memcmp, bcmp), and point cargo at it with RUSTFLAGS=--sysroot=... . That built libm , blake3 and the test crate with plain cargo build --offline [R]. For the rest of the plan, installing the target is cleaner. Trap found: the target JSON must be named x86_64-... [R] blake3 's build script reads the first dash-separated component of $TARGET . A target file called ks-sse2.json gave TARGET=ks-sse2 , the script concluded "not x86_64", configured no SIMD modules, and the build failed with "could not find sse2 in the crate root". Renaming to x86_64-ks-sse2.json fixed it. Any crate with an arch-sniffing build script will do the same. Two custom targets (derived from the builtin x86_64-unknown-none ) x86_64-ks-sse2 : code-model small (the builtin one is kernel , which assumes addresses in the top 2 GB and is wrong for TempleOS, whose code heap is the low 2 GB), relocation-model pic , disable-redzone , panic-strategy abort , SSE and SSE2 enabled, no SSE3 and up, no x87 use for f32/f64. x86_64-ks-soft : same but -mmx,-sse,-sse2 ... +soft-float and rustc-abi x86-softfloat . Float ops become compiler_builtins calls ( __addsf3 and so on). Not built with float code (needs the real compiler_builtins ); built and checked with integer-only code. Route 1 in detail: the .BIN wrapper (format read from source) [S] and run [R] Format, from Kernel/KLoad.HC , Kernel/KernelA.HH:383-427 , Compiler/CMain.HC:534-560 in the extracted ISO sources: Header CBinFile is 32 bytes , not 40 as holyc-improvement-analysis.md section C says (U16 jmp, U8 module_align_bits, U8 reserved, U32 signature, then three I64: org, patch_table_offset, file_size). jmp = 0xEB | (30 << 8) ; signature 'TOSB' = 0x42534F54; org must be INVALID_PTR , which is I64_MAX (0x7FFF...F), not -1 ( KernelA.HH:40 ), or Load copies to a fixed address; module_align_bits 4 gives a 16-byte aligned module_base (needed for SSE constant loads). Image bytes follow at offset 32 ( module_base ). Exports are made visible to HolyC through the hash table. Patch table at patch_table_offset , records U8 type; U32 value; NUL-terminated name , then payload: IET_REL32_EXPORT =16 (value = offset, symbol = base + offset), IET_ABS_ADDR =20 (value = count, empty name, then count U32 offsets; the loader does *(U32*)(base+off) += base , so the 64-bit slot must hold the link-time address in its low 32 bits, which works because the code heap is below 2 GB), IET_END =0 followed by 16 zero bytes. File size rounded to 16. The writer is 25 lines of Python ( mkbin.py : rust-objcopy -O binary , symbols from objdump -t , relative relocs from objdump --dynamic-reloc ). Calling convention: the .BIN is SysV, TempleOS is stack-based, callee-pops. One HolyC asm{} trampoline serves every export ( KseSysV2(fn, a, b) ): load fn from SF_ARG1[RBP] , args from SF_ARG2/3 into RDI/RSI, save RBX/RSI/RDI/R10/R11 (SysV callee clobbers RSI, RDI, R10, R11 that TempleOS expects preserved; R12-R15, RBX, RBP are preserved by SysV), AND RSP,-16 because TempleOS gives no alignment and rustc spills with movaps , CALL RAX , restore, RET1 24 . The exported address is fetched with HashFind("KsEngRun", Fs->hash_table, HTT_EXPORT_SYS_SYM)->val . Generating one trampoline per signature (2 to 6 integer args) is trivial; floats and structs pass through memory pointers. Route notes Route 2, port the sim to HolyC. About 6 k lines for kosmos-sim alone plus the physics (rapier is not portable by hand), and the crowd/airship ports are 14 k lines of f64. HolyC has F64 on x87 only ( analysis section on floating point), no f32, a different operator-precedence table, no continue , one compiler. The hashes would not match the engine's f32 values, which defeats the purpose of the engine's replay contract. Measured float cost today: 67 ns per multiply-add (x87 under TCG) against 6 ns for hand SSE2 ( holyc-improvement-analysis.md ). Rejected. Route 3, host engine, TempleOS client. What the repo already does. kosmos serve --port speaks line-delimited JSON/WebSocket ( apps/kosmos-cli/src/main.rs ; rust-engine.md 4.15); TempleOS has serial only, so the same bridge as the browser spec (framed binary over COM1 with CRC, browser-architecture.md section b1) would carry step , query , hash and a state or display-list stream, with a small Python or Rust bridge on the Mac translating serial to the WebSocket. The TempleOS side draws with its own software renderer. Cost S to M; no determinism question since the engine runs once, on the host. Route 4, Aiwnios. Aiwnios binds native C through PrsAddSymbol(name, int64_t (*)(int64_t *stk), arity) and has no dlopen [S, aiwnios/README.md and the analysis doc], so the engine would be linked into the Aiwnios runtime itself (a static library, crate-type = ["staticlib"] with a C header) and registered at start-up, then called from HolyC like any function. This is the one route where the full engine (std, threads, files, even wgpu) can sit next to HolyC, because it is a normal arm64 process. It costs a patch and rebuild of the Aiwnios runtime for each new entry, but each entry is a few lines. It does not run the x86 TempleOS build and it is not the OS showcase; it is a development vehicle. Not built or run here (the analysis doc records that the Aiwnios build was earlier blocked by the permission classifier). Route 5. Status quo: TempleOS UI in QEMU, everything else on the host. It is route 3 without the dedicated protocol work. 7. Recommendation (section D) Ranked: 1. Route 3 as the product path (now). It is the only route that gives TempleOS users the whole engine, including rendering assets, physics at full speed and the MCP surface, and it adds no new risk. Build the serial protocol once; it also serves the browser. 2. Route 1 as a research spike, sim core only , because it is the only route that puts engine code inside the OS and the experiment shows it works. Value: a TempleOS-native "engine state hash" check, offline deterministic replays, and a stress test of the engine's no_std hygiene that also benefits wasm. Do not promise physics at scale under TCG (25x slower in the test). 3. Route 4 only if Aiwnios becomes the desktop's daily driver; almost free once a staticlib with a C header exists. 4. Route 2: no. Route 5: keep as fallback, it is what runs now. TempleOS fragility : faults are uncatchable and drop to a debugger; an out-of-arena write corrupts the single address space (no MMU protection). TCG speed : 25x on float-heavy code; acceptable for hashes and small scenes only. blake3 SIMD dead code and compiler_builtins float helpers in the soft-float variant are unverified; choose the SSE2 variant, which was verified. And the TempleOS guest is x86_64 under TCG on this arm Mac, so the guest CPU is software-emulated, while a Linux box on the same Mac can be arm64 with hardware acceleration (HVF) at near native speed. That asymmetry is the reason to put the work in the box and keep the guest thin. 3. Terminal (question 1) 4.1 Spec from Kosmos OS /Users/paulbloch/kosmos-os-frame/src/apps/terminal/TerminalApp.tsx (108 lines [V]) is explicitly "one-shot commands, not a pty": it POSTs a command to /api/exec and lists stdout, stderr and exit code, with arrow-key history. That is the floor for us (a run-a-command panel) and proves the workspace exec path exists. It is not enough for vim, htop or ssh, so the Dev Box needs a real pty. 4.2 Hub service term The hub is request/reply, not streaming: one REQ record, one RES record set, the reply chunked at 256 bytes with a one-byte ack per chunk, and a PENDING frame once a second while a slow call runs [V hostd.py docstring]. Records are TAB separated, and esc() drops  and escapes 	 
 \ [V recs.py], so raw terminal bytes cannot ride in a record. Two consequences: Output is polled with a long poll: term read id max_bytes wait_ms returns what the pty produced (immediately, or after at most wait_ms ), or an empty reply. The hub already sends PENDING for slow calls, so a 200 ms wait costs nothing extra. The guest keeps one read outstanding while a terminal window is focused. Binary data must be encoded: hex doubles it, base64 adds 33 percent [M]. Section 4.3 avoids the problem. Ops: text Copy term open cwd cols rows [cmd...] -> TERM id (first open per session needs approval token: scope "term:shell") term write id <b64 or hex bytes> -> OK n term read id max wait_ms -> DATA seq n ... | EOF code term resize id cols rows -> OK (ioctl TIOCSWINSZ, then the child gets SIGWINCH) term close id -> OK Host side is stdlib Python: pty.fork() or os.openpty() plus subprocess.Popen(..., start_new_session=True) , a reader thread feeding a bounded ring buffer (flow control: stop reading the master when the ring holds 64 KB, so the child blocks in write, which is exactly what a real terminal does), fcntl.ioctl(fd, termios.TIOCSWINSZ, struct.pack("HHHH", rows, cols, 0, 0)) for resize, TERM=xterm-256color . Smoke test run here with /bin/echo and /bin/ls in a throwaway directory [V, scratchpad devbox/pty_smoke.py ]: echo returned b'hello devbox
' , ls -la returned four lines with 
 line ends (the pty's tty layer adds the CR), and the winsize ioctl succeeded. The command that open runs is the target : limactl shell devbox (R1), ssh -tt box (R3), docker exec -it c sh (R2), or /bin/echo in the smoke test. One service serves all routes. The hub, not the guest, owns credentials and the allowed target list. 4.3 Where the VT emulation lives A. Emulator in HolyC (parse bytes in the guest) B. Emulator in the host (hub keeps the screen model) Guest code a VT parser plus a cell grid plus a renderer a cell renderer only Link traffic raw pty bytes (any program, any volume) dirty rows only: text plus attribute runs Full-screen app (top, vim) every escape sequence crosses the link only the changed rows cross Aiwnios native pty natural fit not needed Risk a hostile or noisy program can flood the guest host Python parser must be right; pyte (MIT [M]) exists, but stdlib-only would be about 400 lines [M] Recommendation: B first , A later. The hub runs a small VT100/xterm model and sends, per poll, a list of changed rows: ROW y text plus ATTR y x0 x1 fg bg flags runs, plus CUR x y visible , plus ALT 0/1 . The HolyC side is then a grid renderer that never parses an escape. Scrollback also lives on the host (the guest asks term scroll id offset count ). Keys go the other way as bytes: arrows ESC [ A .. D (application mode ESC O A when the host model says DECCKM is set), ctrl-letter as 1..26, F1..F4 as ESC O P .. S , F5.. as ESC [ 15 ~ etc., bracketed paste as ESC [ 200 ~ ... ESC [ 201 ~ when the program enabled mode 2004. The host model also answers queries (cursor position ESC [ 6 n , device attributes) so vim and htop do not hang waiting for a reply. Sequences needed for bash, vim, htop, git, ssh [M, to confirm with a recorded session]: C0 controls (BS, HT, LF, CR, BEL), CSI cursor moves (A B C D H f G d), erase (J K), insert/delete lines and chars (L M @ P), scroll region (r), SGR (0 1 3 4 7 22 27 30..37 38;5;n 38;2;r;g;b 39 40..47 48;5;n 49 90..97 100..107), save/restore cursor (7 8), modes (?1 application cursor, ?7 autowrap, ?25 cursor visible, ?1049 alternate screen, ?2004 bracketed paste, ?1000/1006 mouse optional), ESC c reset, titles (OSC 0, ignored), UTF-8 box drawing (needs glyphs, see 4.4). Acceptance is a recorded corpus: record vim , top , htop , git log --graph , ssh sessions with script , replay into the model, compare the final grid with a known-good emulator such as tmux's capture-pane [M]. 4.4 Monospace face and rendering cost Our faces are Inter ASCII, proportional, at four sizes [V fonts.md]; browser plan h5a stage A+ already names a monospace bitmap face for pre and code (candidates Iosevka or JetBrains Mono, OFL, to check [V browser-architecture.md line 555]). The terminal needs the same asset plus box-drawing and block characters (U+2500..257F, 2580..259F, about 128 glyphs [M]); those can be drawn as lines and rectangles in code, not stored. Use one face at 8x16 and a 2x variant. Cell size 8x16 makes 120x40 equal to 960x640 pixels. Fonts are a host job (fonts.md rule 1), so the face is produced by gen-font.py style tooling and ships as a bitmap atlas; the font manager plan covers licences. Rendering estimates [M, to measure at gate G4]: Full grid: 4,800 cells x 128 pixels = 614,000 pixels per full repaint. At 60 Hz that is 37 million pixel writes per second. In HolyC under QEMU TCG (x86 emulated on arm, roughly 5 to 20 times slower than native [M]) a full 60 Hz repaint is not realistic. Dirty rows only: a typical keystroke or a top refresh changes 1 to 40 rows. At 40 rows it is the same 614k pixels once per refresh, 1 to 2 per second for top; under 10 repaints per second is fine. Draw only the cells in rows the hub reports; keep the previous frame in the window buffer. Therefore: the terminal is event driven, not 60 Hz . The target is under 50 ms from reply to pixels for a one-row change. Aiwnios (native arm, per the build in aiwnios/ ) removes the emulation penalty; full repaint at 60 Hz of 614k pixels is a normal blit there [M]. It can also call a registered native function for a pty (KsExec exists [V README]) and skip the hub for the terminal entirely; that is the better Aiwnios path, with the same approval prompt. 4.5 Bandwidth Link: about 17 KB/s measured end to end on QEMU serial (20,000-byte bench, 1,167 ms at chunk 128 and 1,236 ms at chunk 512, checksum ok [V browser-painter-status.md line 11]). The earlier 47 KB/s figure was not reproduced [V browser-architecture.md b4]. Use 16 KB/s. The channel is the limit only for output floods, not for editing. 5. Files, workspace and git (question 2) Workspace model. One host folder, e.g. ~/devbox/work/<project> , is the single shared directory. Lima mounts it into the box as /work over virtiofs (VZ) or 9p (QEMU); nothing else is mounted [W lima mount doc; V default mounts: [] ]. This is the ai-ide.md 2.4 rule ("the bridge mounts it as the only writable root") with a VM boundary added. File tree and search. Services files list/stat/read/write run on the host against the shared folder (fast, no VM round trip) with the ai-ide.md rule that paths resolving outside the root are refused; grep runs inside the box ( rg ) so it sees the same view the compiler sees. Git. Status and diff run on the host ( git -C ) for speed; commits and anything that needs hooks or the toolchain run in the box. Push is never done by the desktop (ai-ide.md policy). Credentials stay on the host (section 9). File watching. The hub watches with polling on the host side ( os.scandir mtimes every second [M]) or fswatch if installed; virtiofs does not propagate inotify from host edits to the guest on all kernels [M], so tools that watch inside the box (webpack, cargo-watch) may need polling mode; flag it in templates. AI IDE reuse. The agent's tools in ai-ide.md (read, edit, grep, shell, tests) map to files , git , term / exec . The agent shell runs in the box , never on the Mac, unless the user approves; this implements the "Docker or Lima sandbox" setting already in the plan and makes it the default instead of an option. 6. Inside Lima/Colima the socket is forwarded to the host (Colima writes ~/.colima/<profile>/docker.sock [M]); the hub speaks HTTP over a unix socket with http.client (stdlib). Read-only endpoints: GET /containers/json?all=1 , /images/json , /volumes , /containers/{id}/logs?tail=200 , /networks , /containers/{id}/stats?stream=false . Action Approval list containers, images, volumes, ports, logs, stats none (read-only default) start, stop, restart a container the Dev Box created one approval per session per scope docker:control exec shell ( term open with docker exec -it ) scope term:shell compose up/down in the workspace scope docker:compose:<project> ; shows the compose file's images, ports and volumes in the prompt image pull, build with network each pull: prompt names the image, tag and digest if pinned; pulls are the supply-chain gate (section 9) run with --privileged , host network, docker.sock mount, or bind mount outside /work denied , no override in v1 rm, prune, volume delete per-action prompt with the object name The hub must not hand the guest a raw socket: the Engine API is root in the box. Vite, webpack and Next dev servers use a WebSocket back to the page's origin. Chromium on the host handles it natively since the dev server is on the same loopback; the guest only sees painted bands. The costly part is repainting over a 16 KB/s link, so preview is a screenshot/band stream, not a live pixel mirror: a hot reload that changes a region sends only that region. Security. Language tooling (question 5) LSP is JSON-RPC over stdio with Content-Length framing [M]; DAP has the same base framing, with single-session (stdio) and multi-session (port) modes, and requests initialize, launch/attach, setBreakpoints, continue/next/stepIn/stepOut, threads, stackTrace, scopes, variables [W: microsoft.github.io/debug-adapter-protocol/overview]. Both servers run in the box (rust-analyzer, gopls, pyright, typescript-language-server, lldb-dap or debugpy, delve). Our editor is the client. The host service lsp starts a server in the box through term -like exec (no pty, plain pipes), owns the JSON framing, and gives the guest a reduced set: didOpen/didChange (full text or ranges), diagnostics ( publishDiagnostics flattened to DIAG file line col sev msg ), hover text, completion list (top 20), go-to-definition (file and position), symbols. Semantic tokens and code actions come later. That keeps JSON parsing out of HolyC. DAP is the same pattern: dap start , breakpoints set from the editor gutter, stopped events become a status line plus stack and variables lists. A terminal debugger (gdb, lldb, pdb) in the Dev Box terminal is the day-one fallback. Test and build panels. exec (no pty) with line-parsed output ( path:line:col: message ) produces a clickable problems list; cargo test , go test , pytest , npm test all fit. devcontainer.json. The spec's main properties: image or build.dockerfile , features (ids like ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/node:1 ), forwardPorts , postCreateCommand (string, array or object of parallel commands), mounts , and tool-specific customizations [W: containers.dev/implementors/spec]. Support a subset: image , build , features (from an allow-list of pinned ids), forwardPorts , postCreateCommand , remoteUser , containerEnv . mounts entries outside /work are rejected. Implementation is the reference CLI ( @devcontainers/cli [M], Node) run in the box, not our own parser.
