x: Kamiji on the HolyC TempleOS desktop and on Aiwnios: study Date 2026-10-27, branch task/templeos-shell . Research only. Nothing was built, installed, downloaded or pulled; no LFS command was used (sizes are file sizes on disk). The only code run was a 15-line Python script that reads GLB headers. Labels: [V] read in a file or measured today. [R] measured in our earlier notes. [E] my estimate from measured numbers. [I] inference or memory. Effort: S under a day, M a week, L a month. 1. What Kamiji is 1.1 Answer Kamiji is a family . I infer the Projects entry "Kamiji: Rigged 3D hand avatars and the characters around them" means the characters : a rigged cartoon hand with a morph-target face, the Kamikin "mochi" friends and the Rubbernose cast built with the same toolchain. Confidence about 85 percent. "Kamiji UI" is separate : the Longformer lf-* component kit that Kamiji's prototype folder carries (section 4). The game repos are ancestors, not the product. Why: apps/os-styles/projects.json has three character rows (Kamiji, Kamikin, Hands) and one game row (Kamae, prototype); no row is called "Kamiji UI" [V]. The kamiji README opens "A rigged, expressive 3D hand avatar for React, built on three.js" [V]. 1.2 Repo map (under /Users/paulbloch/Documents/github/ ) Repo What Stack Commits kamiji The product : KamijiAvatar React library, a framework-free <kamiji-avatar> element, a status/mood protocol, MCP/ACP/VS Code/JetBrains integrations, site, Blender build scripts, GLBs, prototypes/ui-port TypeScript, three.js 0.186.1, Vite 8, vitest; Python for Blender 90 kamiji-demo , kamiji-game Tamagotchi pet device (Electron) and Lovable RPG, 2D ancestors TS, Vite 0 and 5 kamiji-rig Original 2D SVG face rig; merged into kamiji/legacy/ TS, Vite 2 kamae Browser fencing duel game with its own rules, server and 8x5x7 sprite sheets; not a character project JS, drizzle/D1 40 kechimyaku-lineage-nexus Religious lineage database; unrelated , no kamiji string [V grep] React, Neo4j 3 kosmos-engine Holds a copy of the hand ( assets/models/kamiji/ , 2,359,916 bytes) and the Kamikin mochi source arrays ( assets/kamikin/mochi/ , 14 characters, 14 MB) Rust 2024, wgpu Grepping the engine for kamiji finds only docs, licences, apps/os-styles and our own docs. There is no Rust Kamiji runtime : poses, expressions and motion are TypeScript in the kamiji repo ( kamiji-pose-tween.ts , kamiji-expressions.ts , kamiji-motion.ts ) [V]. The engine's kosmos-model/src/hands.rs targets Mixamo-style bones ( mixamorig:LeftHandIndex1..4 ); Kamiji's skeleton is Root > Palm > {Thumb,Index,Middle,Ring,Pinky}_1..3 plus Face [V]. The engine does consume mochi data ( mochi_import.rs , skinned body, face, baked motions) and any GLB ( gltf_import.rs , kosmos-app --glb , with --clip , --at , --screenshot [V main.rs:22 ]). docs/plans/kamikin-port.md covers the Kamikin game and toon look in kosmos-app . 1.3 The assets From a script that reads the GLB JSON chunk ( .../scratchpad/kamiji/glbinfo.py ) [V]: Asset Size Verts Tris Joints Morphs Clips kamiji.glb hand + face 2.36 MB 27,437 (hand 26,452) 43,514 (hand 41,744) 18 face 22, hand 2 ( shapeSphere , shapeCube ) Idle, Wave, Think, Celebrate (2 to 3 s) mochi/kamikin-pip.glb 634 KB 5,526 10,818 15 none idle, walk, run, hop, happy, wave, sad, sit, dance mochi/kamikin-chochin.glb 1.39 MB 16,069 31,946 8 none same nine mochi/kamikin-hana.glb 721 KB 6,744 12,402 14 none same nine rubbernose-rubby.glb 1.54 MB 8,985 17,386 46 10 idle, strut, run, wave, charleston, cheer, point, shrug, thumbs-up The kamiji repo holds 265 GLBs, 50 MB (rubbernose 25 MB for 16 characters, mochi 11 MB, props 11 MB). Mochi faces are six embedded PNGs mapped by extras.kamiji.faceStates . The 14 hand poses ( open fist point peace thumbsUp rock three one two four five ok thumbsDown callMe ) are curl tables in TypeScript, not in the GLB ; so are the eight expressions, 15 emotes and three shapes [V]. Rendering is cel shading with an inverted-hull ink outline and flat bands [V kamiji-toon.ts ]. That is flat colour in a few tones, a good match for a 16-colour palette and a small software rasteriser. 1.4 Licences [V kamiji/LICENSE.md , assets/PROVENANCE.md ] Code: MIT. Characters and assets: CC BY-NC 4.0 with credit "Kamiji by Paul Bloch"; for-profit use needs a paid Premium Licence. "Kamiji" and "Kamikin" are trademarks. The licence itself lists open items: the hand's base mesh came from Meshy AI and its terms "must permit the licences above before any public release"; Kamikin provenance rows say TODO; twelve mochi exports are git-ignored until cleared. Treat all of it as local use only until the owner clears provenance. 1.5 How it connects to Kosmos and agents The GLB is copied into the engine; kamiji/tools/mochi-export/export.mjs turns engine mochi folders into GLBs. The control surface is small and suits us. Protocol v1 is one JSON object, {"v":1,"agent":"hermes-1","status":"running","mood":"thinking","color":"#4aa8ff","emote":"sparkle","ttl":5000} , with statuses idle running paused waiting finished error stuck , eight moods, 15 emotes, a JSON Schema and a mapping table. integrations/mcp/server.js exposes it over stdio to a loopback bridge; its README says it works end to end in headless Chrome with SwiftShader WebGL [V]. A desktop Characters app can take the same message over our hub in under 200 bytes. The engine's own MCP surface ( scene_load , sim_step , screenshot , hashes) addresses scenes, not Kamiji state, and agent-native.md still lists headless screenshot as a gap [V]. 2. The characters in the OS Goal: a window showing a skinned character or hand with clips, poses, expressions, pointer interaction and a screenshot, on x86 TempleOS under QEMU and on Aiwnios, from one HolyC source. 2.1 Viewport and Scene today [V desk3/03-apps.HC ] Viewport (app 1, lines 38 to 69): 8 cube vertices, 12 edges, F64 Sin/Cos , perspective divide, Line() . Two cubes and a label. No mesh loader, depth, fill or input. Scene (app 3, lines 80 to 96): static text and a tick counter. No state link. Dispatch is AppBody ; NA is 16 and ids 14 and 15 are Weather and Music, so a new app needs NA raised [V 01-core.HC:26 ]. Other agents have uncommitted edits in 01-core.HC , 02-ui.HC , 03-apps.HC , 04-main.HC ; follow the Clock-suite pattern: new files plus one-line hooks. Available: Line , RRFill , Disk , Copy32 , clip rectangles, a 32-bit framebuffer, boot-image assets ( KSICONS.BIN , KSFONT2.BIN ), the style editors [V]. 2.2 Cost model Measured numbers from holyc-improvement-analysis.md [R]: simple integer op 1 to 2 ns; call 9 to 12 ns; pixel by pointer walk 3 ns; F64 on x87 67 ns per multiply-add ; 16.16 fixed point 2 ns. The brief's "30 ns per op" matches neither integers (1 to 3) nor F64 (67); I use measured values and show a 30 ns pessimistic case. Aiwnios: window drag costs 1.5 ms there against 5.7 ms on QEMU, about 4x [R aiwnios/README.md ]. I found no repo evidence for 40 to 60x; I assume 4x to 10x for compute [E]. Aiwnios has no inline asm, U64 multiply truncates to 32 bits, F64 is IEEE not x87; only fixed-point integer maths gives identical pixels on both builds [R]. Unit costs, x86 TCG, fixed point [E]: vertex (two-bone skin, project, 2 divides) 150 ns; triangle (cull, edge setup, 3 calls) 300 ns; pixel (flat span, z compare) 5 ns, 8 ns with three-band shade. Scene Compute x1 With 3x margin At 30 ns/op (about 15x) Hand decimated to 1,500 tris, 800 verts, 140x140 px 0.7 ms 2 ms 30 ms (30 fps) Pip decimated to 3,000 tris, 192x192 1.6 ms 5 ms 70 ms (14 fps) Pip as exported, 10,818 tris, 256x256 4.5 ms 14 ms (40 fps) 200 ms Hand as exported, 41,744 tris 17 ms 50 ms (20 fps) seconds Reading: on x86 the compute of a decimated character is small beside the desktop's own present cost (5.6 ms for a window drag [R]). The un-decimated hand is out of reach on x86, so every guest-drawn route needs decimated rigs. On Aiwnios the same code should be 4x to 10x cheaper, so a 10k-triangle mochi at 60 fps is plausible [E]. Palette: toon shading needs 3 or 4 tones per material, so 8 to 16 entries per character; tint becomes a palette swap at no per-pixel cost. 2.3 Routes R1. Host engine renders, guest shows tiles. kosmos-app --glb kamiji.glb --clip Wave --at T --screenshot out.png ( KOSMOS_SHOT_SIZE=WxH ) renders the real toon look [V]. The tile channel exists: apps-host/stream.py sends EA_TILE (x,y,w,h; enc 0 = 16-colour palette with RLE, two pixels a byte; enc 1 = RGB565 RLE) and takes EA_INPUT back, lockstep with an ACK per chunk [V]. - Bandwidth at 16 KB/s: a raw 256x256 4-bpp frame is 32 KB, 2 s. Toon frames are flat; I guess 4 to 8 KB after RLE [E], so 2 to 4 fps full frame, about 8 fps for a 128x128 dirty rect (2 KB). Our notes quote 47 KB/s, unreproduced, which triples that. Input round trip 100 to 250 ms. - Aiwnios: each host call is a KsExec process spawn ( hostlink-aiw.HC ) [V]. Better: the host rewrites a frame file in T:/kosmos and the guest reads it per frame; 8 KB for a 128x128 tile, no serial limit [I]. - Effort M (needs a kosmos-app build, a render daemon, glue). Fidelity highest. Not replay-hashed. Licence MIT OR Apache-2.0. R2. Host bake to sprite sheets the guest plays. Render turntables and clips offline (Blender is installed at /opt/homebrew/bin/blender , or kosmos-app --screenshot ), quantise to a 16-colour palette per sprite, pack KSCHAR.BIN , blit with palette-swap tint. - Sizes [E]: 96x96 at 4 bpp is 4.6 KB raw, about 1.5 KB RLE. Hand, 8 yaw x 14 poses = 112 sprites, about 170 KB, plus 8 expression decals. Pip, 3 clips x 12 frames x 8 yaw = 288 frames, about 430 KB. Boot image: free; channel at 16 KB/s: 10 s once. - Cost per frame: one blit. Interaction: choose state, rotate by sprite, play a clip; no free camera, no new pose mixes. Kamiji's own protocol is discrete states (mood, status, emote), which map one to one onto sprites. - Byte-identical on x86 and Aiwnios , trivially hashable. Effort S for the hand, M for a library. Derived art stays CC BY-NC. R3. Native skinned-mesh rasteriser in HolyC. Decimated rigs (hand about 1,500 tris, Pip about 3,000) in a compact binary (section 5), 16.16 fixed point, linear blend skinning with at most two bones per vertex, 16-bit z-buffer (painter's sort fails on overlapping fingers and hull outlines), flat or three-band toon shading, outline by drawing back faces pushed along the normal in ink colour (the trick in kamiji-toon.ts ), no texture mapping (face as vertex colour plus decal sprites). - Realistic: hand at 160x160, 30 to 60 fps on x86; Pip at 192x192, 25 to 40 fps on x86, 60 on Aiwnios [E]. Texturing about doubles the pixel term; skip it. - Free orbit camera, any pose blend, finger curls from the same tables as Kamiji, picking with an id buffer. Integer-only code is bit-identical on both builds and aiwnios/golden.py , kernel-test.py can check it [R]. - Effort L: rasteriser about 400 lines (M), skin and clip player (M), decimation and converter (M). Risks: no continue , 10 ns calls, locals not zeroed on Aiwnios; use kslint.py . R4. Engine sim/pose core as no_std in the guest. engine-on-templeos.md ran a Rust .BIN that matched host hashes at 25x slower [R], but for a hash and a float loop only; no engine crate was compiled for bare metal. Kamiji's pose logic is not in Rust, the engine hand rig is a different skeleton, and nothing here draws. Porting 14 curl tables to HolyC integers is cheaper. Aiwnios cannot load x86 .BIN s. Effort L, value low. R5. Aiwnios in-process C rasteriser. Register one native through PrsAddSymbol in aiwnios-sdl32.patch , as KsPresentRect and KsExec are [V]. A 43k-triangle hand at 60 fps is easy, but Aiwnios only. Effort M. Add after R3, as an optional power viewer. R6. Kamiji's web component in host Chromium, shown as tiles. <kamiji-avatar> needs only an import map for three.js, serves from loopback, and its MCP e2e already runs in headless Chrome with SwiftShader [V]. docs/web-apps.md routes WebGL through tiles and plans an appd web run runner (not built) [V]. The avatar is 64 to 128 px, so a dirty rect is about 1 to 2 KB [E]. Gives the real Kamiji (all expressions, emotes, poses, shapes, protocol) with no guest rendering. Latency 100 to 200 ms; serial limits motion on x86. Effort S to M once the runner exists. Three.js is MIT. 2.4 Ranking Rank Route Effort Perf Fidelity Interaction Parity Verdict 1 R2 bake S to M trivial engine toon look, fixed views state, rotate identical bytes first, and the permanent fallback 2 R3 HolyC rasteriser L 30 to 60 fps small window (x86 est.), faster on Aiwnios flat toon, decimated free camera, any pose identical product path; MVP in a week 3 R6 web component S to M 2 to 8 fps x86 serial the real Kamiji full, laggy same decoder best "real Kamiji" if the runner lands 4 R1 engine tiles M same limits highest full, laggy same decoder use as the baker; live later 5 R5 C ABI M native any full Aiwnios only optional 6 R4 no_std core L 25x slower none none x86 only skip 3. Proposed "Characters" app New file desk3/03m-characters.HC , id 16 ( NA to 17). - Left list: Kamiji hand, Pip, Hana, Kumo, Rubby. Centre viewport. Right inspector. - Controls: drag for yaw and pitch; 14 pose buttons; 8 expression buttons; clip list (Idle, Wave, Think, Celebrate; Pip's nine); tint (the style's seven accents plus Kamiji yellow #ffd23f ); emote chips; Screenshot writes a BMP to B:/ for the host to copy; hover makes the hand wave. - Milestones: M0 sprite player (R2); M1 rasteriser (R3) with sprites as fallback and as the test oracle (silhouette comparison); M2 a kamiji hub service speaking protocol v1 so an agent sets mood/status/emote over MCP, also feeding the status bar. - Reuses Viewport's Line and projection for a wireframe toggle, Scene's tick as the clip clock, HostLink for protocol messages (reply cap HL_MAXRX 12,000 bytes) [V]. 4. The Kamiji UI kit What exists [V]: - kamiji/prototypes/ui-port is a prototype pipeline : JSON-schema contracts, --lf-* tokens (light and dark), five Lit components ( lf-button , lf-badge , lf-card , lf-stat-card , lf-empty-state ) plus 39 icons, a conformance runner, a Rust adapter folder. Its README: "Not a release". The roadmap says licence "provisional MIT", IP clearance open. - apps/os-styles/kamiji-ui/ is our vendored copy with three local token patches and the note "local prototyping only: do not publish". Our docs already say "do not ship until cleared". - The tokens are Longformer 's. Our desk already has "Longformer light" and "Longformer dark" ( ks_sn in 01-core.HC ), and apps/os-styles/styles.css has nine styles. The values differ: styles.css accent #234184 , ui-port accent #3b6fe0 , desk3 slot 1 0x1F4FD8 . "Kamiji UI" is a third blue, not the one we ship. Mapping to desk3's 16 slots ( ink accent ok teal bad purple warn surface muted accent2 card border shadow dock amber page ): text-primary / secondary to ink/muted; accent / accent-hover to accent/accent2; success / danger / warning to ok/bad/warn; surface-1 / 2 / canvas to card/surface/page; border-default to border; radii 6/8/12/16 to ks_rad and WinStyle geometry. Missing: a toon "sticker" look (bold ink outline, #ffd23f , chubby corners) that the characters carry but the kit does not define [I: site CSS not audited]; hover, focus and dark states are not compared in the prototype; no table, tabs or dialog. Effort: S to add colours as a sixth row ( ks_pal , ks_sn , ks_kind , ks_rad , ks_glass , and every table sized by NS ; grep first, ks_wallp[NS] and icon defaults are among them). Cheaper and in line with the other agents' work: author it as data in the Window Style editor (geometry, title bar, nine colour schemes; Export writes a ws1 ... line and B:/WINSTYLE.TXT ) and the Icon Style editor, imported as a theme with no HolyC change [V window-style-editor.md , icon-style-editor.md ]. Components: lf-badge , lf-stat-card , lf-empty-state are about 40 lines each in HolyC [E]; the widget kit has button, toggle, radio, slider. Icons are Lucide (ISC) and Feather (MIT), already in KSICONS.BIN . Do not publish while the kit is "provisional". 5. Asset pipeline 5.1 Conversion Host tool scripts/kamiji_pack.py (Python 3, numpy and Pillow are present): 1. Read GLB JSON and BIN chunks: positions, normals, joints, weights, indices, inverse binds, node tree, animation samplers. 2. Decimate hand 41,744 to about 1,500 tris, Pip 10,818 to about 3,000, with Blender's Decimate modifier headless ( blender -b -P ) or quadric collapse; keep top two bone weights, renormalised to 8 bits. 3. Quantise positions to I16 in the bounding box; vertex colour to a palette index; no UVs. 4. Resample clips to 30 Hz; rotations as I16 quaternions; translation only for the root. 5. Face: eight expressions become 2D decals instead of 22 morph targets; hand shapeSphere/Cube become two baked vertex sets. 5.2 Format KMSH (little endian) text Copy u32 'KMSH' u16 version u16 flags u16 nVerts u16 nTris u8 nJoints u8 nPal u8 nClips u8 nMorph i16 bbox[6] u16 off_pal u16 off_vert u32 off_idx u32 off_bind u32 off_clips u32 off_end pal: nPal x (u8 r,g,b) vert: i16 x,y,z | u8 bone0,bone1 | u8 w0 | u8 colour (12 bytes padded) idx: nTris x (u16 a,b,c) bind: nJoints x (u8 parent, i16 t[3], i16 q[4]) clip: name[12] | u16 nFrames | u8 fps | nFrames x nJoints x i16 q[4] (+ root i16 t[3]) Budgets [E]: hand (800 verts, 1,500 tris, 18 joints, 4 clips x 60 frames) about 55 KB ; Pip (1,700 verts, 3,000 tris, 15 joints, 9 clips) about 70 KB ; a 14-character roster about 1 MB. Heap is a non-issue ( -m 1024M ; the desktop's 2880x1800 buffers are about 20.7 MB each [R]). Pip's six face PNGs (3 to 4 KB) become 64x64 decals at 8 colours, about 500 bytes each. 5.3 Getting it in Boot image (precedent KSICONS.BIN , KSFONT2.BIN , built by gen-icons.py , gen-font2.py ): no channel cost; best for the default hand and Pip (about 130 KB). Channel for the long tail: scripts/send-to-vm.sh file push; 70 KB takes about 5 s at 16 KB/s, 1.5 s at 47 KB/s. Hub replies cap at 12,000 bytes, so use the file push, not HostCall . Aiwnios : read from T:/kosmos/ , no channel. LFS: the engine tracks *.glb in LFS; assets/models is 252 MB, assets/human 612 MB, assets/kamikin 87 MB (mochi 14, planet 72). The kamiji repo's GLBs are plain files on disk. The packer reads from the kamiji repo and never touches LFS. 6. Phased plan with gates Day 1 prototype: R2 hand turntable Pick R2 over the Viewport wireframe , on evidence: (a) Viewport's F64 cubes already run, while wireframing a 41,744-triangle mesh needs decimation first, and that step pays off later in week 1 anyway; (b) a wireframe hand is not recognisably Kamiji, a tinted toon sprite is; (c) R2 has no frame-time risk and is byte-identical on both builds, which our golden tooling can check. scripts/kamiji_bake.py plus a Blender helper: blender -b -P ... on /Users/paulbloch/Documents/github/kamiji/assets/kamiji.glb ; 24 yaw views of Idle and 8 frames of Wave; 96x96, transparent, Workbench with flat light [I: untried; EEVEE may need a GPU]. Quantise to 16 colours (Pillow), RLE-pack into assets/KSCHAR.BIN using stream.py enc 0. desk3/03m-characters.HC : loader, SpriteBlit(x,y,id,tint) , drag-to-rotate, Idle/Wave buttons; hook as app 16. Test with scripts/snap.sh and screenshots to shots/characters-*.png ; Aiwnios via aiwnios/run-desk.sh ; hash both. Gate: smooth rotation by mouse on both builds, tint swap works, identical sprite decode, under 3 ms a frame. Approvals needed: running Blender (installed, no download), a new 120 KB binary, the NA raise and AppBody hook in shared files. No LFS, no cargo. Week 1 MVP: R3 on hand and Pip scripts/kamiji_pack.py and KMSH writer; desk3/03n-raster.HC (fixed-point rasteriser, z-buffer, skin, clip player); the app prefers the mesh and falls back to sprites; protocol v1 through the hub; screenshot button. Gate: hand at 30 fps or better and Pip at 25 fps or better on x86 QEMU in a 192x192 viewport; identical frame hash on x86 and Aiwnios for a scripted clip; kslint.py clean; silhouettes match the bake within tolerance. Three months All 14 mochi and the rubbernose cast from a character folder (manifest shape of applications-folder.md ), expression decals, emotes, the 14 poses as a data file ported from the TypeScript tables, hover reactions, the status-bar mood driven by agents over MCP, optional R6 or R1 live viewer on the web-app runner, a Kamiji theme imported through the style editors. Gate: owner sign-off on licences and provenance before anything leaves the machine. Risks Licence and provenance (Meshy, mochi) block any release; shared-file collisions with other agents; speeds are modelled, the day-one blit is the first real number; decimating a 26k-vertex chubby hand may lose fingers; headless Blender on macOS may need a GPU, with kosmos-app --screenshot (a cargo build, so approval) as fallback; avoid F64 in the rasteriser. 7. Verified versus inferred Verified: repo list, commit counts, stacks; GLB statistics; poses, expressions, emotes living in TypeScript; protocol v1 and MCP bridge as documented; licence texts and caveats; the vendored kit and its patches; desk3 style tables ( NS 5, NA 16); Viewport and Scene source; stream.py encodings; the PrsAddSymbol pattern; Blender, numpy, Pillow present; kosmos-app flags; HolyC micro-benchmarks as cited. Inferred or estimated: that Projects' "Kamiji" means the characters (85 percent); every rasteriser cost and frame rate; RLE sizes; Aiwnios 4x to 10x speed-up (the brief's 40 to 60x is in no repo doc); the Aiwnios frame-file route; headless Blender rendering; that the UI kit lacks a toon look (site CSS not read); 47 KB/s serial (reported) against the brief's 16 KB/s. Not examined: kamiji/site CSS, integrations/openclaw-os , longformer , core-design-library , the Kamikin game, prototypes/ui-port/rust .

t: Review of the HolyC-native apps plan
h: Review of the HolyC-native apps plan
x: Review of the HolyC-native apps plan Date 2026-10-27. Read-only review of docs/holyc-native-apps-plan.md (the plan), docs/core-apps-plan.md , docs/os-foundation-plan.md , the two research reports, desk3/01-core.HC to desk3/05-run.HC , spike/KsSpike.HC and scripts/ . Nothing was built or run. Line numbers are of the files as of today. Evidence labels: [V] verified by reading a local file or a primary source fetched today (URL given), [D] reported by documentation or a project README fetched today, [U] unverified (reasoning, memory or arithmetic; treat as a hypothesis). Every speed estimate is [U] unless it cites a measurement. 0. Verdict The plan is a good list of apps and an honest list of gaps , but it is sequenced as an application project when the real risks are in the platform underneath it. Four things are wrong or missing at the root: It solves persistence and file exchange with a bridge that does not need to exist. TempleOS installs itself to a hard drive ( scripts/boot-vm.sh:17 answers "n" to "Install onto hard drive?" [V]). Attach a disk and say yes: notes, settings, bookmarks and the whole dev loop survive reboots, with no channel, no daemon and no protocol. The channel is still wanted for fetch and host services, but it drops from "gate 1, everything depends on it" to "one service among several". It builds the app framework and widget kit before fixing the renderer's cost structure , and the renderer is where every later gate ("render legibly at 2x", editors, a browser page) will hit the wall. The measured 23 to 25 ms per dragged window at 2880x1800 is not the emulator's floor; it is the sum of four fixable things inside 01-core.HC (a bytewise MemCpy , a per-pixel shadow, per-pixel function calls, x87 maths in pixel loops). The cheapest single win in the whole project is replacing TempleOS's MemCpy , which is REP_MOVSB [V], with an 8 or 16 byte per iteration copy: under TCG every rep movsb iteration is one byte. It writes "native" apps against a shell that is a demo, not a framework : fixed NA=9 windows, one window per app, if (a==...) chains in three places, a 500-entry hit list that silently drops entries, no clip stack, no key-up or modifier handling, Esc reboots the desktop, and every dirty rectangle re-executes every app's draw code. The plan knows some of this ("App framework", "Widget kit v2") but underestimates it as M and does not list the event model, clipping, Unicode, threading or memory items at all. It does not say what "a complete operating system that runs and looks like a modern OS" means for TempleOS V5.03, which cannot display this desktop on real hardware at all (the mode set uses QEMU's Bochs VBE ports 0x1CE/0x1CF , desk3/04-main.HC:9-13 , spike/KsSpike.HC:9-13 [V]; V5.03 itself is 640x480 16-colour VGA). If the Temple family stays the base, the base should be ZealOS (variable-resolution 32-bit VBE, AHCI, a networking stack in development, UEFI via Limine, public domain [D]), not V5.03. Recommendation on the base: keep the HolyC desktop as the showpiece and personality , do the renderer pass and the five native apps that TempleOS does well (editor, code editor with Run, terminal, notes, reader-mode browser over a host fetch service), and treat the "complete modern OS" goal as the Linux-plus-own-Wayland-shell track already written up in os-foundation-plan.md , with the HolyC desktop running inside it as one window. The conditions that would change that are in section 3.12. 1. Critique of the plan 1.1 Wrong or shaky assumptions # Plan statement What the evidence says Consequence A1 "Persistence: host file service over the channel" (plan line 23); README: "the live CD has no writable disk" The ISO offers an install to disk at boot and the script declines it ( scripts/boot-vm.sh:17 [V]). TempleOS has an ATA driver and the RedSea file system; an installed system keeps C: / D: across reboots. Persistence is a QEMU flag ( -drive file=temple.qcow2,if=ide ) and a "y", not a channel gate. A host-side RedSea reader (the format is flat: a free bitmap and 64-byte directory entries, Kernel/BlkDev/FileSysRedSea.HC [U, from memory of the source]) also gives file exchange both ways without a protocol. A2 "the lockstep serial loader moves about 1.4 to 2.7 KB/s" is treated as a property of serial The loader acks every 32 bytes over a TCP round trip and sleeps 3 to 4 s per file ( scripts/serial-send.py:13-18 , scripts/send-to-vm.sh:27 [V]). It is a protocol artifact. The 50 KB/s gate is probably easy; it is still the wrong channel for anything but control text (section 3.2). A3 Channel option (b) "a second IDE disk used as a mailbox ... verify raw block access" Right instinct, under-weighted. TempleOS already drives ATA ( Kernel/BlkDev/ listing [V]: it exists; raw BlkRead / BlkWrite on a mounted drive [U]). Both QEMU and a host writer go through the same macOS page cache, so host writes are visible to the next guest read without special cache modes [U]. This is the best zero-driver bulk channel on this QEMU: a few MB/s with PIO, no shared-memory unknowns. Put it ahead of serial streaming for bulk data. A4 "TempleOS has none of it [networking]" True for V5.03. But Shrine has a native TCP/IP stack with a PCnet-PCI II driver, Wget and a package manager (experimental) [D]; ZealOS lists "network card drivers and a networking stack" as in development [D]. All public domain. The "native network stack" track (plan step 8) should start from that code, not from zero. TLS remains nowhere. A5 "the mouse, keyboard and clipboard paths are still hacks ... no key-up, no non-ASCII" The code masks the scan code to 8 bits ( 04-main.HC:267 ), discarding the flag bits TempleOS puts above bit 8 ( SCF_SHIFT , SCF_CTRL , SCF_ALT ; key-up is SCF_KEY_UP , and kbd.down_bitmap holds held keys) [U, from memory of Kernel/KeyDev.HC and KernelA.HH ; verify in the VM]. Modifiers and key-up are probably available today without a kernel change; add them to the framework spike. Non-ASCII stays a real gap (8-bit kernel, Txt handles 32 to 126 only, 01-core.HC:399,420 [V]). A6 "Paint: already largely exists" (browser table) Paint exists for ASCII text in four sizes of one face at two scales, with no clipping other than the dirty rectangle, no scrolling and no images. Paint for a browser is M to L, not "exists": clip stack, scroll offset, image blit with scaling, underline, selection highlight, many fonts. A7 Browser B1 "3 to 5 weeks ... Wikipedia, MDN, a blog, HN, a GitHub README lay out without overlap" MDN and GitHub use CSS grid and flexbox throughout, web fonts, SVG icons and Unicode; Wikipedia needs Unicode and tables. The plan's CSS list has "simple flexbox" only and the font plan is ASCII. B1 is 2 to 3 times the estimate for one person, and the 20-page gate will drive weeks of CSS. Keep the gate but choose pages by what the engine will support (HN, plain blogs, docs sites, our own docs) and make MDN/GitHub stretch goals. A8 "JavaScript: later a small ES5-class interpreter" Even ES5 plus a DOM would not render modern sites; the plan says so. Say "no JavaScript, ever, in the guest" and keep the "display list from a host browser" as the only escape. It avoids an XL item nobody will finish. A9 "A full-screen copy is about 7 ms" is read as the bus limit MemCpy is REP_MOVSB ( Kernel/KUtils.HC [V], fetched today); QEMU's TCG translates a rep movs as one element per loop iteration [U]. 0.5 to 0.75 GB/s is what a byte-at-a-time loop costs under TCG, not what the emulated memory can do. Expect 3 to 8x on every copy from a 30-line assembly routine (section 2). A10 Frame cap 60 ( ks_fcap=60 , 01-core.HC:58 ) QEMU's GUI refresh interval is 30 ms by default ( GUI_REFRESH_INTERVAL_DEFAULT 30 , include/ui/console.h [V]). Nothing above about 33 fps is visible in the QEMU window. Cap at 30 and spend the budget on quality, or on sleeping. 1.2 Missing work Unicode and text. The kernel is 8-bit, the atlas is ASCII, TW and Txt skip anything outside 32 to 126. A browser, an email client and a messenger are mostly non-ASCII text in practice (names, quotes, dashes, accents, emoji). The plan's font row says "non-Latin" once and gives no path. See 3.3. Clipping and scrolling. The only clip is the dirty rectangle ( ks_c0x..ks_c1y , 01-core.HC:36 ). Apps keep content inside windows by arithmetic ( rows in Notes, FROWS in Files). A scroll view, a text field, a list and a browser viewport all need a push/pop clip stack intersected with the dirty rectangle. Not listed. Event model. Clicks are dispatched by numeric id ranges ( 04-main.HC:148-204,218-261 ), keys by FrontOpen index ( :315-361 ), hover by a global ks_hot . There is no event struct, no capture/bubble, no focus object, no double-click, no right button (only ms.lb is read, :378 ), no key repeat policy. The plan's "app table with draw, click, key, close" is the right shape but is listed as M; with text fields, drag and drop, menus and modal sheets it is L. Threading. Everything runs in one task; Draw blocks input; the idle loop sleeps 5 ms ( 05-run.HC:123 ). A fetch, a page parse or a file copy will freeze the desktop. TempleOS Spawn takes a target_cpu ( Kernel/KTask.HC [V]) and tasks share one address space, so a worker per core is cheap. Not mentioned anywhere in the plan. Memory. At 2x the desktop holds ten wallpapers of 20.7 MB plus bb and prev (about 250 MB of the 1 GB in boot-vm.sh:14 ) [V, arithmetic from 01-core.HC:35,655-656 and 04-main.HC:103-104 ], icon masks cached per size forever ( ks_icm , 01-core.HC:514,571 ), and no budget for window layers, glyph caches, images or page DOMs. No -m increase, no eviction policy. Failure. TempleOS is ring 0 with one address space: a stray pointer in any app takes the desktop and the OS with it. HolyC has try / catch (used in 03-apps.HC:271-275 ), which is the only tool. The plan has no crash policy (auto-restart the desktop task? reboot to a snapshot?). For an OS that runs an AI agent and a browser against untrusted input this is the first security fact, and it is absent. Testing. scripts/snap.sh and the monitor socket exist [V]; there is no golden-screenshot test, no frame-time regression check, no per-commit boot. The browser gate ("20 pages lay out") needs exactly this harness. Real hardware. Nothing in the plan says where the OS eventually runs. V5.03 plus this desktop cannot display outside QEMU (A4, verdict point 4). 1.3 Sequencing The plan's order is channel, framework, services, browser B0, B1, editors, mail, network. Better: Install to disk (hours). Removes the persistence gate. Measurement harness and renderer performance pass (1 week, section 2). Every later item is cheaper to build against a renderer whose costs are known and whose primitives will not change under it. Framework, event model, clip stack, input fix (modifiers, key-up, Esc no longer quits), widget kit v2 (3 weeks, not 2). Text: host-built atlases for more ranges, sizes and weights; glyph cache by (face, size, codepoint); UTF-8 strings throughout (1 week). This is the first thing that makes the editor, the browser and mail possible. Channel: raw-disk mailbox for bulk, serial for control (3 days), host service v0 (file exchange, fetch). Browser B0 (reader mode) and the editor family. B1 only after a B0 user test, with the page set chosen to fit. 1.4 Is desk3 a sound base? Code audit Keep: the logical/native unit split ( 01-core.HC:31-36,331-367 ), clipped spans and the corner coverage table ( :130-176 ), the dirty-rectangle loop ( 02-ui.HC:24-71 , 05-run.HC:28-54 ), immediate-mode widgets with hit registration ( 02-ui.HC:117-177 ), the Lucide stroke rasteriser with a per-size cache ( 01-core.HC:530-597 ), the per-phase timers for Monitor ( 05-run.HC:5-25 ). These are good ideas done simply. Redesign now (cheaper now than after six apps are written against them): Item Where Problem Change App = window = array slot 02-ui.HC:4-15 , NA at 01-core.HC:26 One window per app, fixed size, nine of them; ToFront copies arrays ( 04-main.HC:28-41 ) A window table (id, app, rect, z, flags, layer bitmap) and an app table of function pointers; HolyC has function pointers ( Spawn takes one). Dispatch by if-chain 03-apps.HC:585-597 , 04-main.HC:148-204 , :315-361 Three places to edit per app; keyboard rules differ per app app->draw/click/key/wheel/close through the table; one focus rule. Draw re-runs per dirty rect 05-run.HC:33-36 Ten rects means ten full passes over every window's draw code; text and icon loops run and get clipped per glyph Per-window retained layers (section 2.4): a dirty rect becomes a composite of overlapping layers, and only the window whose content changed re-executes its draw. Hit list 02-ui.HC:74,94 MAXH 500 , silently dropped when full; linear scan per hover; rebuilt only inside the first dirty rect's draw ( ks_reg set at 05-run.HC:32 , cleared at :50 ) by accident of ordering Per-window hit lists owned by the layer, invalidated with the layer; Hit reports overflow in Monitor. Clip 01-core.HC:36 One rectangle, equals the dirty rect ClipPush(x,y,w,h) / ClipPop intersecting with the current clip; scroll offset in the window's draw context. Text 01-core.HC:369-489 ASCII only; Wrap is O(n^2) (calls TW on the growing buffer per character, :475 ) with a 200-byte buffer; Notes re-lays out the whole buffer every frame ( 03-apps.HC:422-449 ) and every 500 ms for the caret blink ( 05-run.HC:109-113 ) UTF-8 decode; glyph cache keyed by face, size, codepoint; a line-layout cache per paragraph; the caret blink dirties a 2 by 17 rectangle, not the body. Keyboard 04-main.HC:319-321,267 Esc and Shift-Esc reboot; flag bits masked off; no key-up; no repeat policy Esc is an app key; a system chord (Ctrl-Alt-Q) quits; keep sc whole and expose modifiers; read kbd.down_bitmap for key-up if it exists [U]. Mouse 04-main.HC:367-378 Relative deltas times 3 times scale, re-centred with MsSet ; no right or middle button; wheel from ms.pos.z Keep the relative scheme (it works) but add acceleration curves and read ms.rb / ms.mb [U, field names from memory]. Absolute positioning needs a tablet device, which needs USB, which TempleOS lacks. Shadow 01-core.HC:287-329 Per-pixel Px call with a table lookup over the whole blur band, per window, per dirty rect 9-slice cache keyed by (w,h,r,blur) and span blends with constant alpha on the straight edges (section 2.3). Blend 01-core.HC:60-65,85-92 Mix is a function call per pixel from Px , RRTexN , Txt , LIcon , Up4 , BuildWall Inline the two-multiply blend; precompute src*a per span; a 16-entry table per glyph colour for the 4-bit alpha. Floating point in pixel loops DiskN :235-246 (a Sqrt per pixel), LineN :248-272 , SegMask :530-552 HolyC F64 is x87 ( Compiler/OpCodes.DD has FLD/FADD/FSQRT and no SSE [V]); TCG emulates x87 in software Integer coverage tables for disks (like CornerTab ), DDA in fixed point for lines; icons are already cached so SegMask only pays once per size. Memory 01-core.HC:649-717 , 04-main.HC:90-121 Wallpapers never evicted; no budget Keep one style's wallpaper, rebuild on switch (0.3 s today, less after the pass); raise -m . The verdict on the base: the primitives are fine, the shell structure is a demo. Do the redesign in the framework step, before the editor, because the editor is the first app that needs clipping, focus, modifiers, UTF-8 and a line cache, and it will otherwise be written around the demo's limits and then rewritten. 2. Performance 2.1 Where the time goes today (reasoning from the code and the measured numbers) 64000 pixel loop in 1 ms ( spike/KsSpike.HC:67-71 , README) is 15.6 ns per back[j]=back[j]+0x010101 . HolyC keeps j in memory and emits about ten instructions for that statement [U]; TCG on Apple Silicon runs a translated guest instruction in roughly 1 to 2 ns [U]. So the cost is HolyC's code generation times TCG, not TCG alone: a register-resident assembly loop should do the same in 3 to 5 ns per pixel, and a 16-byte SSE2 move in about 1 ns per pixel if the assembler had SSE (it does not [V]; 64-bit MOV pairs then, two pixels per instruction). A full 1280x800x4 copy in 7 ms is 0.59 GB/s, consistent with one translated loop iteration per byte ( REP_MOVSB [V]). A dragged window at 2x (23 ms): per dirty rect (two per move, each about the window plus 88x90 logical of shadow margin, 02-ui.HC:68-71 ), Draw copies the wallpaper span by span ( 05-run.HC:7-8 , MemCpy per row), then for every open window draws the shadow band (a 560x400 window at 2x with blur 68 native is about 280k Px calls [U, arithmetic]), the rounded fill, the ring, the app body, then the menubar backdrop and the dock. Estimate for one window: shadow 8 to 12 ms, body and fill 4 to 6 ms, copies 4 to 6 ms, the rest 2 ms. The shadow and the byte copies are the two biggest items. 2.2 Ranked wins Rank Change Estimated gain Reasoning Cheapest experiment 1 Run on x86 with hardware virtualisation (a Linux PC or server with KVM, an Intel Mac with HVF, or a bare-metal cloud instance). Apple Silicon cannot accelerate an x86 guest (HVF is same-architecture only; Rosetta does not apply to system emulation). 10 to 20x on HolyC code, 10 to 30x on copies; a 2x frame drag from 23 ms to 1 to 2 ms; the 20.7 MB full-frame copy from about 35 ms [U, extrapolated from 0.59 GB/s] to 2 ms TCG costs 10 to 30 host instructions per guest instruction and software MMU on every load and store; KVM runs the guest natively Copy spike/KsSpike.HC to any x86 Linux box, qemu-system-x86_64 -accel kvm , read the three numbers. One hour plus access to a machine. A cheap mini PC or a used Intel Mac is the development-host answer if the HolyC route continues. 2 Replace MemCpy / MemSetU32 with 64-bit, unrolled assembly ( REP_MOVSQ at least; an 8-way unrolled MOV loop better). Kernel/KUtils.HC uses REP_MOVSB and REP_STOSD [V]. 3 to 8x on every copy and fill: card copy, wallpaper spans, layer composites, prev snapshot in SetStyle TCG executes string instructions one element per iteration [U]; 8 bytes per iteration is 8x fewer iterations; an unrolled plain loop avoids the per-iteration flag and counter work 30 lines of HolyC asm in the spike; time 100 copies of 4 MB with each variant. Half a day. Caveat: QEMU may have grown a bulk fast path for rep movs in recent versions [U]; the measurement settles it. 3 9-slice shadow cache. Alpha of the shadow depends only on (w,h,r,blur), so cache four corner tiles and two edge profiles; blend straight edges with a per-row or per-column constant alpha span. Shadow cost from about 10 ms to 2 ms per 2x window Replaces 280k Px calls (bounds check, function call, Mix call) with table reads and span loops Set ks_focus shadow strength to 0 and Shadow to a no-op, read ks_pt[1] in Monitor before and after; that is the upper bound. Then implement. One day. 4 Retained window layers and tile damage. Each window draws into its own bitmap (stride-aware), re-executed only when its content changes; a frame is composite-by-copy of the layers that touch each dirty tile (32x32 tiles with per-tile dirty bits instead of 10 merged rects, 02-ui.HC:25-55 ). Drag, raise, focus animation and overlaps become copies: with win 2, about 3 to 5 ms for a 2x window; text-heavy windows stop re-rasterising their text on every neighbour's change Separates "content changed" from "position changed"; the browser's scroll becomes a memmove plus one strip Prototype on one window (Notes): draw it to a side bitmap, composite with a stride-aware SpanCopy . Two days. 5 No function calls or x87 in pixel loops. Inline blend in Px -callers, premultiplied source per span, 16-entry alpha tables for glyph blending, integer disks and lines. 1.5 to 2x on corners, glyphs, icons, disks; the dock's disks and radios lose their per-pixel Sqrt HolyC function calls push a frame and pass arguments on the stack; x87 under TCG is software floating point Time DiskN with r=20 at 2x 1000 times, then with a coverage table. Half a day. 6 Multicore rasterisation. -smp 4 ; Spawn(fn,data,name,core) three workers; split the dirty tiles by row bands; the main task composites. MTTCG is supported and on by default for the i386 target in current QEMU ( target/i386/tcg/tcg-cpu.c : .mttcg_supported = true ; accel/tcg/tcg-all.c enables it when supported and not icount [V, master source; assume the same in 11.0.2 [U]]). 2 to 3x on the draw phase on a 4-core slice of this Mac; nothing on the single card copy unless split too Pixels are embarrassingly parallel; TempleOS tasks share memory so no marshalling -smp 4 , spawn three tasks that each fill a quarter of bb , time against one task. Half a day. Risk: TempleOS's own SMP code paths under MTTCG are lightly tested; a wrong result means stay single-core. 7 Frame pacing. Cap at 30 (QEMU refreshes the window every 30 ms [V]); only sleep when nothing is dirty; measure input-to-pixel latency not frame time. No speedup; removes wasted frames and makes animations even Frames that the display never shows cost CPU and heat Set ks_fcap=30 , watch Monitor. Minutes. 8 Cursor and drag latency. With layers, the two cursor rectangles are composites, not draws; keep the cursor in its own tiny layer; read the mouse at the top of the loop and composite last. Hover and drag feel: from "one full Draw of everything under 16x21 px" to two tile copies Latency is dominated by the frame, which win 4 shrinks Comes with win 4. 9 Memory bandwidth. 2x doubles pixel count and quadruples bytes per logical area; keep blurred backdrops at quarter resolution (already), evict unused wallpapers, keep layers only for open windows, and consider 1.5x logical scales for large displays. Frees about 200 MB; avoids swapping to a bigger -m for layers Arithmetic from 01-core.HC:655-656 -m 2048M and one wallpaper at a time. Minutes. 10 GPU path. This QEMU has virtio-gpu-pci without GL [V, task statement]. A virtio-gpu 2D driver in HolyC (virtqueue setup, RESOURCE_CREATE_2D , TRANSFER_TO_HOST_2D , SET_SCANOUT , RESOURCE_FLUSH ) is 500 to 1000 lines and gives a second way to put a guest-rasterised frame on screen, with explicit flush rectangles instead of dirty-page scanning. No drawing acceleration. virgl would require emitting a Gallium command stream from HolyC: not a project. About zero for rendering; maybe saves the host some dirty-page scanning All the cost is in the guest's rasterisation, which no 2D scanout device helps Do not do it. If the display path ever matters, measure the host-side cost of vga_update_display with perf on Linux first. Combined, wins 2 to 5 should bring a 2x window drag on this Mac from 23 ms to roughly 4 to 6 ms and a full-screen style crossfade from about 60 ms to about 15 ms [U]; win 1 makes the whole question go away and is the only one that gives headroom for a browser layout engine in HolyC. Win 6 is a multiplier on whatever remains. 2.3 Emulator configuration, briefly -accel tcg,thread=multi is the default when supported; no flag needed. -accel tcg,tb-size= larger translation cache helps only if the working set thrashes (unlikely at this code size) [U]. -cpu choice: keep a plain x86-64 model; AVX emulation exists but is slow and the assembler cannot emit it anyway. -display cocoa,zoom-to-fit=on scales 2880x1800 on the host each refresh; that is host time, not guest time. For measurement use -display none and screendump . QEMU 7.2 and later show TCG regressions for some x86 guests on Apple Silicon (a Windows 3.11 hang report, QEMU issue 2996 [D]); not our symptom, but pin the QEMU version used for measurements. 3. Better solutions by component 3.1 Display and input path Plan: keep the Bochs VBE framebuffer, fix input "in the framework step". Right for QEMU. Add: the layer compositor (2.2 win 4), a clip stack, a proper cursor layer, modifiers and key-up from the scan code flags and kbd.down_bitmap [U], right and middle buttons, and a system chord instead of Esc. For real hardware the display path must be a boot-time VBE mode set in the boot loader, which is what ZealOS did [D]; V5.03 cannot do it. 3.2 Host channel Plan: serial streaming spike, else an IDE mailbox, else a NIC. Better order: Installed disk for persistence (not a channel at all). Raw second disk as a mailbox for bulk bytes both ways: guest BlkRead / BlkWrite through the existing ATA driver on a -drive if=ide,format=raw file the host also opens. A 4 KB header with sequence numbers, then a ring of blocks. Expected several MB/s with PIO under TCG [U]; no driver, no shared-memory ordering questions, works on any QEMU and on real hardware with a USB-free ATA disk. Cheapest experiment: write 1 MB from the host, read it in the guest, compare hashes, time it. One day. Serial for control lines and events (it is duplex and already wired): stream with the FIFO, no acks, measure drops. Shared RAM ( memory-backend-file , share=on ) only if latency below 1 ms matters (a live viewport). Unproven under TCG on macOS, as the earlier report says. A virtio driver (serial or blk) later for interrupts and DMA; not first. 3.3 Fonts and text shaping Plan: port stb_truetype (about 5k lines) or keep host-built atlases. Better: host-built atlases now, a small rasteriser later, shaping never in the guest. Now: extend scripts/gen-font.py to emit a glyph index keyed by codepoint and more ranges (Latin-1, Latin Extended, Greek, Cyrillic, general punctuation, arrows, a monospace face, bold and italic), at the sizes a browser and editor use, plus a Noto Sans CJK subset if CJK is wanted (about 20k glyphs at two sizes is a few MB in 4-bit alpha). Add the kern pairs for the main face. This is days, not weeks, and covers email, chat and most of the document web. Later: a quadratic-outline scanline rasteriser in HolyC (TrueType glyf only, nonzero winding, 4x vertical oversampling, about 1500 lines) with an LRU glyph cache, for arbitrary sizes and web fonts. Under TCG a 24 px glyph rasterises in well under a millisecond [U]; cached, it does not matter. Shaping (ligatures, Arabic joining, Indic reordering), bidi and IME: do not write these in HolyC. If the OS ever needs them, the host service returns positioned glyph runs for a string (a "shape" request), which the guest paints with its cache. That keeps the guest honest about what it can do and matches the plan's own service model. 3.4 Web browser engine scope Plan: reader mode first, then HTML/CSS subset, then maybe JavaScript. Agree with reader mode first and with "document web" as the ceiling. Changes: Make B0 the product: reader mode plus a host-side HTML-to-display-list service for pages that reader mode mangles. A display list (text runs with font and colour, boxes, images, links with rectangles) painted natively is not screen capture; it is what the plan already names as the "clean fallback". With it, B1's layout engine becomes an optimisation, not a prerequisite for usefulness. B1 native layout: scope it as "block, inline, lists, tables, images, simple flex", with a conformance set chosen from pages that use only that. Drop "position basics" and "simple flexbox" from the first cut; add them after the page set passes. JavaScript: never in the guest (A8). Images: a host decode-and-resize service (the plan's option two) is right; PNG and JPEG decoders in HolyC are a later nicety. 3.5 Network and TLS Plan: host fetch service first, native stack optional. Right. For the native track, start from Shrine's stack (PCnet driver, TCP/IP, Wget [D]) or ZealOS's work, both public domain; write an E1000 or virtio-net driver against QEMU. TLS in HolyC (X25519, AES-GCM, SHA-256, certificate parsing, a root store) is months and will be slow under TCG; it is justified only on real hardware or KVM, and only if the OS is meant to be self-contained. Keep credentials on the host regardless. 3.6 Persistence and file systems Plan: host file service. Better: installed RedSea disk (3.2.1), plus a host RedSea tool to read and write the image when the VM is stopped and a mailbox file for live exchange. RedSea has no journaling, no permissions and no long-name hashing; fine for a single-user OS, not for a "complete OS" (section 4). 3.7 Audio Plan: host plays, guest controls (mpd/mpv). Right. A guest HDA or AC97 driver for QEMU ( -device intel-hda plus hda-duplex , or AC97 ) is a few hundred lines of ring-buffer DMA and would let the music player be genuinely native for decoded PCM; decoding MP3 or AAC in HolyC under TCG is too slow to be worth it (an MP3 frame decoder is around 10 million operations per second of audio [U]). Order: host playback now, an AC97 driver as a weekend spike later, decoding on the host always. 3.8 Apps SDK Plan: app table and widget kit. Add: a written contract (draw context with clip and scroll, event struct, focus, invalidation API, timers, a worker-task helper), a component gallery that doubles as the golden test, UTF-8 everywhere, and a size limit per app file so the single concatenated build ( scripts/send-to-vm.sh:14 [V]) stays fast to compile. HolyC's #include at run time already gives hot reload; use it: each app a file, reloadable without a desktop restart. 3.9 Packaging and updates Not in the plan. For the HolyC desktop: a manifest per app (name, icon, files, version), apps stored on the installed disk under one directory, an updater that pulls a package through the fetch service and verifies a hash. Shrine's Pkg is a public-domain reference [D]. Signatures need a hash and a signature verifier in HolyC (Ed25519 is about 1000 lines of C and runs fast enough once per package [U]). 3.10 AI agent integration Plan: host agent, approval for every write and command, native chat and diff panels. Right, and the only safe shape given ring 0. Add: the agent must never drive guest input directly without the "agent is driving" banner the earlier report proposed; all tool calls and their approvals logged on the host; the guest shows the exact command before approval. The engine's editor.* protocol and kosmos-mcp are the obvious transport once the channel exists. 3.11 Security and permissions In TempleOS there are none: no user separation, no memory protection, no sandbox, any app can read all memory and the whole disk. The plan's rule (nothing sent, deleted or purchased without a UI prompt) is therefore only as strong as the host daemon's enforcement of it. Write the permission broker on the host with per-app manifests, make the guest unable to reach the network or credentials by construction (it cannot), and treat anything the guest sends as untrusted input. Say this in the plan, because "security" for this OS is a host property. 3.12 The base OS question Option Can look modern Can run a modern browser, TLS, drivers, GPU Keeps the HolyC work Runs on real hardware Years to "complete OS" TempleOS V5.03 (today) yes, in QEMU no, by design (ring 0, no libc, no network, 8-bit text, BIOS only) all of it no (VGA only) not reachable ZealOS (fork; variable-resolution 32-bit VBE, AHCI, networking in development, UEFI via Limine, public domain [D]) yes, with a port of the renderer to its VBE path partly: network yes (later), TLS no, GPU no, protection no most (HolyC dialect is close [U]) yes [D] the "hobby OS" end state: a modern-looking single-address-space OS with native apps and a document web browser; 2 to 3 person-years for that, never a daily driver for web apps Linux base plus own Wayland shell ( os-foundation-plan.md ) yes yes, all of it exists the design, tokens, assets, app list; the HolyC desktop as a VM window or personality yes 1 to 2 person-years to a usable shell and store on an existing distribution; the OS underneath is already complete Modern host app embedding a HolyC runtime (a Rust or Swift app that runs TempleOS in QEMU or a HolyC interpreter as a "personality" with our shell around it) yes yes (host) all, as content it is an app, not an OS months; useful as the development vehicle and demo, not the goal Bare-metal Rust unikernel reusing the renderer design yes no, you write drivers, a network stack, TLS, a browser, a GPU stack from scratch (or pull in Rust crates like smoltcp, rustls, embedded-graphics) the design yes 3 to 5 person-years for parity with the ZealOS end state plus TLS; still no web platform Hybrid: Linux base, our shell, TempleOS VM as a first-class app with shared channel yes yes all yes as Linux base; the HolyC desktop keeps its showcase role Recommendation: hybrid . Keep the HolyC desktop as the showpiece on the Temple family (move to ZealOS when the showpiece should leave QEMU), finish the renderer pass and the native apps that fit (editor, code editor, terminal, notes, reader browser, calculator, files, settings, music control), and put the "complete OS" ambition on the Linux-base track, where the same shell design becomes a Wayland compositor and the HolyC desktop runs inside it as one window, with the host services the plan already needs. That gives the user the two things they asked for without pretending one base can do both. Conditions that change it: If the goal is really "a TempleOS that looks modern and runs on a PC" (an art and hobby OS, accepting no web apps, no TLS in the guest and no protection): go ZealOS, develop on x86 with KVM, skip the Linux track. If the user gets an x86 development host with KVM: the TCG penalty disappears and the HolyC native-app scope (including B1 layout) becomes comfortable; the base question is unchanged. If the user will accept a host app as the "OS" (a kiosk-style shell on macOS or Linux running the HolyC desktop and web apps side by side): the embedding option is the fastest path to a daily-driver feel, at the cost of not being an OS. 4. x: Improving HolyC on all of its deficits: analysis and ranked plan Written 2026-10-27. Evidence labels: [V] verified today (file and line in the TempleOS V5.03 source mirror, a measurement in a scratch VM, or a page opened today), [D] reported by documentation or a README, [U] unverified. Source paths are relative to the TempleOS mirror ( Compiler/ , Kernel/ , Adam/ , Doc/ ); line numbers are from the cia-foundation/TempleOS archive branch checked out in the scratchpad. Measurements were taken in a headless scratch QEMU (TCG, Apple Silicon, -m 1024M , TempleOS V5.03 live CD, no display); the raw outputs are in /tmp/tvm-lang/E1.out to E4.out and the test programs in the scratchpad ( lang-vm/files/E1.HC to E4.HC ). Verdict The compiler is not the 30x problem. Measured in the same VM, the blend loop costs 11 ns a pixel written the way the spike wrote it, 3 ns as a pointer walk, and 0.8 ns a pixel as two-pixels-a-pass HolyC with reg variables, against under 1 ns for the hand assembly . The TempleOS compiler already keeps locals in registers (RSI, RDI, R10 to R15, chosen by use count, Compiler/OptPass3.HC:512-560 [V]); the 30x figure came from a loop in a large function with more live locals than register slots, an index loop instead of a pointer walk, one pixel a pass instead of two, and (probably) a visible QEMU window. The real, measured deficits are elsewhere: x87 floating point under TCG is 11x slower than SSE2 (67 ns versus 6 ns per multiply-add) , a call costs 9 to 12 ns, there is no continue , the precedence table differs from C, faults are uncatchable, and tooling is a single in-OS compiler. Two things make the compiler far more fixable than expected, both verified today: The compiler rebuilds and hot-loads on the live CD in under three seconds : copy ::/Compiler and ::/Kernel to the RAM drive (157 ms), Cmp("B:/Compiler/Compiler") (2.36 s, 0 errors, 179 KB of code), Load(...) (51 ms), then re-resolve the kernel's 19 import sites with a 30-line HolyC relinker. The prompt then compiles with the patched compiler (a changed warning string proved it). No install, no ISO rebuild, no snapshot change. So family A (modify the in-OS compiler) is a daily-loop activity, not a project. The precedence table is runtime data ( cmp.binary_ops , Compiler/CInit.HC:286-310 , public extern CCmpGlbls cmp in Compiler/CompilerB.HH:13 [V]). Sixteen assignments switch the live compiler to C precedence, verified with a*b>>1 , a&b+c , a+b<<1 , a==b|1 ; sixteen more restore it. No rebuild. Recommended direction: keep HolyC as the language of the desktop, fix the compiler in place for the handful of things that matter (SSE2 for F64, continue , C precedence as an option, cheaper calls, a few peepholes), move only floating-point kernels and two or three blit loops to assembly (hand-written or NASM-assembled on the Mac and embedded as bytes), and build the tooling (lint, format, test, profiler) on the host against the compiler's own tables. Do not build an LLVM front end or a transpiler for this project: the measured gain over fixed HolyC is 2 to 4x on integer loops and the cost is the loss of the in-OS edit-and-run loop that the whole workflow is built on. Summary table Deficit Best fix Effort Expected gain Evidence 1 Slow generated code (a) Write hot loops as pointer walks, two pixels a pass, in small functions; (b) add SSE2 scalar F64 to the backend and enable CR4.OSFXSR; (c) three peepholes in OptPass789A / BackLib (drop the MOV R8,RAX echo, LEA-fold [RSI+R11*4] , keep F64 locals in XMM) S / L / M 3 to 14x on the blend from (a) alone, measured; 8 to 11x on F64 from (b), measured; about 1.5x more from (c), estimated E1, E2 2 Operator precedence Runtime switch of cmp.binary_ops to C precedence around our compile, plus a host lint that flags mixed & ^ \| << >> with + - * without parentheses S removes the bug class E2, CInit.HC 3 Missing features Add continue to PrsStmt.HC (loop parsers already carry lb_break ; add lb_continue ); host preprocessor for function-like macros; keep the rest as lint rules S (continue), M (macros) fewer gotos, fewer bugs PrsStmt.HC:1133 4 No memory safety Fault policy: replace Fault2 for the desktop task so a page fault throws into the desktop's try and the frame is dropped; guard pages are available ( MemPagAlloc plus the 4K lowest-2 MB mapping is the only 4K region, so true guard pages need a page-table edit); host-side bounds-check mode via a lint-inserted KsChk macro for debug builds M survives the common crash; does not protect the OS E4, KInts.HC:61-93 , KDbg.HC Fault2 5 Tiny ecosystem A host-built blob format (TempleOS .BIN with the IET_ patch table, Kernel/KLoad.HC ) and a 200-line libc shim; port stb_image and stb_truetype through C to HolyC by a transpiler is more work than writing them in HolyC-with-asm-kernels L PNG, JPEG, TrueType in the guest KLoad.HC , ABI section 6 Weak tooling Host lint and formatter driven by a HolyC parser written in Python (the lexer is simple, Compiler/Lex.HC ), a test runner that boots the snapshot and reads results over serial (already done for this report), a sampling profiler from a timer IRQ ( IntEntrySet ) writing Fs->rip histograms M catches the two bug classes that have bitten; measurable changes this report's harness 7 Portability Stay on x86 emulation for the showcase; Aiwnios is the only native aarch64 HolyC (JIT, Apple W^X handled) but it is 640x480 8-bit, no asm blocks on arm, no continue ; a port of desk3 is L to XL and loses the OS none now n/a Aiwnios source 8 Community Treat V5.03 as frozen upstream, keep our compiler patches as a small series against the mirror, borrow ZealOS's SSE enable ( KStart64.ZC:6-8 ), ignore the rest S low risk ZealOS 1. The compiler as it is (what the source says) Pipeline ( Compiler/Compiler.PRJ [V]): Lex to PrsExp / PrsStmt / PrsVar producing a reverse-Polish intermediate code (IC) list, then OptPass012 (constant folding, address-mode merging, the CALL,FS/GS,... patterns), OptPass3 (register-variable scoring and assignment), OptPass4 , OptPass5 , OptPass6 , then OptPass789A which emits x86-64 bytes through BackLib / BackA / BackB / BackC (integer) and BackFA / BackFB (x87). Terry's own description: "The compiler's parser makes RISC code which it optimizes to CISC" ( Doc/Charter.DD:75 [V]); the IC is "rev polish stack machine in nature" ( Doc/Glossary.DD:183 [V]). Register model ( OptPass3.HC:512-525 comment, Kernel/KernelA.HH:1801-1805 [V]): RAX, RBX, RCX, RDX, R8 are clobber scratch; RAX and R8 link IC nodes; R9 is the stack-machine temporary; RBP the frame; RSI, RDI, R10, R11, R14, R15 hold register variables; R12, R13 hold non-pointer register variables only. Variables are chosen by a use-count score with the address-taken ones excluded ( OptPass3.HC:535-560 ); reg / noreg only force or forbid ( REG_ALLOC , REG_NONE , KernelA.HH:1797-1798 ). Eight slots total; a function with more hot locals spills the rest to [RBP] . Functions containing try get no register variables at all ( PrsStmt.HC:852 , "TODO: Currently no reg vars in funs with try/catch" [V]). Options ( KernelA.HH:1546-1558 [V]): the only codegen options are OPTf_NO_REG_VAR , OPTf_GLBLS_ON_DATA_HEAP , OPTf_NO_BUILTIN_CONST and the half-implemented OPTf_USE_IMM64 . There is no optimisation level, no inlining, no loop pass, no CSE. PassTrace shows the IC per pass ( Doc/DbgOverview.DD:35 ). Floating point : all F64 goes through x87 ( BackFA.HC , BackFB.HC ); OpCodes.DD has FXSAVE , MOV_CR4_RAX and friends but no SSE arithmetic (plan-review already verified no MOVAPS , PADDB and so on). The kernel never sets CR4.OSFXSR ( Kernel/KStart64.HC:45-47 sets OR EAX,0xB0 : PAE, PSE, PGE only [V]), so SSE instructions fault with #UD until a program sets bit 9. The scheduler already does FXSAVE / FXRSTOR per task ( Kernel/Sched.HC:87,119 [V]), so XMM state survives task switches once SSE is on. ZealOS turns it on at boot ( BTS RAX,CR4f_OSFXSR , src/Kernel/KStart64.ZC:6-8 [V]). Calling convention ( PrsExp.HC:545-583 , OptPass789A.HC:323-330,398-416,698-704 , PrsStmt.HC:116-121 , KernelA.HH:577-586 [V]): every argument is a 64-bit PUSH , pushed so that argument 1 is at 16[RBP] ( SF_ARG1 ), CALL rel32 (or MOV RBX,imm64; CALL RBX for far targets), result in RAX (F64 as raw bits in RAX), callee pops with RET imm16 when Ff_RET1 is set (default for any non-variadic function with arguments; variadic functions use caller ADD RSP ). The prologue is PUSH RBP; MOV RBP,RSP; SUB RSP,n; PUSH <used reg vars> and the epilogue pops them, LEAVE , RET1 . Callee must preserve RBP, RSI, RDI, R10 to R15 ( Doc/GuideLines.DD:117 ). There is no stack alignment requirement and no red zone. Measured cost: 9 to 12 ns per call under TCG (E1/E2), five instructions ( PUSH; CALL; ...; LEAVE; RET1 ). Linking and loading ( Kernel/KLoad.HC [V]): a .BIN is a CBinFile header ( jmp , module_align_bits , 'TOSB' , org , patch_table_offset , file_size ; KernelA.HH:384-394 ), code, and a patch table of records {U8 type; U32 rip; U8 name[]; ...} with types IET_REL_I32 / IET_IMM_I64 imports, IET_*_EXPORT exports, IET_ABS_ADDR (add module base at each listed offset), IET_DATA_HEAP (allocate and add), IET_MAIN (call). Load() reads the file, allocates in the code heap (below 2 GB so CALL rel32 works, Doc/Glossary.DD:169 ), runs LoadPass1 (exports into Fs->hash_table , imports resolved by HashFind , which returns the newest entry because HashAdd inserts at the bucket head, KHashA.HC:169-189 [V]) and LoadPass2 ( IET_MAIN ). Unresolved imports are parked as HTT_IMPORT_SYS_SYM and fixed when a later module exports the name ( SysSymImportsResolve ). Reading of the BlendB body (E1 disassembly): the IC-to-CISC emitter produces the pattern MOV RAX,R13; IMUL R8; MOV R8,RAX; ADD RAX,R14; MOV R8,RAX; SAR R8,8 for (x*ia+srb)>>8 , that is two redundant MOV R8,RAX per subexpression and a one-operand IMUL that clobbers RDX; the mask constants are re-materialised each use ( MOV R8u32,0x00FF00FF twice per pixel). A hand version needs 14 instructions; the compiler emits 27. Under TCG, instruction count is roughly the cost, so the per-instruction codegen gap is about 2x, not 30x. Where the 30x came from (decomposition from the table): window open versus headless, about 3x [U, inferred from 31 versus 11]; 17 live locals forcing spills and an index loop, 11 to 3 (3.7x) [V]; one pixel a pass versus two with 64-bit loads, 3 to 0.8 (3.7x) [V]; residual codegen quality, about 1.0 to 1.3x on the final form [V]. Conclusion: rewrite the hot loops, do not rewrite the compiler, to get 90 percent of the gain ; the last 2x in integer code and the 10x in floating point are compiler work. 3. Family B: a host-side toolchain B.1 ABI facts a host compiler must match (all [V], section 1) Stack-passed 64-bit arguments, argument 1 at 16[RBP] , callee pops ( RET imm16 ) for fixed-arity functions, RAX result, RBP frame, callee-saved RBP/RSI/RDI/R10-R15, caller-saved RAX/RBX/RCX/RDX/R8/R9, no alignment, code below 2 GB, globals reached by RIP -relative or absolute 32-bit addressing. This is not System V, so clang / rustc output cannot be called directly; a shim is needed in one of two forms: Per-function trampolines written as HolyC asm blocks: load SF_ARGn[RBP] into RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9, align RSP to 16, CALL the SysV symbol, restore. About 12 instructions per entry point, generated by a script from the C prototypes. The callee must be built -ffreestanding -fno-builtin -mno-red-zone -fno-stack-protector -mcmodel=small -fPIC (or -mcmodel=kernel ) with no libc, no TLS, no unwinding, no SSE unless CR4.OSFXSR is set (set it; see A.2) and no x87 state assumptions. -mno-red-zone is required because TempleOS interrupts run on the current stack ( KInts.HC INT_FAULT and the timer handler save context in place). A HolyC-ABI target : patch the host compiler's calling convention. holyc-lang (section 8) emits text assembly and uses SysV; changing its backend to push-and- RET1 is a day of work in its emitter [U]. For LLVM there is no HolyC CC; adding one is XL and not worth it. Loading a host-built blob : emit a .BIN (header plus code plus patch table) from the host: the format is 40 bytes of header, raw code, and the IET_ records; imports of TempleOS functions become IET_REL_I32 records naming MAlloc , Free , MemCpy and so on; exports become IET_REL32_EXPORT ; relocations become IET_ABS_ADDR lists. Then Load("B:/KSBLOB") resolves and the functions are callable by name from HolyC after an extern declaration (or by _extern to an exported label). A Python writer for this is S. Simpler still for kernels with no relocations: send the raw bytes over serial, MAlloc from Fs->code_heap , copy, and call through a function pointer; that works today with no format at all. Family C: dialect and tooling on the host (no OS change) What the host can do with the compiler's own tables: Precedence lint (S) : a token-level checker (lex rules from Lex.HC : identifiers, numbers, 8-char char constants, $...$ commands, strings with \ escapes) that flags any expression mixing & ^ | << >> with + - * or a comparison without parentheses. False positives are cheap to silence with parentheses, which is what we want anyway. Also run the runtime precedence switch (section 2) around our own compile so that HolyC-written code is parsed as C: CPrec; ExeFile("B:/KSDESK3.HC"); HPrec; . Preprocessor (M) : a Python pass that adds function-like macros, continue (rewrite to goto to a generated label before the increment, which is what the compiler would do), ?: to if , and #include <...> ; keep line numbers with #line -like comments so compiler errors still point to the source (the compiler reports file,line via LexExcept ). Output is plain HolyC, so nothing in the OS changes. Family D: safety Facts [V]: everything is ring 0 in one identity-mapped address space with 2 MB or 1 GB pages ( Doc/MemOverview.DD:3 , Kernel/Mem/PageTables.HC ); only the lowest 2 MB is 4 KB pages ( MemOverview.DD:56 ); page 0 is mapped, so *(0) reads BIOS memory (E4: reads F000FF53F000FF53 , no fault); mem_mapped_space was 0x10100000000 with 1 GB of RAM, so addresses above it page-fault. A CPU fault goes INT_FAULT ( KInts.HC:61-93 ) to Fault2 ( KDbg.HC ) which enters the debugger in the faulting task; try/catch does not see it (E4: the page fault inside try dropped to "TempleOS Debugger", Fault:0x0E Page Fault , and the task stayed there). throw is a software unwind through Fs->next_except ( KExcept.HC:84-114 ). Options: Option How Cost Benefit Risk Catchable faults for the desktop task (M, recommended) Patch the first bytes of Fault2 with a JMP to a HolyC KsFault2 (code heap is writable), or better IntEntrySet(I_PAGE_FAULT/I_GP, &KsIntFault) with a copy of the INT_FAULT stub; in the handler, if Fs is the desktop task and Fs->next_except is non-empty, SetRFlags to re-enable interrupts and throw('Fault') ; otherwise fall through to the original Fault2 . The desktop's frame loop wraps each app callback in try , logs the fault address and RIP, closes the window.
