Backend quality : reverse-Polish IR ("THIS COMPILER USES REVERSE POLISH NOTATION", README [V]); c/optpass.c has OptPassConstFold , OptPassMergeCommunitives , OptPassRemoveUselessArith , OptPassMergeAddressOffsets and OptPassRegAlloc , whose comment says "AIWNIOS will not do fancy register allocation shenanigins. We will get a score for REG_MAYBE|REG_ALLOC" ( c/optpass.c:1066-1073 [V]); the developer manual's "Sexy Register Allocator: Live Variable Analysis, Graph Coloring" sections exist ( DEVMAN.MD:910-920 ) but are headings in a WIP manual, so treat graph colouring as [U]. Temporaries are spilled depth-first ( PushTmpDepthFirst , c/arm_backend.c:4757 ). Expect code quality in the TempleOS class, that is use-count register variables, not LLVM class. No benchmark published. Inline asm on aarch64 : no. KW_ASM in Src/PrsStmt.HC:1042-1056 is wrapped in #ifdef TARGET_RISCV with the comment "TODO gutted by nrootconauto in favor of his own assembler"; on aarch64 and x86-64 an asm{} block is not compiled [V]. Our asm{} routines (one block in desk3/01-core.HC with 11 _extern entry points, plus the spike files) would have to become C or HolyC. Src/AsmARM64.HC and Src/UAsmARM64.HC exist (an ARM assembler and disassembler in HolyC, 36 KB and 28 KB) and the README says "I plan on adding something lit like an arm assembler from HolyC", so the pieces exist but are not wired to asm{} . Graphics, mouse, keyboard : SDL2 window created at 640x480 with a 4:3 letterboxed viewport ( c/windows.c:82-116 ); the screen is an 8-bit paletted SDL_CreateRGBSurface(0,640,480,8,...) ( :95 ) and UpdateScreen(px,w,h,w_internal) memcpys w bytes per row into it and presents via SDL_CreateTextureFromSurface ( :170-192 ); GrPaletteColorSet sets the 16 colours ( :195 ). Mouse events are scaled to 640x480 and delivered through FFI_CALL_TOS_4(ms_cb, x, y, z, state) with a relative mode available ( :623-636 , SDL_SetRelativeMouseMode :709 ). There is no 32-bit framebuffer path and no resolution other than 640x480 ; adding one is a change to windows.c (new surface format and size, a HolyC-visible UpdateScreen32 ) plus the HolyC side; M. Native C functions : registered at start-up with PrsAddSymbol(name, int64_t (*)(int64_t *stk), arity) which binds a C function taking an array of 64-bit arguments ( c/main.c:122-127 , hundreds of uses such as PrsAddSymbol("PrintI", STK_PrintI, 2) :202 ), and PrsAddSymbolNaked for functions called with the native convention; the README's "Extending Aiwnios" shows the same mechanism plus how to add IR nodes. No dlopen (0 hits in c/*.c ), so adding a NEON blend means editing main.c and rebuilding the runtime; S per function. The trampoline for calling HolyC from C is asm/ffi_call_tos_aarch64.s ( FFI_CALL_TOS_n ) [V]. Completeness : Src/ carries the TempleOS user land file by file (DolDoc Doc*.HC , Gr*.HC , Win.HC , WinMgr.HC , KTask.HC , Sched.HC , KExcept.HC , Menu.HC , Mouse.HC , Keyboard.HC , Sprite*.HC , God*.HC , file systems FAT/RedSea/virtual, sockets) with its own KernelA.HH (224 KB), AIWNIOS_CodeGen.HC , AIWNIOS_PrsExp.HC , a profiler ( Profiler.HC ) and ScrnCast.HC ; there is no PCIBIOS , no port I/O, no KStart* , so anything that touches hardware (our Bochs VBE driver, OutU16 , PCIReadU32 ) has no equivalent [V, directory listing]. try/catch , Spawn , MAlloc , Fs-> are provided ( except.c , multic.c , mem.c , Src/KTask.HC ). Language : TempleOS precedence; no continue ; reg / noreg honoured as scores; 8-char char constants (lexer is a port); F64 through NEON scalar ( ARM_fmulReg in the README's example; AArch64_ops.csv 448 KB opcode table). Build and benchmark : not done. The build was going to run in the scratchpad through a sub-agent; the request was refused by the session's permission classifier ("Code from External"). Dependencies per README: a C compiler, SDL2 development headers (Homebrew on macOS: "Your on your own"), cmake; then ./aiwnios -b to bootstrap HCRT2.BIN , ./aiwnios to run, --tui for a terminal mode, -c for a command. So the ns-per-pixel number for a HolyC blend loop on Aiwnios is not measured ; the expectation from its allocator design is the same instruction mix as TempleOS's compiler executed natively, that is about 0.5 to 1 ns a pixel for the pointer-walk form (TCG costs roughly 5 to 10x on this loop, [U]). Porting desk3 to Aiwnios : (1) a 32-bit, arbitrary-size framebuffer path in windows.c and a HolyC UpdateScreen32 binding, M; (2) replace the Bochs VBE and PCI code ( desk3/01-core.HC , 04-main.HC , 05-splash.HC , 06-run.HC : 8 port-I/O sites) with the new binding, S; (3) rewrite KsBlendRow/Col/A/A2D , KsMix3 , Copy32 , Fill32 and the other 11 _extern asm entry points as C registered through PrsAddSymbol (NEON optional), M; (4) input: relative mouse already exists, keyboard key-up and modifiers are better than TempleOS's, S; (5) the splash, serial go-byte, savevm boot image and the TempleOS mirror window ( gr.dc2 ) have no meaning there, rework the boot story, M; (6) timing and the Monitor app use cnts.jiffies , available; (7) persistence becomes real files, S; (8) the Files app browsing ::/ becomes the host directory, S. Total L to XL, and the result is a macOS app, not an OS, which plan-review section 3.12 already lists as "the embedding option: months; useful as the development vehicle and demo, not the goal". Off x86 emulation for the OS itself : an ARM64 or RISC-V backend for the TempleOS compiler is XL and the kernel ( KStart16/32/64 , KInts , paging, PIT, PS/2, ATA, VGA) is x86 through and through; no fork has tried. KVM on an x86 host removes the TCG penalty entirely (plan-review condition 2). WebAssembly: Aiwnios's bytecode build, "slow" by its own README. Nothing here changes the recommendation to stay on QEMU for the showcase. 9. Ranked list of improvements by payoff per effort Rank Improvement Effort Payoff Evidence 1 Rewrite remaining hot HolyC loops as pointer walks in small functions, two pixels a pass where the maths allows; add reg only where the disassembly shows a spill S 3.7x to 14x on those loops, measured E1, E2 2 Set CR4.OSFXSR and move F64 kernels ( LineN , anti-aliasing, blur, layout maths) to SSE2 assembly assembled by NASM on the Mac and embedded as bytes; or to 16.16 fixed point where exact S 11x on float loops (67 to 6 ns), 30x to fixed point, measured E2 3 Test harness over serial plus benchmark set (section 11) in send-to-vm.sh S every later claim becomes a number; this report's harness is the prototype E1 to E4 4 Precedence: C table switched in around our compile, restored after; host lint for mixed operators S removes the bug class that has bitten twice E2 5 continue and OPTf_C_PREC in the compiler, built and hot-loaded with the A.1 loop S language quality; proves the compiler-patch loop E3 6 Catchable faults for the desktop task plus a crash policy M the demo survives a bad pointer E4 7 Peepholes in OptPass789A / BackLib (dead MOV R8,RAX , LEA folding, constant reuse) M about 1.4x on integer loops E1 disassembly 8 Sampling profiler (timer IRQ, RIP histogram, symbolised with Fs->hash_table ) M finds the next 46-ms-a-frame surprise without guessing renderer pass history 9 SSE2 F64 in the compiler backend L 8 to 11x on all F64 code without asm E2 10 fastcall register arguments for flagged functions M 2x on call-heavy paths (callbacks, widgets) E1 call cost 11 .BIN writer on the host plus clang freestanding trampolines; port stb_image , stb_truetype L images and fonts in the guest section 7 12 Debug allocator with canaries, lint-inserted bounds checks S + M fewer faults to catch section 6 13 More register-variable slots (RBX after audit) M fixes the "17 locals" case without rewriting E1 14 Inlining of leaf functions L removes calls where fastcall is not enough 15 Aiwnios port of desk3 L to XL a native Mac demo, not an OS section 8 not LLVM/Cranelift front end, HolyC-to-C transpiler, ARM kernel XL the measured gain is already available from 1, 2, 7, 9 10. Recommended architecture for the next six months Language : HolyC, compiled by a lightly patched TempleOS compiler ( continue , OPTf_C_PREC , peepholes, later SSE2), carried as a small patch series applied to ::/Compiler on the RAM drive during image build ( build-image.sh step: copy, patch, Cmp , Load , relink, savevm ). The desktop is compiled with C precedence; the loader restores TempleOS precedence before handing the prompt back so Demo/ and user programs keep their semantics. Hot code : assembly kernels assembled on the Mac by NASM (SSE2 allowed after the one-line CR4 enable at desktop start, per core if -smp is used), embedded as DU8 byte strings with the source kept alongside; the existing hand asm{} routines stay. Rule: anything that runs per pixel or per glyph is a kernel; HolyC does per-span, per-widget and per-frame work. Host-built C only for ported libraries (image decoders, TrueType), through the .BIN writer and trampolines, after the fetch channel exists. Tooling on the host : kslint (precedence, ASCII, $ , unused reg , functions over the register budget), ksfmt , kstest (serial harness), ksbench (section 11), a profiler in the guest reporting over serial. All Python, none touching the OS. Safety : fault policy and debug allocator in the desktop; snapshot restore as the backstop; no attempt at memory protection. Stop doing in HolyC : per-pixel loops with more than eight live variables; F64 arithmetic in anything that runs per frame (use fixed point or an SSE2 kernel); per-pixel function calls; goto -based continue once the keyword exists; expressions mixing & , | , ^ , shifts with arithmetic without parentheses (lint). First week : items 1 to 5 of the ranked list; they are all S and each is checkable with the benchmark set. 11. Benchmark set (measured now; rerun after every change) All in the headless scratch VM, 1,000,000 elements, 20 repetitions, cnts.jiffies ; report ns per element and the Uf instruction count of the loop body. The E1/E2 programs are the reference implementations. Kernel HolyC today (ns) HolyC best form today (ns) Assembly (ns) What it measures Constant-alpha blend (spike/KsBlend.HC formula) 11 (spike form) 0.8 (two pixels, reg ) under 1 (README) integer codegen, register pressure memcpy 4 MB 2392 ms per 168 MB MemCpy (README) HolyC I64 loop: in KsBench REP MOVSQ 7.5x, unrolled faster (README) string ops under TCG Per-pixel alpha blend ( KsBlendA form, alpha from a mask) to measure branchy per-pixel Glyph blit (8-bit coverage into 32-bit, KsBlendA2D ) to measure 2D loops, strides Box blur (separable, three passes) to measure accumulator loops, division or shift Text layout (measure 10,000 glyph advances with kerning lookups) to measure pointer chasing, small calls Function call s=Add1(s) 9 to 12 per call 5 instructions call convention F64 multiply-add loop 67 2 (16.16 fixed) 48 (x87), 6 (SSE2) floating point under TCG Index loop big[i]+=k 4 3 (pointer) loop overhead Rules: repeat three times and report the median (E1's 531 ms outlier); headless only, the Cocoa window changes the numbers by about 3x; same ISO, same -m , same QEMU version (11.0.2 on this Mac per plan-review). 12. Risks and the conditions for leaving HolyC in an area Compiler patches diverge from upstream : TempleOS is frozen; ZealOS has not touched the compiler either. Keep patches under 500 lines total and rebuild-tested by the harness; if a patch breaks Cmp of the kernel (the Charter's own metric), revert it. A patched compiler can be loaded half-built (E3 hazard): gate on Cmp()==0 and keep HolyCPrec -style restore paths; the image build must fail loudly, not snapshot a broken compiler. SSE in a kernel that never used it : FXSAVE/FXRSTOR are already in the scheduler; interrupt handlers do not touch XMM; the only unknown is -smp (each core must set CR4). Test with the Monitor app running on a second core before relying on it. Precedence switch is global : any TempleOS program compiled while it is on misparses; restore in the loader, add a lint that refuses to send a file compiled under the wrong table. Fault catching hides bugs : log every caught fault with RIP and address over serial; a fault counter that restarts the desktop after three. TCG numbers are not hardware numbers : a 2x change in instruction count can be 1.2x on KVM or metal; the only user-facing target is the frame time in QEMU on this Mac, so measure that. Leave HolyC for an area when: (a) the kernel is floating-point heavy and the SSE2 backend is not done, use NASM; (b) the code is a port of more than 2,000 lines of C (decoders, fonts), use clang plus trampolines; (c) the loop needs more than eight live registers and the RBX audit is not done, use assembly; (d) a crash in that code would corrupt heap or lock state (allocator, scheduler hooks), keep it tiny and in assembly with no allocation. Stay in HolyC for everything else: the in-OS loop (edit, send, run, Uf , PassTrace ) is the asset this project has that no host toolchain offers. 13. What could not be verified Aiwnios was not built or run; its blend speed on this Mac is an estimate. The 31 ns figure's exact cause (window versus other conditions) was inferred from headless re-measurement of the same loop (11 ns), not re-measured with the window open. holyc-lang's precedence table and the LSP's behaviour on our sources. Whether a custom fault handler can throw out of Fault2 cleanly (interrupt flag, stack state): designed from KInts.HC and KExcept.HC , not tested. -smp plus CR4.OSFXSR on every core; the single-core case was tested. The compile time of the full desk3 (8,000 lines) under the patched compiler; the serial transfer dominates the measured 20 s today. QEMU TCG's x87 implementation being 80-bit softfloat is the standard explanation for 48 to 67 ns per op [U]; the SSE2 number (6 ns) is measured.

t: Porting kosmos-app into the TempleOS desktop: feasibility report
h: Porting kosmos-app into the TempleOS desktop: feasibility report
x: Porting kosmos-app into the TempleOS desktop: feasibility report Date 2026-10-27. Read-only research; nothing built, run or launched. Paths are relative to the repo root. "Unverified" marks anything not read from code or measured here. 0. Verdict A source port of kosmos-app to HolyC is not feasible (it is a 27.5k-line Rust, egui and wgpu program plus roughly 45 crates). Running it inside the guest is impossible (no network, no GPU, no Rust). It can be made to appear inside a TempleOS window by running it on the Mac and bridging two things: its widget tree (as data, drawn by HolyC in the desktop's own style) and its 3D viewport (as a small pixel stream). Input flows back through the existing editor.event grammar. The cheapest honest demo is a read-only mirror of editor.tree plus one viewport crop, which takes about 3 to 5 days, not weeks. Naming caveat. "Kosmos" at kosmos.computer is a different public product (Arco, a generative-UI OS). kamiji/docs/kosmos-context.md lines 7 to 8 say the engine is not in that org. This report concerns apps/kosmos-app , the engine's editor. 1. What kosmos-app is Rust, edition 2024. apps/kosmos-app/Cargo.toml lines 1 to 12 and 31 to 90. Binary kosmos-app , 27,535 lines in src/*.rs ( wc -l ), plus about 130 files in src/editor/ . A winit window with an egui editor drawn over a wgpu scene ( egui , egui-wgpu , egui-winit , winit , tiny-skia , ab_glyph ; Cargo.toml lines 79 to 86). About 45 workspace crates are linked ( kosmos-render , -sim , -physics , -anim , -body and more). The editor is immediate-mode egui, not the kosmos-ui tree. crates/kosmos-ui is "Retained HUD tree for the Solid host" that "does not layout, paint, or talk to Hermes" ( crates/kosmos-ui/src/lib.rs lines 1 to 7). No Cargo.toml in crates/ or apps/ depends on it (grep, only its own manifest matches). NodeKind has 28 variants ( crates/kosmos-ui/src/kind.rs lines 14 to 44). It describes game HUD screens, not the editor. The HUD (game UI) has its own live path. apps/kosmos-app/src/hud.rs (3,036 lines) replays a hud.json op log (create, set, insert, remove) and paints on the CPU with tiny-skia. Hud::paint(width, height, ui_scale) -> Vec<u8> returns RGBA ( hud.rs line 457). hud-element/1 is only a proposal: "Not built: nothing in this document exists as code yet" ( docs/plans/hud-native-format.md line 3). The schema is schemas/hud-element.schema.json . The HUD painter belongs to the HUD session, and "Do not rewrite the painter" ( docs/plans/rust-engine.md line 1305). How the editor is exposed. The editor's widgets are egui's AccessKit tree, flattened to JSON ( apps/kosmos-app/src/editor/introspect.rs lines 1 to 10, struct Widget lines 91 to 113). Fields per widget: id , parent , role , label , value , rect [x0,y0,x1,y1] in points, disabled , toggled , src , src_guess . Nodes with no label, value or action are folded away (lines 5 to 6). Roles are not typed beyond a string. interesting() keeps Button, TextInput, CheckBox, Slider, TreeItem and Window (lines 114 to 130). There are no colours, fonts, icons, z-order, clipping or styles in the tree. That detail exists only in pixels. Protocol. editor.tree , editor.at , editor.event {steps} , editor.view {tab,bottom,theme,select} , editor.shot ( crates/kosmos-protocol/src/message.rs lines 311 to 345). editor.shot writes a PNG to an engine-owned directory and replies {path,w,h,bytes,hash} . There is no inline or raw-RGBA editor frame request (lines 340 onward). The step grammar is click:Label , hover: , click@x,y , drag@x1,y1>x2,y2[>x,y...] , key:cmd+z , type:text , wait:n ( apps/kosmos-app/src/editor/script.rs lines 1 to 20 and 141). Two hosts answer it. The open window serves it with --serve-port N ( apps/kosmos-app/src/main.rs line 908, window_link.rs ). A headless EditorServer serves it with --serve-editor ( apps/kosmos-app/src/editor_host.rs lines 1 to 80). The headless one keeps one renderer, scene and egui editor alive per connection and draws a fresh frame per request. kosmos-mcp --connect 5878 is the MCP bridge to all of the above ( .mcp.json lines 1 to 8). apps/kosmos-cli/src/mcp.rs lines 274 and 522 define the editor tool. .claude/skills/drive-window/SKILL.md documents a 5 s reply limit. The first event after launch can return window_busy although it landed. Rendering path. The 3D scene goes through kosmos-render (wgpu, Metal on this Mac), then egui-wgpu draws the panels over it. The headless editor shot size defaults to 1600x1000 ( main.rs lines 138 to 139). The committed reports/editor-shot.png is 253,567 bytes ( ls -la ). Split of UI shell versus engine and viewport. Part Where Notes UI shell src/editor.rs (3,289 lines), src/editor/* (menus, docks, inspector, timeline, labs, cast, chat) Described by the AccessKit tree; looks need pixels Viewport and engine main.rs (4,041), kosmos-render , kosmos-sim , kosmos-physics , kosmos-anim and others Real GPU work. Only pixels can cross to the guest Control plane editor.* and command , undo , redo , list_commands Already text, already agent-driven 2. Transport facts about the guest Today the host-to-guest path is COM1 over -serial tcp:127.0.0.1:4555 ( scripts/boot-vm.sh line 17). The guest receiver Rx busy-polls InU8(0x3FD)&1 and reads InU8(0x3F8) ( scripts/send-to-vm.sh line 27). It answers one dot per 8 bytes, and serial-send.py lines 14 to 17 waits for each dot. The measured 1.4 KB/s is therefore the lockstep design (a TCP round trip per 8 bytes, plus the slow cocoa-window guest). It is not a hardware or baud limit. QEMU's 16550 model has no baud throttle on receive (unverified). A streamed, un-acked protocol with the FIFO enabled and a bounded per-frame drain loop is untested. Rough guess, unverified: 1 to 3 us per byte for two port reads under TCG, so about 100k to 500k B/s when draining flat out and about 40 to 130 KB/s with a 4 ms per frame budget. This is the first thing to measure. The guest already has a linear framebuffer address and a full-frame copy. ks_fb comes from PCI BAR0 ( KsDesk2.HC line 919). The frame loop does MemCpy(ks_fb,bb,SW*SH*4) (lines 951 to 952), and README says that costs about 7 ms for 5.2 MB. A 640x400x4 blit would be about 1.5 ms. The Viewport window in the desktop is a stub: AppViewport draws a rounded rectangle and two cubes ( KsDesk2.HC lines 609 to 617). That is the natural place to blit host pixels. The guest can already scan PCI ( PCIClassFind , PCIReadU32 , line 917 to 919). It does raw port I/O with no driver (COM1). Input in the guest comes from ms.pos and key reads in Input() (line 853 onward). The mouse is read as relative deltas. 3. Candidate architectures (a) Host-driven pixel mirror Run kosmos-app (or --serve-editor ) on the Mac, take editor.shot , convert, push to the guest, blit into a window. Bytes per frame, for a 640x400 window (256,000 px). Format Bytes At 1.4 KB/s At 40 KB/s (guess) RGBA 1,024,000 12 min 26 s RGB332 256,000 3 min 6.4 s 4 bpp palette 128,000 91 s 3.2 s Tile deltas (for example 16x16 tiles, hash per tile) help a mostly static editor chrome a lot, but not a spinning viewport. They need a host differ, a protocol and a guest decoder. A typical 3D viewport redraw touches most of its tiles. Serial alone gives a still image or about one frame every few seconds. A smooth 10 fps needs about 128 KB x 10 = 1.3 MB/s even at 4 bpp, so a shared-memory channel is mandatory for live pixels. Host-to-guest channels, ranked: 1. ivshmem-plain. -object memory-backend-file,share=on,mem-path=/tmp/ks.shm,size=16M,id=hm -device ivshmem-plain,memdev=hm . The host mmaps the file and writes at memory speed. The guest finds it with the same PCI scan it already uses (vendor 1af4, device 1110) and reads BAR2 with MemCpy . Unverified: that SeaBIOS places the BAR below TempleOS's identity-mapped range, that TempleOS maps it writable or readable, and that TCG respects the shared mapping coherently. Cost: about 1 day to prove. Latency below 5 ms plus the guest blit. 2. gdbstub memory writes ( -gdb tcp::1234 , packet M addr,len:hex ). Needs the VM stopped per write in system mode, hex doubles the bytes, and the guest buffer address must be sent back on serial. Works as a fallback; jittery (unverified). 3. Raw second drive or ISO. Needs a mounted second block device in TempleOS. The earlier ISO9660 route failed with an ISOInit exception ( README.md "Things learned the hard way"), and the guest's cache behaviour is unknown. Lowest priority. 4. Serial tuned (streaming, FIFO on, no acks). Good enough for the tree (below) and stills. 5. Writing into the VBE framebuffer from outside QEMU. Not possible: VGA RAM is an internal RAMBlock with no shared mapping (unverified in detail, but nothing in scripts/ exposes it). The QEMU monitor can read memory ( pmemsave ) but I know of no stock command that writes it. Look: the app appears as its own pixels (egui theme), not in the OS style. That is the weakest fit with apps/os-styles , which is the point of the Desk2 work. Cost: bridge about 2 days (Rust or Python on the host), guest decoder about 2 days, shared-memory spike about 1 day. Risk: medium, mostly ivshmem. (b) UI-tree-driven (recommended core) Send only the widget tree and events; draw it in HolyC with the toolkit that exists ( Rect , RRFill , RRRing , Txt , Icon , Shadow in KsDesk2.HC lines 85 to 352). Size: unverified, because I did not run the app. A 300-widget tree at about 40 bytes binary (id, parent, role, rect, flags, label) is about 12 KB, which is 9 s at 1.4 KB/s once and sub-second as deltas (changed widgets only). That fits the serial link as it stands. Cleanly mapped AccessKit roles and what to draw: Role or field HolyC drawing Window Frame() -style window, title from label Button RRFill plus centred TxtC , disabled greys it CheckBox / toggled box plus tick, or a switch Slider ( value , numeric) rail plus knob; drag@ back TextInput well plus caret; type: back TreeItem indented row; click:Label back Label / value Txt What is lost: colours, icons ( src/editor/lucide.rs ), the viewport, timeline lanes, node graphs, gizmos (the skill says handles are "painted, not widgets"), custom egui painting in Cast, face boards and the labs. These are drawn by egui directly and appear in the tree as nothing or as one big rect. Expect the panels, menus, buttons, tree and inspector to look right and every custom canvas to be an empty box, which is where (a) fills in. Free benefit: it picks up the five desktop styles (Longformer light and dark, macOS, Windows 11, Kosmica glass) with no extra work. Cost: bridge 1 day, guest tree renderer 2 to 3 days (layout is given by rect , so no layout engine). Risk: low to medium. Rect clipping, scroll regions, popups and z-order need a rule (draw in tree order, clip children to parent). (b2) NodeKind (hud-element/1) tree The kosmos-ui tree and hud-element/1 are the game HUD, not the editor. They map cleanly only for HUD screens. Cleanly mapped kinds: Panel, Label, Bar, Divider, Swatch, Dots, Button, Switch, Slider, TextField (rect, rounded rect, text, caret). Needs host-side resolution before sending: Row, Column, Stack, At, Pad, Center, Spacer, Scroll, Overlay (layout kinds; the painter in hud.rs resolves them, kosmos-ui does not). Needs a bitmap or vector sprite: Icon, Image, Drawing, Wedge, FadeMask, Glyph, Slot. A clean design would tap the painter's resolved layout as a display list of rect, text and image commands. That means a change in apps/kosmos-app/src/hud*.rs , which is owned by the HUD session ( rust-engine.md line 1305). Do not start there. Mirror the HUD as pixels instead, because Hud::paint already returns RGBA at any size ( hud.rs line 457). Use (b2) only if the user later wants the game HUD in the guest. (c) HolyC reimplementation of a subset Reasonable for a few panels only after (b) exists, and only for panels that are pure data (for example the Scene tree, Inspector fields, command list). Every panel reimplemented duplicates egui code and the command semantics ( model.* , scene.* , undo steps). Not recommended as a first move; (b) with editor.event gets the same behaviour for free. (d) Something better Hybrid (b) plus a thin (a): the chrome from the tree, the viewport as a low-rate pixel stream into a window rect. This is the recommended end state. Do not use: running a second QEMU display or placing the Mac window beside it. That shows the app but is not "inside" the desktop. Possible later: a request editor.frame returning raw RGBA of a region (a new protocol message and an EditorHost change in crates/kosmos-protocol , apps/kosmos-app/src/editor_host.rs ). The demo avoids it by reading the PNG file the existing editor.shot writes. Do not add it without the user's go. 4. Input flow back Reuse the existing plumbing end to end; no new engine API is needed. Guest Input() ( KsDesk2.HC line 853) already knows the mouse position in screen pixels, the buttons and the keys. Convert to window-local points by subtracting the window origin and dividing by the mirror scale. Guest writes event lines on COM1 ( OutU8(0x3F8, ...) ; the same port the loader reads, so the link is already duplex): for example M x y b , K name , T text , one line each. A ring in ivshmem is the faster option later. A host bridge (small Python or Rust process holding both the QEMU socket 4555 and a websocket or TCP to kosmos-app --serve-port 5878 ) maps events to steps and sends {"t":"editor.event","steps":"..."} . - A press and release without movement maps to click@x,y , or to click:Label when the tree gives a unique hit (more robust). - Press, moves and release map to drag@x1,y1>x2,y2>... . Drags are batched at release, so there is no live orbit while holding the button. A true live drag needs a down/move/up step type (unverified whether script.rs has one; the grammar seen has only atomic drag@ ). - Keys map to key:cmd+z and type:text ; hover maps to hover@x,y . The reply {ran, log} then triggers editor.tree to refresh. Alternatively kosmos-mcp can be driven by an agent in parallel on the same socket (one editor client at a time; unverified for multiple concurrent clients on --serve-port ). - Latency estimate, unverified: serial event to bridge below 10 ms; editor.event plus a fresh frame in the live window is the unknown, and the skill notes a 5 s reply window and a slow first event. 5. Smallest demo (recommended) Goal: the editor's real widget tree, drawn in a TempleOS window in the Desk2 style, with click-through to the real editor, plus one still viewport image. Steps and effort: Host: start KOSMOS_EDITOR=1 KOSMOS_SPLASH=0 KOSMOS_TITLE=0 kosmos-app --serve-port 5878 (from .claude/skills/drive-window/SKILL.md ), or --serve-editor for headless. 0.25 day. Bridge tools/templeos-bridge (or a script under apps/templeos-holyc/scripts , Python 3): call editor.tree , scale rects into a 640x400 box, pack a compact binary or line text format (role code, rect as 16-bit ints, flags, label), diff against the previous tree and write deltas to the QEMU serial socket. 1 day. Spike the serial: write a streaming guest drain (no acks, FIFO on, bounded loop) in spike/ and measure bytes per second with the desktop running. 0.5 day. Gate: at least 20 KB/s, else send the tree once on demand. Guest: new AppKosmos window (replacing or beside AppViewport , KsDesk2.HC line 609) that holds the parsed widgets in arrays and draws them with existing primitives by role. 2 days. Viewport: bridge reads the PNG at the editor.shot path, crops the viewport rect, quantises to 4 bpp, sends one still over serial (128 KB, about 90 s at today's rate, faster after step 3) or through ivshmem if that spike passes. 1 day plus 1 day for the ivshmem spike (optional). Input: guest sends click and key lines; the bridge turns them into editor.event and re-sends the tree. 1 day. Capture screenshots into apps/templeos-holyc/shots/ . 0.25 day. Total about 5 to 6 days for a first-pass demo, about 3 days if the viewport still and ivshmem are dropped. A smaller first proof of 1 day: read-only, one editor.tree snapshot as a text file sent with the existing loader, drawn as labelled boxes. 6. Blockers, unknowns, constraints Licence. The workspace is MIT OR Apache-2.0 ( Cargo.toml line 109). TempleOS is public domain (not verified here). The Inter font in the guest is SIL OFL ( README.md ). apps/os-styles/kamiji-ui is "local prototyping only: do not publish it" ( PROVENANCE.md ). None block this work. Plan constraints. Do not start phase work before the go gate ( rust-engine.md §1.5, lines 86 to 97). The gate is already ticked go on 2026-10-15 (line 1475), so the engine track is open, but the protocol and apps/kosmos-app changes are engine work. The bridge and guest code live in this repo's apps/templeos-holyc and are not on a phase card. §8.6 questions the user must answer (line 1278): none are triggered by a read-only bridge in apps/templeos-holyc . They would be triggered by adding a runtime dependency with a non-allowed licence, a required CI check, deploying, or a pre-release crate ( rust-engine.md §8.7 line 1285 lists winit 0.31 beta and wasmtime rc as not to use). Using Python or QEMU on the host adds no workspace crate. Protected paths ( docs/agents/recipes.md lines 55 to 57, docs/agents/verifier.md line 16): .github/ , deny.toml , Cargo.lock , rust-toolchain.toml . The demo needs none. The HUD files ( apps/kosmos-app/src/hud*.rs , assets/hud/ ) are owned by the HUD session ( rust-engine.md line 1305). A new editor.frame request would be a protocol change; ask first. Base branch and repo rules: branch from local proto , not main ; Yakopop must not receive kosmos-* crates ( CLAUDE.md ). Current branch is task/templeos-shell . Unverified (not measured or read): guest serial drain rate without acks; ivshmem BAR placement and TempleOS mapping; real editor.tree size and widget count for the editor; latency of editor.event and editor.shot on the live window; whether the step grammar has separate mouse-down and mouse-up for a live drag; whether --serve-port accepts a second concurrent client; TempleOS paging identity mapping above 4 GB; gdbstub write behaviour on a running VM. Product risks. The tree is a lossy view of the editor (custom-painted canvases vanish), the guest is TCG-slow (30 to 40 ms frames at 1440x900, README.md ), and the wasm or kosmos-web route ( docs/plans/os-frame.md "Later") remains the cleaner way to run the engine itself in a browser desktop. The guest can never be the engine host. 7. Recommendation Build the hybrid. Draw the editor chrome natively in HolyC from editor.tree , driven over the existing serial link with deltas, and feed editor.event from guest input through a small host bridge. Add a viewport pixel stream through ivshmem only after a one-day spike proves it. Start with the read-only tree mirror demo in section 5, because it needs no change to kosmos-app, kosmos-protocol or the HUD code, and it proves the hardest question (does the tree look right in the desktop's styles) first.

t: Running Electron and Tauri apps inside the TempleOS desktop: research and route
h: Running Electron and Tauri apps inside the TempleOS desktop: research and route
x: Running Electron and Tauri apps inside the TempleOS desktop: research and route Date 2026-10-27. Research only: nothing was built, launched, installed or committed. The only commands run were read-only queries ( qemu-system-x86_64 -device help , -machine pc,help , -object ...,help , uname , sw_vers , sed , grep ). Paths are relative to apps/templeos-holyc/ unless absolute. Web pages were accessed 2026-10-27. Evidence labels used on every claim: [V] verified here (read in a local file, or a command run on this Mac), [D] reported by documentation I fetched (URL given), [S] reported by a search result snippet only, [U] unverified (from general knowledge or inference; treat as a hypothesis to test). 0. Summary The previous plan's transport is dead on this machine. ivshmem-plain and ivshmem-doorbell do not exist in the Homebrew QEMU 11.0.2 on this Apple Silicon Mac: -device ivshmem-plain,help answers "Device 'ivshmem-plain' not found" [V] . QEMU's own page says "On Linux hosts, a shared memory device is available" and documents only Linux setups [D] (https://www.qemu.org/docs/master/system/devices/ivshmem.html). The same QEMU does ship memory-backend-file with share= and mem-path= and the pc machine accepts memory-backend= (use a file as the guest's main RAM) [V] . So the best candidate transport is guest main RAM backed by a shared file that a host process also maps ("ramshm"). Whether that works on macOS under TCG is the first thing to prove [U] ; memory-backend-file has compiled on macOS since a 2018 patch [S] . Source of pixels is replaceable; build the guest side once. Whatever captures the app (ScreenCaptureKit, Chromium DevTools screencast, an Xpra client in a Linux container), the guest only needs "a surface in shared RAM, a list of changed rectangles, and an event channel back". Build that guest contract first and keep capture behind a host "surface provider" interface. Recommended route: a Swift host daemon captures real macOS app windows with ScreenCaptureKit (works for Electron and Tauri/WKWebView alike, no app changes), writes BGRA surfaces plus dirty rectangles into shared RAM, and injects input back; Electron apps can later be upgraded to CDP (no focus stealing, device-metric resizing) and risky or Linux-only apps moved into a Linux ARM64 container behind Xpra. Do not compile Chromium, Node or Rust apps into TempleOS. 1. Facts about our guest that bound every design The desktop works in logical units at scale ks_s of 1 or 2 and owns the whole framebuffer; the card address comes from PCI BAR0 ( desk3/05-run.HC:58-66 , ks_fb=PCIReadU32(...,0x10) ) [V] . Windows are fixed size, held in arrays sized by NA ( #define NA 9 , desk3/01-core.HC:26 ; arrays ks_aw/ks_ah/ks_wx/ks_open/ks_z in desk3/02-ui.HC:5-15 ) [V] . Apps are AppXxx(a,x,y,w,h) draw functions dispatched by an if-chain in AppBody ( desk3/03-apps.HC:584-597 ( AppBody at :585)) and by AppClick ( desk3/04-main.HC:148 ) [V] . A frame is: for each dirty rectangle, set the clip ( ks_c0x..ks_c1y ), run Draw (wallpaper, every window frame with shadow, app body, menubar, dock), Cursor , then MemCpy each row to the card ( desk3/05-run.HC:3-54 ) [V] . So a dirty rectangle inside a video-like window still repaints the wallpaper, the shadow and the card under it unless a fast path is added. SpanCopy ( desk3/01-core.HC:114 ) and RRTexN ( :178 ) already copy from a full-screen-sized source with a rounded mask, but assume the source has the screen stride [V] ; a stride-aware variant is needed. Hit regions are rebuilt every drawn frame ( Hit , desk3/02-ui.HC:92 , max 500 MAXH ) and the hit test is a linear scan ( HitAt , :101 ) [V] . Input: mouse is relative, re-centred each loop ( MsSet(320,240) ), cursor moved by dx*3*s ( desk3/04-main.HC:364-373 ); only ms.lb (left button) and wheel ms.pos.z are read ( :378 , :367 ) [V] . Keys come from ScanKey(&ch,&sc) ( desk3/04-main.HC:315-318 ), used with sc&0xFF PS/2 scancodes in NotesKey ( :264-270 , for example 0x4B left, 0x4D right, 0x53 delete) [V] . ScanKey returns key-down only as far as these uses show; whether key-up and modifier state are readable ( kbd globals, KeyDown() ) is [U] . Measured by earlier agents and the README: full 1280x800x4 copy to the card about 7 ms; 700k pixel redraw about 20 ms; 7 ms redraw at 1440x900 and about 25 ms at 2880x1800 for moving a window ( README.md:7 , :23-24 ) [V as documented measurements, not re-run] . 1 GB RAM ( -m 1024M , scripts/boot-vm.sh:14 ) [V] ; at 2x the desktop already holds a back buffer, a prev buffer, low-res blur buffers and 5+5 wallpapers of 20.7 MB each (about 290 MB, my arithmetic from desk3/01-core.HC:35 ) so remote surfaces need a RAM increase. Serial: lockstep loader about 1.4 KB/s because it acks every 8 to 32 bytes ( docs/kosmos-app-port-research.md:37-40 ) [V as reported by that file] ; a streaming drain loop is unmeasured. Audio: PC speaker only (task statement). Network: none. The guest build is one concatenated file: cat desk3/0*.HC ( scripts/send-to-vm.sh:14 ) [V] , so a new file named desk3/03b-remote.HC sorts between 03-apps.HC and 04-main.HC automatically. 2. Q1: architectures for getting Electron and Tauri apps into a window Common baseline numbers (my arithmetic): a 1000x700 logical window is 2.8 MB at 1x and 11.2 MB at 2x per full frame. All approaches below end in "BGRA surface plus changed rectangles", so Q2 and Q6 apply to all. (a) Native macOS app, ScreenCaptureKit capture, CGEvent or Accessibility input What you see: the real app window, native fonts, native GPU, macOS menus. SCContentFilter(desktopIndependentWindow:) captures one window regardless of what covers it, minimumFrameInterval up to 60 fps, frames arrive when content changes, BGRA output, optional app audio since macOS 13, Screen Recording permission required [U: the Apple page https://developer.apple.com/documentation/screencapturekit/ returned no body to my fetch; the details come from the fetch tool's general-knowledge summary. Verify with an Apple sample before relying on them.] Sunshine, a GPL-3.0 streaming server, uses ScreenCaptureKit as its only macOS capture backend and requires macOS 14.2 or later [D] (https://github.com/LizardByte/Sunshine), which is evidence that SCK capture is a mainstream route in 2026. It does not say whether it captures single windows [D] . Latency/FPS: capture is GPU-side and cheap; readback of 2.8 MB at 30 fps is about 84 MB/s of memcpy on the host [U] . The chain click to pixel is guest poll (up to 5 ms idle sleep, desk3/05-run.HC (the idle Sleep(5) in Main )) + serial/shm event + host injection + app render + SCK frame (up to 16 ms at 60 fps) + shm write + guest blit (about 10 ms): estimate 60 to 120 ms [U] . Input: CGEventPostToPid for mouse and keys to a specific app, or Accessibility ( AXUIElement ) actions such as AXPress for robust button clicks. Needs the Accessibility permission [U] . Unicode and IME: host can set a Unicode string on a key event; the guest cannot compose non-ASCII, so a host-side "paste or type text" path is needed [U] . Clipboard: NSPasteboard bridged by the daemon, gated by consent (Q5). Audio: the app plays through the Mac speakers (free); per-app mute only [U] . Cursors: SCK can hide the cursor; shape needs a query ( NSCursor.currentSystem ) or a guess from the AX element role [U] . Multi-window and popups: a per-window capture excludes the app's other windows. Menus, drop-downs, tooltips, dialogs and native context menus are separate windows. Handle by listing all windows of the same pid and exposing each as a child surface at an offset, or by capturing at application level and cropping the union rectangle [U] . HiDPI: ask SCK for width and height = window logical size x ks_s so the guest does 1:1 copies. Resize: set the real window size via Accessibility AXSize [U] . Drag and drop: not feasible except through a shared folder and the app's own open dialog (captured as another window). What breaks: windows must be on-screen to be captured (minimised and fully off-screen windows are a risk) [U] , so the user's real desktop gets cluttered unless windows live on a virtual display (private CGVirtualDisplay API, risky [U] ) or another Space; focus stealing when injecting keyboard events; the app runs in the user's own profile with the user's files (security, Q5); permission prompts that macOS re-confirms periodically [U] . Cost: S/M for a single-window prototype, L with popups and resize. Best compatibility: everything installed on the Mac, including Slack, Discord, Notion, 1Password, and Tauri apps (WKWebView). (b) Linux ARM64 VM or container on the Mac, headless compositor, pull frames over a remote-display protocol Electron officially documents running under Xvfb with DISPLAY set for headless CI [D] (https://electronjs.org/docs/latest/tutorial/testing-on-headless-ci). A forum report says headless Obsidian needed --disable-gpu --no-sandbox besides Xvfb [S] (https://forum.obsidian.md/t/one-solution-to-segmentation-fault-when-launching-headless-obsidian/117276). Tauri v2 on Linux needs WebKitGTK 4.1 and the docs give an arm64 install line ( libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev:arm64 ) [D] (https://v2.tauri.app/distribute/debian/). Software GL only (no GPU in a container on macOS) means Chromium uses SwiftShader or llvmpipe, so heavy pages burn host CPU [U] . Xpra is the strongest tool here: seamless per-window forwarding of individual X11 apps, built-in HTML5 client, clipboard and audio forwarding, macOS arm64 client builds, GPL-2.0+ [D] (https://github.com/Xpra-org/xpra/). Older tickets show encodings rgb (zlib or lz4), png, jpeg, webp, h264, vp8, vp9 [S] ; latest release notes seen mention 6.5.3 and AV1 decoders [S] (https://github.com/Xpra-org/xpra/releases). Per-window damage regions and window move/resize/title/icon/cursor events are the protocol's native vocabulary, which map one-to-one to our "remote window" contract [U] . The cost is writing a custom client (Python, speaking Xpra's protocol) that decodes window updates and copies them to shared RAM. waypipe : a Wayland proxy with lz4/zstd/video compression and DMABUF transfer [S] (man pages, e.g. https://man.archlinux.org/man/waypipe.1.en); it needs a Wayland compositor at the receiving end, which we are not (our "compositor" is HolyC). Poor fit. Its project page returned an anti-bot "Access Denied" so licence and macOS status are [U] . Weston RDP backend plus FreeRDP: RemoteApp-style RAIL/VAIL support was developed for WSLg; whether mainline Weston ships it is not confirmed [S] (https://www.mankier.com/1/weston). Weston and FreeRDP licences: FreeRDP is Apache-2.0 [D] (https://github.com/FreeRDP/FreeRDP); Weston is MIT [U] . wayvnc with sway or another wlroots compositor: WLR_BACKENDS=headless WLR_LIBINPUT_NO_DEVICES=1 , one display per wayvnc instance [S] ; a wlroots issue reports a grey screen with the headless backend in some versions [S] (https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/wlroots/wlroots/-/issues/3712). One container per app under cage (single-app kiosk) plus wayvnc yields a per-app stream by construction [U] ; popups and dialogs live inside that one output. TigerVNC (GPL-2.0, Xvnc is an X server with a virtual framebuffer, Tight encoding with libjpeg-turbo) and noVNC (MPL-2.0, Raw, CopyRect, RRE, Hextile, Tight, TightPNG, ZRLE, JPEG, Zlib, H.264) are whole-desktop [D] (https://github.com/TigerVNC/tigervnc, https://github.com/novnc/noVNC). VNC rectangles include CopyRect, which is a natural dirty-rectangle source. Latency 50 to 150 ms typical on localhost [U] . Host CPU: one container with Xvfb, a window manager and a software-rendered Chromium can use one to two cores while active [U] . Input: X11 events through xdotool, XTest or the protocol (Xpra/VNC both carry keysyms and button masks); IME and clipboard are native to Xpra. Multi-window: native in Xpra, absent in VNC. Audio: PulseAudio over TCP to a Mac player [U] . What breaks: only apps with Linux ARM64 builds (Q4); app looks like a Linux app (fonts, no macOS menu bar, tray icons need a tray host); Rosetta for Linux in Apple's Virtualization framework or qemu-user could run x86_64 Electron apps, slowly [U] ; keychain/biometric integrations differ. Benefit: real isolation (own filesystem, own network namespace, kill switch, cgroup limits), the right answer for untrusted or noisy apps. (c) Electron specific Offscreen rendering webPreferences.offscreen : delivers each frame through webContents.on('paint') with the dirty rect and image, windows are always frameless, setFrameRate up to 240 fps in software mode, no frames while the page is idle, GPU mode supports WebGL with a copy cost, and a useSharedTexture mode needs a native Node module [D] (https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/tutorial/offscreen-rendering). It must be set where the BrowserWindow is created, so it works for apps we own or can patch, not for closed apps like Slack (and ASAR integrity or OnlyLoadAppFromAsar fuses may block patching [U] ). beginFrameSubscription exists in webContents with an onlyDirty flag; the fetched page was truncated so callback details are [U] ; the page also lists capturePage(rect, {stayHidden, stayAwake}) and isBeingCaptured() [D] (https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/api/web-contents). CDP Page.startScreencast over --remote-debugging-port : frames are only emitted when the browser renders something new, every frame must be acked with Page.screencastFrameAck , the method is flagged experimental [S] (search results quoting Puppeteer recorder code and Chromium page_handler.h ; the protocol viewer page fetch returned only a redirect notice). Input via Input.dispatchMouseEvent / dispatchKeyEvent / insertText ; resize via Emulation.setDeviceMetricsOverride without moving the real window; no native chrome, native menus, OS dialogs, <select> popup widgets or tray [U] . Wins: no Screen Recording or Accessibility permission, no focus stealing, can run hidden [U: background throttling of hidden pages may stop frames] . JPEG frames are cheap to decode on the host but we want raw BGRA so decode costs host CPU only. Playwright Electron : experimental, _electron.launch() , Electron v21 or later, firstWindow() , electronApp.evaluate() runs in the main process (so Menu.getApplicationMenu() could feed our menubar), native dialogs are not intercepted and must be stubbed through evaluate() , and the EnableNodeCliInspectArguments fuse set false breaks launch [D] (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-electron). Apps built with that fuse off (hardened apps) cannot be driven this way; they would still accept --remote-debugging-port unless stripped [U] . Electron on Linux arm64 is a supported target for packagers [S] (https://www.electron.build/docs/architecture). (d) Tauri specific wry is the webview layer: WKWebView on macOS ("WebKit is native on macOS"), WebView2 on Windows, WebKitGTK on Linux, child webviews on macOS, Windows and Linux (X11 only); dual MIT or Apache-2.0; the README says nothing about offscreen/headless rendering [D] (https://github.com/tauri-apps/wry). tao is its window crate [U] . No CDP : the Tauri debugging page documents Safari's inspector on macOS (private API on macOS, blocks App Store), Edge DevTools on Windows, WebKitGTK WebInspector on Linux, and mentions no remote protocol [D] (https://v2.tauri.app/develop/debug/). Production builds disable devtools unless the devtools feature or a debug build is used [D] (same page). WebDriver : tauri-driver supports Windows and Linux only; there is "no WKWebView driver tool" on macOS; CrabNebula sells a cross-platform fork needing a paid key on macOS; the docs recommend WebdriverIO with @wdio/tauri-service [D] (https://v2.tauri.app/develop/tests/webdriver/). Screenshots are not mentioned there; W3C WebDriver has a standard screenshot endpoint [U] but it is a poll, not a stream. WebKitGTK remote inspector : WEBKIT_INSPECTOR_SERVER=host:port with enable-developer-extras , client is another WebKitGTK browser at inspector:// ; WebKitWebDriver uses the same remote protocol [S] (https://trac.webkit.org/wiki/RemoteInspectorGTKandWPE, https://blogs.igalia.com/carlosgc/?p=936, dated 2017). This is WebKit's protocol, not CDP. Linux aarch64 build: Tauri's docs give the arm64 dependency line [D] ; whether a given third-party Tauri app publishes aarch64 Linux binaries is app-specific (many publish only x86_64 AppImages) [U] . Building from source in a container is possible for open-source Tauri apps [U] . Idea: Tauri frontend as a plain page in headless Chromium, Rust backend on the host. The frontend talks through window.__TAURI_INTERNALS__ and a custom IPC protocol [U] ; Tauri ships mockIPC for tests and a tauri::test mock runtime [U] . In principle the backend's #[tauri::command] functions run in a process with a mock runtime and a shim forwards invoke over a WebSocket. This needs the app source (to build a headless backend) and per-app work; it also loses plugins that need a real window (dialogs, tray, window management). Feasible for a few open-source Tauri apps we choose, not a general route. Rate: a research spike, not a platform feature. For closed Tauri binaries on macOS: only (a) ScreenCaptureKit works. Cost the same as for Electron. (e) Semantic route: redraw natively from accessibility or DOM Data sources: macOS AXUIElement trees of any app [U] ; for Chromium Accessibility.getFullAXTree , DOM.getDocument , DOMSnapshot.captureSnapshot (nodes with bounding boxes and computed styles) [U] ; our own egui precedent in docs/kosmos-app-port-research.md:70-90 already shows the loss profile (no colours, fonts, icons, canvases, z-order) [V] . What is lost: everything custom drawn (VS Code editor canvas, Slack message virtualisation, images, video, fonts, shadows); web layout cannot be reproduced by walking rectangles at 15 ns per operation with a single font atlas. What it is good for as an adjunct: the app's menu bar items into our menubar ( desk3/02-ui.HC:238 ), window titles, focus and caret rectangles for IME, cursor shape by element role, robust button activation ( AXPress ), and an agent/reader mode that sends styled text. Verdict: not a primary route. (f) Better ideas found Web-first apps in one host Chromium. Slack, Discord, Notion, Element and VS Code (through vscode.dev or code-server) all have web clients, so a single headless Chromium (Playwright) with one tab per app and CDP screencast covers many "apps" with no per-app install, no ScreenCaptureKit permission and a clean cookie jar per profile. The core-apps plan already contains this as spike 2 ( docs/core-apps-plan.md:117-119 ) [V] . Loses Electron-only features and may breach some web-client terms (Q4). Host-side overlay. Skip pixels in the guest entirely: the guest sends window rectangles over serial and a borderless host window sits over the QEMU window showing the real app. Zero guest cost and perfect speed; but z-order with guest windows, menus and shadows is wrong, screenshots of the VM miss it, and it is not "inside". Useful only as a stop-gap demo [U] . Surface-provider abstraction (recommended): the host daemon exposes one contract (create surface, resize, dirty rects, title, cursor, close, child surfaces) and implements it with SCK, CDP or Xpra. The guest never learns which. 3. Q2: the transport Bandwidth needs (my arithmetic) Quantity Bytes 1440x900x4 full frame 5.18 MB 2880x1800x4 full frame 20.7 MB 1000x700 logical window, 1x / 2x 2.8 MB / 11.2 MB Typical typing or cursor-blink update (a few percent of a window) 20 to 200 KB at 1x 30 fps of a full 1000x700 window at 1x 84 MB/s 30 fps at 2x 336 MB/s Serial at an optimistic 100 KB/s moves one 2.8 MB window in 28 s, so serial can never carry pixels; with zlib/RLE on a mostly static UI it could carry small deltas (about 1 to 10 KB each) at a few fps [U] . LZ4 and RLE decoders are 30 to 60 lines of HolyC but cost about 10 to 30 ns per output byte under TCG so decoding a 1 MB delta costs 10 to 30 ms [U] ; they only pay when the channel is the bottleneck, which shared RAM removes. Options Option Exists in our QEMU Guest code needed Bandwidth Verdict ivshmem-plain No [V] (not found; docs say Linux hosts [D]) PCI BAR map memory speed Dead on this build. Do not plan on it. A Linux QEMU build could add it, not a macOS one [U]. Main RAM as shared file ( -object memory-backend-file,id=ram,size=2G,mem-path=...,share=on -machine pc,memory-backend=ram ) Yes [V] (object and property exist) Allocate a buffer with MAlloc , write a magic header, tell the host the address over serial (or let the host scan for the magic) memory speed Best candidate. TempleOS kernel memory is identity mapped (reported [U]), so a pointer is a physical address; the host mmaps the same file. No driver, no PCI. Unknowns [U]: TCG store visibility to the host process (use sequence numbers and a release store order; x86 TSO on an ARM host under TCG), RAM-file write-back to the SSD on macOS (mitigate with a RAM disk hdiutil attach -nomount ram://... or memory-backend-shm , which also exists [V]), and that the guest GC of the heap does not move the buffer (HolyC does not move memory). nvdimm device backed by memory-backend-file,share=on Device exists [V] Parse ACPI NFIT or probe the physical range; region sits above RAM so the guest must map it (TempleOS identity maps above 4 GB: unverified, docs/kosmos-app-port-research.md:152 ) memory speed Fallback if RAM-as-file misbehaves; more unknowns. Serial streaming (16550 COM1 or pci-serial , FIFO on, no acks) Yes [V] Existing Rx drain, InU8(0x3F8) maybe 100 to 500 KB/s drain [U], 40 to 130 KB/s with a 4 ms/frame budget [U] ( docs/kosmos-app-port-research.md:39 ) Keep for control, events, clipboard text, thumbnails. Measure with the spike in section 8. Monitor socket ( pmemsave , screendump , xp ) Yes [V] (used by scripts/vmkeys.py ) None Host reads guest memory slowly; HMP has no memory write that I know of [U] Debug and screenshots only. human-monitor-command pmemsave could pull the guest's output, not push input [U]. gdbstub M packets ( -gdb tcp::1234 ) Yes (option) [U] None tens of MB/s at best, stops the CPU [U] Fallback only. Second IDE disk ( piix3-ide , ide-hd exist [V]) with ATA PIO or bus-master DMA Yes [V] Raw ATA sector read/write from HolyC: PIO is rep insw (cheap under TCG [U]); bus-master DMA gives memory-speed copies straight into guest RAM [U]. The README notes mounting a second disc failed once ( README.md:115 , ISO9660 ISOInit ) but that is a file system issue, raw sectors avoid it Host writes a raw file; QEMU re-reads it on each guest request when cache is none / directsync [U] Second-best transport. A real block device with bounded latency; no shared-mapping questions. Guest to host writes show up in the same file. virtio-vsock No device in this QEMU [V] ( vsock absent from -device help ; the vhost backend is Linux only [U]) virtio + vsock stack n/a Not available. virtio-serial / virtio-9p / virtio-blk / virtio-net ( virtio-*-pci present [V]) Yes [V] A legacy-virtio PCI driver in HolyC: scan PCI ( PCIClassFind , PCIReadU32 already used at desk3/05-run.HC:58-66 ), set feature bits via port I/O, allocate descriptor rings in identity-mapped RAM, kick through a port write, poll the used ring. Estimate 300 to 600 lines of HolyC and 3 to 5 days for one queue, polled, legacy mode [U]; modern/transitional devices need MMIO BAR parsing too virtio-serial/9p are limited by host QEMU copy, roughly 100s of MB/s [U] A reasonable Phase 3 upgrade: virtio-blk or virtio-serial gives a clean DMA channel with interrupts-free polling. Frame budget in our guest (derived from README.md:7 , :23-24 and arithmetic) Surface-in-shared-RAM to back buffer to card = two copies. Our measured raw copy is about 5.2 MB per 7 ms (about 0.75 GB/s). A 2.8 MB window costs about 4 ms per copy, so about 8 ms if both copies are needed; the back buffer copy can be skipped by a fast path that blits straight to the card when nothing overlaps the dirty rectangle. Full-window redraws: 1000x700 at 1x about 8 ms, so 30 fps is plausible (the frame cap ks_fcap defaults to 60, desk3/01-core.HC:58 ). At 2x the same window is 11.2 MB, about 15 ms per copy and about 30 ms for both, so 20 to 30 fps with the fast path, 15 to 20 without. Typical UI use updates 5 to 20% of a window, so 30+ fps is realistic for typing, scrolling a small region and hover effects. Video-like content (a scrolling web page) is the stress case. Never upscale in the guest: nearest 2x upsample of 700k source pixels in HolyC at about 15 ns per op is 30 ms or more [derived from README.md rates] . The host renders at the final physical size. Overlap cost: if another window or the dock overlaps a dirty rectangle, Draw must repaint those layers clipped to that rectangle; rounded corners and shadows use RRTexN style code. Expect 2 to 4x slower in that case. 4. Q5: security and permissions design Principles: the guest is a display and input terminal with no network and no secrets; the host daemon is the only holder of credentials and the only place that can reach outward. Credentials stay on the host. Each app runs with its own profile directory on the host (or in its container volume). Login happens inside the remote window by the user. The guest never receives cookies, tokens, keychain items, or app files; it receives pixels and sends events. Sandboxing. macOS route: run each app under a dedicated profile (separate --user-data-dir for Electron, separate app-specific data dir) and, where practical, sandbox-exec with a deny-default profile (deprecated but present [U] ) or a separate low-privilege macOS user account (but windows from another login session cannot be captured [U] ). Linux route: one container per app, read-only root, a single writable volume, no host mounts except the share folder, dropped capabilities, CPU and memory limits, no network unless the manifest asks for it (allow-list by hostname through a proxy for apps that need only one service). Per-app permission manifest. Fields: network (none, allow-list), files (none, share folder only), clipboard (none, ask, allow-paste-only), notifications (off, on), camera/mic (never in v1), automation (can agents drive it: default no). The launcher shows the manifest on first run and stores the approval on the host. Outward-facing actions need a prompt in the desktop UI. Anything that sends a message, mail, post, purchase or file upload, or that is initiated by software rather than the human at the keyboard (an agent script, a clipboard paste, a scripted click) shows an approval sheet with the exact action and the target app. Human keystrokes and clicks in the focused remote window are the user acting directly and need no extra prompt. The agent API of the daemon ( click , type , drag ) must be a separate, opt-in, logged channel; the desktop shows an "agent is driving" banner. This matches the rule at the end of docs/core-apps-plan.md:122 . Clipboard. Guest to host: only on an explicit copy gesture in the desktop with the remote window focused. Host to guest: only when the user presses a "Paste from Mac" action; the daemon shows the first 80 characters in a toast first. Clipboard contents are never logged and are cleared from the daemon after 30 seconds. Never auto-sync (password managers copy secrets). File share. One folder per app ( ~/KosmosShare/<app>/ ); guest Files app can list and drop files there through the daemon; no path outside the share is ever accepted; size and type caps; the remote app sees it through its normal open dialog. Notifications. Forward only the title and first 120 characters of apps enabled in their manifest; never forward OTP-looking text when a manifest flag says so. macOS permissions. The daemon needs Screen Recording and Accessibility; ask once, document in README, and show a banner if the OS revokes it [U] . Use the least capable path: CDP needs neither. Audit log of every cross-boundary event (clipboard, file, agent action, launch, kill) on the host, viewable from a desktop app. ToS and licences. Respect each vendor's terms before enabling agent driving; GPL components (Xpra, Sunshine, TigerVNC) stay out of any shipped binary unless the licence is accepted. 7. Q7: recommended route, phases, spike, risks Phases Phase 0 (spike, 4 days): prove shared RAM plus one live window. Details below. Phase 1: guest contract and framework. Items 2, 7, 8, 9, 14 (minimal), 17 (basic resize), 19. Deliver: two remote windows (host test patterns), keyboard and mouse round trip, Monitor shows fps. Uses a fake provider that renders a test page so the guest work does not wait on capture work. Phase 2: macOS native provider. Items 3, 4, 10, 16; run a Tauri hello-world, Obsidian, VS Code natively; child popups; clipboard and file share (11, 12). Phase 3: safety and breadth. Items 15, 18, 13; the Chromium/CDP provider for Electron and web apps (5); then the Linux container provider with Xpra (6) for apps without macOS-native safety, isolation, or arm64 packaging. Phase 4 (optional): virtio channel driver in HolyC to replace polling; audio routing; second-monitor and virtual display experiments. Smallest spike (time box 4 working days) Goal: a live, interactive window of a real Tauri or Electron app inside a desktop window, over shared RAM, at usable speed. S0 (1 day): boot QEMU with the shared RAM file (flags in item 1). A host Python script mmaps the file. Guest HolyC ShmFind allocates a 64 KB buffer, writes the magic and its address; host finds it (scan or address from serial). Gate: host reads guest-written 4 KB blocks with sequence numbers 1,000,000 times with zero mismatches, and the guest reads host-written blocks the same way; sustained throughput at least 20 MB/s each way (the gate already set in docs/core-apps-plan.md:116 ); round trip under 5 ms. Fail (no visibility, corruption, or SSD write storms that a RAM disk does not cure) means switch to the second-IDE-disk transport (Section 3) for one more day or stop and use the serial thumbnail plus host-overlay stop-gap. S1 (1 day): host writes an 800x600 BGRA surface with a moving test pattern and dirty rectangles; guest AppRemote window blits it. Gate: at least 20 fps full-window at 1x with a Monitor-reported frame cost under 40 ms, and at least 12 fps at 2x. S2 (2 days): Swift CLI captures one window of a Tauri hello-world and Obsidian (or VS Code) with ScreenCaptureKit into the surface; guest click, wheel and key events return via the event ring (or serial) and are injected with CGEvent. Gate: typing and button clicks work; median input-to-pixel latency at most 150 ms at 800x600 1x; at least 15 fps while scrolling; no more than 5% frames with visible tearing. Overall pass: S0, S1 and S2 gates all met inside four days. Anything else means reporting the failure mode before building more. Main risks (ranked) Shared main RAM on macOS under TCG is unproven (visibility and ordering of stores between the TCG thread and a host process; write-back of a file-backed 1 GB mapping; TempleOS identity mapping assumption). Mitigation: S0 first; RAM disk or memory-backend-shm ; fallback second IDE disk transport. Guest-side cost and input fidelity. Retina surfaces are 11 MB per window; overlaps force slow repaints; there is no key-up or non-ASCII input path known to work, one pointer path with a hacked relative-delta scheme, and shortcuts like Esc already reserved ( desk3/04-main.HC:319 ). Mitigation: fast-path blit, host-side scaling, 1x default for remote windows, a text-injection field, a keyboard-release chord. Host capture permissions, focus and policy. Screen Recording and Accessibility permission, windows that must be on-screen to be captured, popups as separate windows, apps that block automation or forbid it in terms of service, secrets visible in pixels. Mitigation: CDP or container providers for sensitive or noisy apps, per-app manifests, explicit approval for outward actions. Lesser: Electron fuses blocking CDP; auto-update; memory ( -m 1024M too small); sync of frame pacing between host capture rate and guest loop sleeps. What not to attempt Compiling or porting Chromium, Node, Electron, WebKit or a Rust/Tauri runtime into TempleOS. HolyC only, ring 0, no libc, no threads, no network stack, no GPU, 15 ns per simple operation; Chromium is tens of millions of lines of C++ that need all of those. There is no path that ends in a usable browser. The guest should stay a display and input terminal. Writing a NIC driver plus TCP/IP and TLS in HolyC to let the guest talk to services directly: large, and it moves secrets into the guest. Rendering web pages by reimplementing a layout engine from DOM or accessibility data (Section 2e). Streaming pixels over the serial port (Section 3). Relying on ivshmem (not in this QEMU build) or on a Linux-only QEMU build. Embedding GPL code (Xpra, Sunshine) in a product we would distribute without a licence decision. Controlling 1Password or other credential managers through the remote window. 9.
